items.content_html:
At a glance

  • Formal methods for everyday software. PDD Kit helps you turn your intent into a formal spec, then proves the code your agent writes for every input and uses tests where a proof can’t reach. It takes formal methods beyond niche, specialist work to engineers without a formal methods background and to everyday applications, like the full-stack web app shown here.
  • Exhaustive line-by-line human review can become difficult to scale as AI agents generate increasingly large amounts of code. The plan is supposed to be the contract between you and a coding agent, but nothing actually forces the agent to follow it. The tests it writes usually check what it built, rather than what you asked for.
  • PDD Kit makes the agent keep the plan. It works with you to turn your intent into a formal specification in Verus (opens in new tab), proves the agent’s code meets that spec for every input, and falls back to tests where a proof can’t reach.
  • We tried it on a full-stack web app. Inside GitHub Next’s Chopin (opens in new tab), we used PDD Kit to formally verify the login logic of Pet Store, a Rust (opens in new tab) storefront. Verus hardened the code and uncovered existing bugs, proving the absence of login bugs with respect to the specification. The developer reviewed the intent and never read the generated code line-by-line.

The plan is the contract the agent should follow, but nothing constrains the agent to follow it.

Coding agents now ship whole features in one sitting often spanning tens of thousands or hundreds of thousands of lines of code. As a result, reading every line of the pull request doesn’t scale to this new way of work. Now, most teams invest in the plan and relevant testing instead: describe to an agent what they want, go back and forth until the plan and proposed tests look right, and hand them off to the agent for implementation.

This plan or natural language spec is meant to be the contract that an agent holds. However, in practice, the agent can drift from it. It implements something slightly different, then writes tests that pass for its implementation rather than the code you intended it to write. Continuous integration (CI) grows due to a profusion of low quality and high quantity of tests, coverage looks healthy, and the gap between what you asked for and what shipped stays hidden until a bug report or a nasty edge case shows up.

So, how do you reliably scale review as agents generate increasingly large amounts of code? Agent code fails in two ways a careful reviewer would usually catch: it leaves out something obviously necessary, or it does something obviously wrong. Tests alone don’t close that gap, because they only exercise a tiny slice of what a program can do. Closing it needs a different kind of machinery, which is where proofs come in.

Review asks “does this look right?” A proof answers “is this right?” A mathematical proof shows that code meets its specification for every input, including the ones your test suite can miss. That provides stronger assurance for specified properties than testing alone, especially when line-by-line review isn’t practical.

Proofs used to be too expensive for everyday software. You needed specialists, unfamiliar languages, proofs many times larger than the code, and proofs took years to develop, but two things have changed since. First, recent advances in coding agents have made it increasingly practical for them to help generate formal proofs from well-defined specs. Secondly, agents can now better help you write formal specs. We call this new software development paradigm Proof-Driven Development (PDD). PDD Kit is our toolkit for it.

How PDD Kit works

PDD Kit is to formal methods roughly what Spec Kit (opens in new tab) is to Spec-Driven Development. It runs as a partner inside Chopin (opens in new tab), GitHub Next’s real-time, multiplayer planning environment, where a team and agents can plan in one shared document.

The workflow has two halves (Figure 1). First, team members review intent in plain language. PDD Kit asks the questions a careful reviewer would ask, explains the relevant code as it goes, and records the answers in an intent artifact, a document that bridges the user’s intent with the formal specification or tests. The parts of the user’s intent that can be formalized are converted into formal specifications and the rest, which must be taken on trust, are converted to informal specifications for tests. PDD Kit automatically generates proofs that the code satisfies the derived formal specs and high-quality tests for the informal specs. You don’t need a formal methods background for any of it.

Figure 1. Proof-Driven Development with PDD Kit. Team members settle intent. Verus and the test suite hold the code to it.

Consequently, every result in PDD Kit says which kind of verification it rests on:

  • Formal verification is a mathematical proof that code satisfies its specification for every possible input, checked by a tool called a verifier. For PDD Kit today, that verifier is Verus (opens in new tab), a proof language for Rust co-developed by Microsoft Research, Carnegie Mellon University, VMware Research, ETH Zurich, MPI-SWS, UNSW Sydney, the University of Texas at Austin, the University of Michigan, the University of British Columbia, the University of Wisconsin–Madison and the Weizmann Institute of Science.
  • Empirical verification checks code by running it and observing what it does. It covers what a proof can’t reach, such as a third-party cryptography library or a user interface. It uses unit and end-to-end tests, terminal automation, browser agents, and computer-use agents for anything a browser can’t drive. A passing test only shows the code worked on the inputs it tried, so PDD Kit labels it as evidence rather than proof.

The line between the two is the Trusted Computing Base (TCB): the code that the proof assumes behaves as described. PDD Kit makes that line explicit and asks you to sign off on each piece.

The capstone: a full-stack web app

To show PDD Kit integrating with existing codebases, we built Pet Store, a full-stack web app written entirely in Rust (opens in new tab). The backend uses Axum (opens in new tab) and SQLite (opens in new tab) and handles inventory, promotions, orders and checkout. The storefront is a Leptos (opens in new tab) app compiled to WebAssembly (opens in new tab). Together they come to about 5,000 lines of Rust.

For brevity in this blog, we focus on formally verifying the login logic of the app, but the same process can be used to verify functional correctness of the entire app. PDD Kit recommends starting with the most sensitive parts of your application and incrementally verifying your application. A login bug can hand an attacker a customer’s account or an admin’s controls, so that’s where proof effort pays off first. The developer’s whole request in Chopin was two sentences:

Verify the login logic in backend/src/handlers/auth.rs. Here are my requirements:

  • You only get a token with the right password.
  • Only admin accounts get admin tokens.

We kept the request rough on purpose. Capturing the intent of the user and turning the user request into something a proof can check is PDD Kit’s job.

Step 1: Questions before code

PDD Kit’s planning workflow, pdd-plan, reads the code and comes back, before writing anything, with questions in a Decisions tab. When a question depends on how the code works, the card explains that part first: the goal, how the pieces fit, and the exact function involved, so you can answer without opening the source.

Figure 2. The first decision card. “Only with the right password” on its own is also met by a login that refuses everyone. Proving both ways rules that out.

The question looks pedantic, but it matters. “You only get a token with the right password” rules out the bad case, a wrong password getting a token, and a login that refuses everyone keeps that promise perfectly. “The right password always works” is the half that rules it out. Formally, the first is an implication (token ⇒ right password) and the second is its converse. Together they make an “if and only if.” An agent left alone would pick one without telling you, but here the developer picked both ways.

Step 2: A human readable intent map

As the conversation goes on, PDD Kit keeps a rough work section at the top of the plan current, so a user can keep track of important concepts without having to scroll back through a long chat to find what was agreed. It includes a flowchart of the login being specified, a spec landscape of what will be proved and what will be trusted, and, when a picture helps, a mental model. For login, PDD Kit drew a ticket desk (Figure 3).

Figure 3. PDD Kit’s mental model for login. The field you send picks the window, the window picks the table and with it the role, and nothing prints until the password matches.

Below it, the intent map ties each requirement back to the developer’s own words and records how it was settled (Figure 4). Each entry links to the section of the formal spec that models it and to the tests that cover it, and the spec section shows snippets of the Verus contract, annotated so the developer can see how the formal spec models their intent.

Figure 4. An intent map entry after the decision: a login gets a token only with the right password for that account, and always with it. The flowchart shows every way the password check can end.

The decision card in Figure 2 is the kind of ambiguity an agent would otherwise settle silently. Figure 5 shows how small the difference looks on paper: the two readings disagree in a single cell, a right password that gets no token.

Figure 5. Two readings of the same sentence. They differ in one cell, and that cell changes what the proof has to establish.

Step 3: Proving the login function

Before anything gets built, PDD Kit asks the team to sign off on the plan as a whole. Its first draft proved the decision at the center of login, picking the table and gating on the password, and kept the handler around it trusted and tested. That’s a sensible default, and it’s what PDD Kit recommended, but the developer wanted more. The handler is where the lookups get awaited and the token gets signed, and that glue is exactly where a refactor can quietly swap two lines. So at intent review the developer chose to give the login handler its own async spec, so the proof covers that glue too instead of trusting it (Figure 6).

Figure 6. Proving more of login means trusting more small wrappers. The card says so before the developer chooses.

That choice moved almost everything into the proof and left the login handler with nothing to do but unpack the request. A new async function, login_flow, carries the contract from the request’s fields all the way to the token or the HTTP error. PDD Kit then brought the revised plan back for a fresh sign-off, because matching your intent isn’t proof, and it doesn’t approve new trust or a wider scope.

Step 4: Where proof stops

There are plenty of things you can’t prove about a program, and login runs into most of them:

  • Code the verifier can’t see. bcrypt’s hashing, sqlx’s queries and jsonwebtoken’s signing live in other crates, outside the proof.
  • Facts about the outside world. What SQLite holds right now and what time the clock says are inputs to the program, not something its code can establish.
  • Whether, and how fast, something finishes. The spec says what you get if login answers. A hung query, or a slow one, breaks nothing in it.
  • Anything a person has to judge, like whether an error message helps or a screen makes sense.
  • Whatever nobody wrote down. A proof covers its spec and says nothing about requirements outside it.

That’s where empirical verification comes in. PDD Kit spells out the trusted boundary, the part of the TCB this proof leans on. It wraps each trusted piece in a small function with an assumed contract, using Verus’s #[verifier::external_body] or external_fn_specification, asks the developer to accept each one on its own, and writes a test for every assumed clause into the plan. For login, the developer signed off on six pieces:

  • The two lookups, Customer::find_by_email and Admin::find_by_username. Each awaited, successful lookup returns exactly the row its own table holds for that email or username, or none.
  • check_password, a thin wrapper around bcrypt::verify. It errors only on a stored hash bcrypt can’t read, and Ok(true) means exactly the right password.
  • generate_token, which signs exactly the claims it is given under the configured secret and reports a signing failure as a 500.
  • expiry_from_now, which reads the clock and writes an expiry exactly 24 hours later.
  • database_error, which turns a failed lookup into today’s 500 with sqlx’s message.
  • The login handler shell, which unpacks the request and passes its fields to login_flow unchanged.

In the spec, a lookup keeps its code where it is and gets a contract from the outside with external_fn_specification:

/// Looks up a customer by exact email. /// Trusted, not proved: the SQL query runs in sqlx, which Verus cannot check. /// Every customer promise of login_flow rests on it. #[verifier::external_fn_specification] pub async fn ex_customer_find_by_email(pool: &sqlx::SqlitePool, email: &str)     -> (r: Result, sqlx::Error>)     ensures         // When the query succeeds, it returns the customers row on         // file for exactly this email, or None when there is none.         r matches Ok(found) ==> found == customer_on_file(email@), {     Customer::find_by_email(pool, email).await } 

The clock is a small wrapper marked #[verifier::external_body]. Verus uses its ensures clause and never reads the body:

/// Reads the clock and computes a token's expiry 24 hours ahead. /// Trusted, not proved: chrono's clock is outside the proof. /// It panics if the time is out of range, as today's login does; /// that panic is not promised against. #[verifier::external_body] pub fn expiry_from_now() -> (r: Expiry)     ensures         // The expiry is exactly 24 hours (86,400 seconds) after the clock reading.         r.exp as int == r.now as int + 86_400, {    ... } 

Figure 7 puts the three layers together: what Verus proves, what people accept and tests check, and what nobody is promising.

Figure 7. Where the login proof stops. Verus proves the core for every input. People accept the trusted ring and tests check it. The plan lists what nobody is promising.

Figure 8 maps what gets proved and what gets trusted. Each trust decision is its own card. It shows the clauses Verus will take on faith, what the developer is accepting, and which promise falls apart if the assumption is wrong (Figure 9). Every assumed clause then gets an empirical check in the plan’s Empirical verification section, written as Given/When/Then scenarios before any test exists (Figure 10). An entry says planned until it has run, and then it records the command’s result and the commit it ran against.

Figure 8. What gets proved and what gets trusted in login. Green functions are proved by Verus for every input. Amber pieces are trusted, accepted by the developer, and checked by the planned tests in the plan’s §4.1.

Figure 9. A trust card for check_password. Verus takes these two clauses on faith, so a person accepts them and two tests check them.

Figure 10. A planned test for the trusted check_password, written before the test exists. The plan labels a passing test as evidence rather than proof.

The plan is just as explicit about what nobody is promising: that the login future ever completes, that an out-of-range clock won’t panic, anything about the timing or rate of attempts, and how other endpoints read the role.

Step 5: Reading the spec

The intent artifact is what the team reviews. It’s the plain-language version of the formal spec PDD Kit writes as Verus contracts. You might be wondering whether someone now has to read the proof instead of the code. Nobody does, because the coding agent writes the proof and Verus checks every step of it. If Verus accepts the proof, it holds whether or not anyone reads it. The spec is what the proof is held to, so that’s what people review, and this one is short enough to learn to read in a few minutes. Each function gets an ensures block: statements about its result, r, that must hold for every possible input. Verus checks them when you build, and if any clause could fail for even one input, the build fails and Verus points at that clause. Each clause reads as an if-then, and Figure 11 takes apart the clause for the developer’s first requirement.

Figure 11. The ensures clause on login_flow for “You only get a token with the right password.” The same account a appears on every line, which ties the password check to the token.

Notice that the same a appears on every line, which ties the password check to the token. For example, imagine a bug where login checks the password against one account but signs the token for another. Bob logs in with his own, correct password and gets back a token for Alice’s account. Each step looks fine on its own, but this clause catches it, because the password check and the token have to name the same account. That’s the kind of wiring bug a test suite rarely thinks to look for. The spec also has to talk about SQLite, bcrypt and JWTs without running any of them. It does that with uninterpreted functions, names with no body: customer_on_file(email) and admin_on_file(username) for the rows the database holds, bcrypt_verdict(password, hash) for what bcrypt would say, and token_claims(token, secret) for what a token carries. Verus knows nothing about them except what the trusted contracts from Step 4 promise. The proof says “whatever the database holds, login does the right thing with it,” and a trusted contract says “the lookup returns what the database holds.”

/// The customers row the database holds for /// exactly this email, if any, when login looks. /// Left abstract: only Customer::find_by_email's /// trusted contract says what it is. pub uninterp spec fn customer_on_file(email: Seq) -> Option; ... /// What bcrypt says about password against a /// stored hash: Some(true) when it is the password /// the hash was made from, Some(false) when it is /// not, None when bcrypt cannot read the hash. /// Left abstract: its meaning is bcrypt's, taken on trust through check_password. pub uninterp spec fn bcrypt_verdict(password: Seq, hash: Seq)     -> Option;  /// The password is the right one for the stored hash, by bcrypt's verdict. pub open spec fn password_matches(password: Seq, hash: Seq) -> bool {     bcrypt_verdict(password, hash) == Some(true) } 

On top of those, named_account(email, username) says which account a login names: the customers row for the email when one is sent, otherwise the admins row for the username, otherwise none. It’s written like Rust, but it’s a mathematical definition that never runs and only appears in contracts. Code like this is called ghost code, since the verifier checks it but the compiler erases it from the program. With it, the developer’s two-sentence request ends up as eight ensures clauses on login_flow (Figure 12).

/// The account a login names: the customers row for /// the email when one is sent (role "customer"), /// otherwise the admins row for the username (role "admin"), otherwise none. pub open spec fn named_account(email: Option, username: Option)     -> Option {     match email {         Some(e) => match customer_on_file(e@) {             Some(c) => Some(NamedAccount {                 id: c.id@, password_hash: c.password_hash@, role: customer_role() }),             None => None,         },         None => match username {             Some(u) => match admin_on_file(u@) {                 Some(a) => Some(NamedAccount {                     id: a.id@, password_hash: a.password_hash@, role: admin_role() }),                 None => None,             },             None => None,         },     } } 

Figure 12. The two-sentence request and the Both ways decision ended up as eight ensures clauses on login_flow. Four of them keep today’s refusals, so the storefront and the existing API tests keep working.

Here’s the whole contract, with its doc comment trimmed. Each clause has the plain-English comment above it that the intent artifact shows the team:

/// The whole login, awaited end to end: from the /// request's fields to the token or the HTTP error. ///... pub async fn login_flow(pool: &sqlx::SqlitePool, config: &Config,     email: Option, username: Option, password: &str)     -> (r: Result)     ensures         // Neither an email nor a username: 400 with today's message.         email is None && username is None             ==> (r matches Err(AppError::BadRequest(m))                 && m@ == missing_identity_text()),         // A token only for the account the login names, with its right         // password; it carries that account's id and its table's role.         r matches Ok(t) ==> (named_account(email, username) matches Some(a)             && password_matches(password@, a.password_hash)             && token_claims(t@, config.jwt_secret@) matches Some(c)             && c.sub@ == a.id && c.role@ == a.role),         // The right password for the named account always gets a         // token, unless a lookup or signing failure gives 500.         (named_account(email, username) matches Some(a)             && password_matches(password@, a.password_hash))             ==> (r is Ok || r matches Err(AppError::Internal(_))),         // A login naming an account nobody holds gets         // 401, unless the lookup fails with 500.         ((email is Some || username is Some) && named_account(email, username) is None)             ==> (r matches Err(AppError::Unauthorized)                 || r matches Err(AppError::Internal(_))),         // A wrong password for an account whose hash bcrypt         // can read gets 401, unless the lookup fails with 500.         (named_account(email, username) matches Some(a)             && bcrypt_verdict(password@, a.password_hash) == Some(false))             ==> (r matches Err(AppError::Unauthorized)                 || r matches Err(AppError::Internal(_))),         // An account whose stored hash bcrypt cannot read gets 500 and no token.         (named_account(email, username) matches Some(a)             && bcrypt_verdict(password@, a.password_hash) is None)             ==> r matches Err(AppError::Internal(_)),         // The admin role only for an admins row         // found by username, with no email sent.         (r matches Ok(t) && token_claims(t@, config.jwt_secret@) matches Some(c)             && c.role@ == admin_role())             ==> (email is None && username matches Some(u)                 && admin_on_file(u@) is Some),         // An email login's token always carries the customer role.         (r matches Ok(t) && email is Some)             ==> (token_claims(t@, config.jwt_secret@) matches Some(c)                 && c.role@ == customer_role()), {     unimplemented!() } 

The trusted boundary shows up in the code too. check_password is one of the functions whose body Verus doesn’t check. Its contract ties it to bcrypt_verdict, an uninterpreted model of bcrypt with no axioms:

/// Asks bcrypt whether password matches the stored hash. /// Trusted, not proved: Verus cannot check bcrypt's hashing, /// so this wrapper's contract is assumed. /// Every password promise of login_flow rests on it. #[verifier::external_body] pub fn check_password(password: &str, hash: &str) -> (r: Result)     ensures         // bcrypt answers (Ok) exactly when it can read the stored hash.         r is Ok <==> bcrypt_verdict(password@, hash@) is Some,         // Its answer is its verdict: true for the         // right password, false for any other.         r matches Ok(b) ==> bcrypt_verdict(password@, hash@) == Some(b), {     bcrypt::verify(password, hash).map_err(|e| e.to_string()) } 

The doc comment above it says what rests on it: every password promise of login_flow. Every login ends in one of a handful of places, and only one of them has a token (Figure 13). The proof covers all of them at once.

Figure 13. Every way a login can end, from the plan.

login_flow is async: it awaits a database query. Verus can put contracts on async functions, with one rule worth knowing (Figure 14). requires is checked when the call creates the future. ensures describes the value you get when you await it. Nothing promises the future finishes, so a hung query breaks no clause.

The doc comment on login_flow says so in as many words:

///... No promise the future completes. pub async fn login_flow(...) -> (r: Result) 

Figure 14. When a contract is checked, for a sync fn and an async fn.

login_flow stays short because it’s built from smaller proved pieces. lookup_target picks the table. login_core awaits the lookup and calls decide_login, the password gate. issue_token signs the token, or maps a refusal to today’s HTTP error. Each piece has its own contract, and Verus proves login_flow using only those contracts, without re-reading their bodies. Change the body of decide_login and only decide_login gets proved again.

Here’s the smallest piece, whole, and the start and end of the password gate:

pub fn lookup_target(email: Option, username: Option)     -> (r: Result)     ensures         // An email, when sent, wins: customers are searched for exactly that email.         email matches Some(e)             ==> r == Ok::(LookupTarget::CustomerByEmail(e)),         // With no email, a username sends the search         // to admins for exactly that username.         email is None && username matches Some(u)             ==> r == Ok::(LookupTarget::AdminByUsername(u)),         // With neither, the login is refused for missing an identity.         email is None && username is None             ==> r == Err::(LoginError::MissingIdentity), 

pub fn decide_login(target: &LookupTarget, found: Option, password: &str)     -> (r: Result)     ensures         // No row found: refused as Unauthorized,         // the same answer as a wrong password.         found is None             ==> r == Err::(LoginError::Unauthorized),         // Claims come back only for a found row         // whose stored hash matches the password.         r is Ok ==> found is Some             && password_matches(password@, found->Some_0.password_hash@),         // The right password for a found row always gets claims.         found matches Some(a) && password_matches(password@, a.password_hash@)             ==> r is Ok,        ...         // An admins-table search gives the role text "admin".         r matches Ok(c) && target is AdminByUsername ==> c.role@ == admin_role(),         // A customers-table search gives the role text "customer".         r matches Ok(c) && target is CustomerByEmail ==> c.role@ == customer_role(), 

An overview of login.rs

Figure 15 maps the whole spec file, verified/src/login.rs. It reads top to bottom in four layers: headers, imports and types Verus needs to know about, an abstract view of the outside world, the trusted contracts that connect that view to real code, and the five contracts the proof has to meet.

Figure 15. The parts of login.rs, in file order. Gray is header and types, purple is math that only appears in contracts, amber is trusted, and green is proven.

Here are two of the less obvious parts, abridged. external_type_specification introduces a type Verus didn’t define. The pool stays opaque, while a customers row keeps its fields visible:

/// The connection pool, opaque to the proof: only /// the lookups' contracts say what it returns. #[verifier::external_type_specification] #[verifier::external_body] #[verifier::reject_recursive_types(DB)] pub struct ExPool(sqlx::Pool); ... /// A customers row, with its fields visible to the proof. #[verifier::external_type_specification] pub struct ExCustomer(Customer); 

And LoginError keeps the decision separate from the HTTP response, which is what lets issue_token pin each refusal to today’s status code:

/// Why a login gets no token. pub enum LoginError {     /// Neither an email nor a username was sent: 400 Bad Request.     MissingIdentity,     /// No such account, or the password does not match: 401 Unauthorized.     Unauthorized,     /// bcrypt could not read the stored hash, with its message: 500 Internal.     UnreadableHash(String),     /// The lookup query failed: 500 Internal, with sqlx's message.     Database(sqlx::Error), } 

Before the plan comes back to you, two reviewer agents poke holes in the derived formal spec from the intent artifact to ensure a high-quality translation, so that the spec matches what you asked for and doesn’t promise more than a proof could show. The spec refinement runs in the background and takes live user feedback, iterating until reviewers agree that the spec is sound.

Step 6: Prove, check, close the gaps

Signing off on the spec is where the developer’s review ends. Everything after it, the implementation and the proof, is checked by machines, which is why this post spends its time on the spec and not the proof. Once the developer signs off, a Build plan stage (Figure 16) hands the approved plan to pdd-prove, which turns it into a small task graph (Figure 16). For login, that’s seven tasks: get login.rs building under Verus inside the backend crate, prove the decision, the token and the whole flow, then write the tests for the trusted wrappers and the end-to-end login.

Figure 16. Build plan turns the approved spec into seven tasks on a development machine. The first gets login.rs building under Verus without changing what any contract promises, and stops to ask rather than weaken a contract.

Each task runs the same loop:

  • A coding agent writes the implementation and the proof, and Verus checks them against the derived formal spec.
  • Anything in the trusted boundary gets the tests the plan called for.
  • An LLM verifier reads the plan, the specification and the results side by side, and looks for gaps: requirements with no proof and no passing check. Gaps go back to the coding agent until none remain. If the specification itself has a gap, such as two requirements that contradict each other, it comes back to the developer as a decision.

A proof is only as good as its spec, so pdd-prove checks the spec too. When a model writes its own spec, or is tuned to produce proofs, it tends to land on weak invariants: clauses that verify but rule out almost nothing. They prove something, just rarely the thing you care about. We call that “vibe verification.” That’s why it’s so important to make sure your intent is aligned with the agent and what PDD Kit is great for.

The loop is strict about not moving the goalposts. If an async construct can’t be expressed in the pinned Verus, the task stops and asks the team instead of switching to a non-async helper or weakening a contract.

How does PDD Kit remove classes of bugs? The mutation check is how PDD Kit guards against vibe verification. pdd-prove plants one bug per ensures clause in a scratch copy of the code, like refusing everyone or checking the username before the email, and Verus has to reject each mutant on the clause it targets. A mutant that gets through means that clause constrains nothing, and it comes back as a gap.

Step 7: Review intent alongside verified code

When the tasks pass, pdd-prove opens pull requests. They add a verified/ crate with login_flow, its pieces, their proofs, and the trusted wrappers with their tests, and route the real login handler through login_flow, keeping the existing HTTP status codes. Your verified logic integrates with and hardens your production login path, not a copy of it.

The developer was able to merge without relying on exhaustive line-by-line review of the generated code. The review had already happened on the intent artifact this whole time, where the team has the final say. We shifted more of the review focus from code review to intent review. The pull request works as a receipt, and its description marks every login requirement as either formally verified or empirically checked.

Merging is where the proof joins the team’s normal workflow. PDD Kit’s pdd-ship workflow adds the Verus check to CI next to the empirical tests, so every later change to login, by a person or an agent, has to keep proving against the same spec, and a broken proof fails the build like a failing test. And because a proof covers every input, PDD Kit prunes tests that only re-check what’s already proved, such as example-based tests of the password gate, and keeps the ones that guard the trusted boundary, so CI gets stronger and leaner at the same time.

What the proof does and doesn’t say

“Fully verified” is easy to oversell, so here’s exactly what we’re claiming.

  • Proved. The bodies of login_flow, login_core, lookup_target, decide_login and issue_token meet their contracts for every input. Login picks the right table, compares the request’s password against the stored hash of the account it names, issues a token with that account’s id and the role its table gives, and refuses everything else with today’s 400, 401 or 500 and no token.
  • Trusted and tested. The two database lookups, check_password over bcrypt, the clock, token signing, the database error message and the handler’s request unpacking sit outside the proof, each behind an assumed contract the developer accepted. Tests against the real bcrypt, the real SQLite schema and the real router cover them.
  • Assumed. The Verus, Rust compiler and Z3 (opens in new tab) toolchain, and Verus’s standard library vstd (opens in new tab).

Why Rust

PDD Kit only verifies Rust today, since that’s the language Verus works on. If your codebase is already Rust, there’s nothing to migrate. Code in other languages can be ported to Rust and checked against the same spec, and non-Rust projects can call verified Rust through bindings.

There’s also a less obvious upside. Once reliance on exhaustive line-by-line review has been reduced, readability stops being the main reason to pick a language. You can pick one for speed and safety, and optimize as hard as you want, because any change that breaks the spec fails the proof.

What to Expect from PDD Kit

PDD Kit is a research prototype, and it only verifies Rust today since that’s the language Verus works on. Code in other languages can be ported to Rust and checked against the same spec, and non-Rust projects can call verified Rust through bindings. Proofs still take real effort, mostly in producing the proof itself, and a clear spec is what keeps that effort down, which is why so much of PDD Kit is about getting intent right first. We’d start where a bug costs the most, such as login, payments, or permissions, and verify the rest of a codebase one piece at a time.

Pet Store’s login is one piece of one app: a spec anyone can read, a Verus proof that the code matches it, and tests for everything the proof takes on trust. We want to be upfront about the weakest links. The guarantees are only as strong as the six trusted pieces, and two carry most of the weight: check_password for every password promise, and the two lookups for every promise about which account a token names. Tests support them, but nothing proves them. We expect that trusted boundary to shrink significantly over time, so a growing share of the code can be formally verified, and we want to find out how far this scales.

What we’re really changing is what people review. Instead of relying mainly on line-by-line review of agent-generated code, a team reviews what it meant, in plain language, and a proof holds the code to it. The plan was always supposed to be the contract, and now the agent actually has to keep it.

Acknowledgments

This work is a collaboration between the Microsoft Research Catalyst Lab, GitHub Next, and the Research in Software Engineering (RiSE) group. We would like to thank Maggie Appleton and Krzysztof Cieślak of GitHub Next for their collaboration on Chopin, and Nikhil Swamy, Lef Ioannidis, Janardhan Kulkarni, and Shuvendu Lahiri for their feedback and discussions on formal verification and intent formalization. We also thank the F*/Pulse and Verus teams for their support. Finally, we thank Idan Gazit of GitHub Next for supporting this collaboration.

FAQ

  • If AI writes the spec, who makes sure the spec is right, and doesn't a wrong spec just give me the wrong verified code? You do, and yes, it would. A proof shows the code meets the spec, not that the spec is what you meant. That’s why PDD Kit is built around existing research in intent formalization. The pdd-plan workflow reads your code, asks questions before writing anything, and turns your answers into a Verus spec plus a plain-language plan you approve, flagging ambiguity instead of guessing. Two reviewer agents check the spec, and the pdd-prove workflow plants one bug per clause to catch clauses that verify but rule out nothing. A wrong spec is still possible, which is why PDD Kit emphasizes making requirements explicit, identifying ambiguities, and keeping developers involved in reviewing and approving the spec before verification begins.
  • How is this different from Spec-Driven Development (SDD), Test-Driven Development (TDD), or just telling the agent to check its own work? The difference is what holds the code to the plan. Approach What checks the code Spec-Driven Development Nothing enforces the spec Test-Driven Development Tests on a sample of inputs, often written to match what was built Agent checks its own work The same model that wrote the code Proof-Driven Development Verus automatically verifies the proof that your code satisfies the spec your approved PDD keeps the planning loop from SDD and still uses tests where a proof can’t reach. A test checks some inputs, while a proof establishes that the code satisfies specified properties for all inputs covered by the formal model, under its stated assumptions.
  • What exactly is the proof? Where does it run? Is it deterministic or another language model (LM)? And how long does it take? The proof is Rust code annotated with Verus constructs, checked mechanically by Verus using the Z3 solver. It runs wherever your Rust builds: the pdd-prove workflow runs it while proving, and the pdd-ship workflow adds it to your build and CI so a broken proof fails the build. The check is deterministic, with no model involved. Models write the spec, code, and proof, but only a deterministic Verus run decides whether it passed. How long the check takes varies with the size of the code and how hard the proofs are: usually seconds for a small module, up to minutes for a larger codebase.
  • If verification replaces line-by-line code review, what do I actually review? PDD Kit shifts more of the review process toward validating what the code should do, while using formal verification to provide additional assurance that the implementation meets those requirements. Developers review the natural-language plan, the formal spec, and the trusted components that fall outside the scope of the proof. The resulting pull request documents what was formally verified, what was tested, and where additional review may be needed. On the Pet Store full stack web app, this approach reduced reliance on exhaustive line-by-line review of the generated code.
  • Is it Rust only? And why Verus instead of other verification tools or formal languages? We chose Verus because it allows us to verify Rust code directly, aligning with PDD Kit’s focus on integrating formal verification into existing Rust development workflows. Other proof languages (e.g., Lean, F*, Rocq) take different approaches to formal verification, each with its own tradeoffs. The techniques behind PDD Kit could help put them to work as well.

items.title: Beneath the Surface: What We Overlook When We Talk About Agent Evolution
items.content: arXiv:2611.07624v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Agent harness evolution enables recursive self-improvement (RSI) without updating model weights. We examine whether higher benchmark scores yield reliable, efficient, and transferable improvement. We evaluate four methods across harnesses, general and coding tasks. Repeated evaluations, controlled agent expansion, component interventions, and admission replays reveal recurring patterns. All sixteen evolved agents gain previously uncovered tasks while losing previously covered ones. In one general-task case, reliability rises by 5.2 points despite losing ten previously covered tasks. Most reliability gains also increase deployment cost. Specific changes usually outperform generic reminders, but their benefits can change when combined. The highest-scoring agent does not yield the largest mean improvement in any of our four pools, and stricter admission can discard useful alternatives. Transfer selectively preserves gains: coverage usually falls on the general-task target across both harness types and paradigms, but rises on the coding target with the outer-layer-only harness. These findings motivate preservation-aware evaluation, tested decision rules, and explicit applicability conditions. As a constructive follow-up, EvoAudit turns these diagnostics into revisions of select, analyze, mutate, and gate, achieving the best performance.
items.author: Xiaobo Wang, Zimu Wang, Siyu Ye, Jiaqi Li, Min Tang, Jun Bai, Yuling Shi, Ruobing Wang, Jingjing Zhang, Chaofan Wang, Kai Wu, Mengnan Qi, Kai Cai, Xiaodong Gu, Qi Liu, Zilong Zheng

It matters because it challenges the common assumption that rising agent benchmark scores indicate real, durable capability improvements.

items.title: The Last Mile to the Real World: Agent-Native Primitives as Reusable Building Blocks for Solving Real-World Tasks
items.content: arXiv:2611.07461v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: How can an agent handle a real-world task end to end? Frontier models with their own harnesses still fall short on real-world benchmarks: on Terminal-Bench 4.0, GPT-5.6 Sol with Codex resolves 37.3% of the tasks and Claude Opus 5 with Claude Code 51.8%. These tasks fail at the step from reaching a resource to applying it, which we call the last mile to the real world. Existing approaches put the resource within reach but leave the competence to apply it with the caller, so each harness rebuilds that competence. We introduce agent-native primitives, reusable units that equip a resource with a resident LLM that applies it in context and communicates with other primitives, and HEELO (Harness Engineering around Evolving Agent-Native Primitives for the Last Mile to Real-WOrld Tasks), a harness engineering framework that builds each task's harness from a library of such primitives. HEELO composes the primitives a task needs into a task-specific graph, verifies the result against evidence from the environment, revises the primitives a failure implicates, and admits new or improved primitives after validation. We instantiate HEELO with eight primitive families, each built for one kind of task, and evaluate them on more than twenty benchmarks. Dev-Primitives raise Terminal-Bench 4.0 resolution from 37.3% under Codex to 55.5% on the same backbone, Harness Primitives composed per task raise Terminal-Bench 2.0 Pass@1 from 60.0% for the seed harness to 72.2%, Tool Primitives raise ToolBench pass rate from 55.8% to 75.1%, and Navigation Primitives raise GAIA-Text-103 accuracy from 45.6% to 58.3%. On the 46 real-world tasks of our heelo.dev platform, Claude Opus 5.5 with Claude Code and GPT-6.1 Sol with Codex complete 9 each on their own and 39 and 35 when connected to HEELO through our MCP server, with 1.9$\times$ and 2.3$\times$ less time and 1.55$\times$ lower cost per completed task.
items.author: Haibo Jin, Peng Kuang, Xiaopeng Yuan, Lucheng Fu, Jerry Wang, Xucheng Yu, Yaoning Yu, Dehao Wu, Runguo Li, Colin Su, Jingxuan Sun, Xuyang Liu, Haojing Luo, Haohan Wang
items.summary: Identifies the gap between an agent reaching a resource and competently applying it, and proposes agent-native primitives: reusable units that bundle a resource with a resident LLM that applies it in context and communicates with other primitives. Their HEELO harness shows strong results on real-world benchmarks, where existing frontier systems like GPT-5.6 Sol with Codex (37.3%) and Claude Opus 5 with Claude Code (51.8%) fall short on Terminal-Bench 4.0. Both models are established systems released months before this analysis, so the paper is evaluating the known limitations of existing agents rather than accompanying a new release.
items.reasoning: Directly relevant to the fast-moving agent-harness space, with a crisp diagnosis of a real failure mode and evaluation against current frontier agents on a credible benchmark. The idea of embedding competence into resources rather than harnesses is architecturally interesting, though it remains a preprint from an academic-industrial group and adoption is unproven.

items.title: Stress Testing Chain-of-Thought Monitoring Against Covert Misalignment
items.content: arXiv:2611.07586v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: As LLM agents advance rapidly in autonomy, the risk of hidden objectives that bypass safety constraints becomes increasingly plausible. Chain-of-thought (CoT) monitoring offers a key control mechanism by reading the agent's reasoning and flagging misalignment before it materializes into action, yet its reliability depends on the realism of the red-team it is stress-tested against. Existing red-teaming efforts rely on shared templates, such as casting a side task as a prerequisite, which treat the side objective as an exogenous insertion and leave task-specific, contextually grounded evasions underexplored. We therefore ask: How robust is CoT monitoring against agents that strategically conceal misalignment? To answer this, we introduce TraceMRT, an automated Trace-level Monitor Red-Teaming framework that reframes the side task as a coherent sub-goal of the primary task and searches trace-shaping strategies whose induced trajectories complete the misaligned objective while reading as natural execution. Through black-box attacks on state-of-the-art monitors such as GPT-5.2 and Claude-4.5, we reveal substantial vulnerabilities even in top models. To counter these vulnerabilities, we propose a Bayesian Trajectory Monitoring framework, integrating global context and local segment evidence to detect covert misalignment. Empirically, our method significantly consolidates monitor robustness with 0.91 AUC and 0.74 TPR@FPR=0.05.
items.author: Yao Huang, Yifan Wang, Yitong Sun, Yichi Zhang, Yinpeng Dong
items.summary: The paper stress-tests chain-of-thought monitoring by building more realistic red-team attacks: rather than exogenously inserting side objectives via shared templates, agents strategically conceal contextually grounded misalignment. The introduced framework probes how robust CoT-based oversight is against agents that actively hide hidden objectives.
items.reasoning: Directly addresses a central open question in AI safety oversight—whether CoT monitoring survives adaptive adversaries—and improves red-team realism over prior work; from a recognized safety research group, though evaluation scope is limited to current model capabilities.

Empirically, our method significantly consolidates monitor robustness with 0.91 AUC and 0.74 TPR@FPR=0.05.

items.title: Optimistic Hedge in General-Sum Games: Fundamental Limits and Regret Bounds via Temporal Approximation
items.content: arXiv:2611.07078v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Optimistic Hedge, a multiplicative weight update with one step of extrapolation, is one of the most natural regret-minimizing dynamics for games, and characterizing its regret has been a longstanding open question. Daskalakis, Fishelson and Golowich proved that if all $m$ players in a finite general-sum game follow Optimistic Hedge with a fixed learning rate, each player's regret is polylogarithmic in the horizon $T$. Subsequently, Ha showed that an appropriate choice of learning rate makes each player's regret bounded independently of $T$. This bound, however, is non-constructive and its dependence on the number of actions $n$ is not explicit, leaving open whether Optimistic Hedge can achieve a constant regret bound which is polynomial in the size of the game.   We show that the answer hinges on the number of players. In two-player games, there is a learning rate for which Optimistic Hedge guarantees $O(n\log n)$ regret independent of the horizon. In three-player games, however, no such bound is possible: for any learning rate up to an absolute constant and for sufficiently large horizon $T$, there is a game with $n$ actions per player in which some player's regret is $2^{\Omega(n)}$, and more generally, for every $m\ge3$ we construct $m$-player games in which some player's regret is $2^{\Omega(mn)}$; for learning rates above $2^{-\Omega(mn)}$, that player's regret even grows linearly in $T$.   Our upper bound is based on a temporal approximation framework for the analysis of Optimistic Hedge. Starting from the variance-based RVU bound of Daskalakis et al., we approximate the losses over time-localized windows by well-behaved functions, whose total variation is a small fraction of their cumulative variance. In $m$-player games, the same framework gives a significantly simplified proof of the recent $O(\sqrt{m}\log n\log T)$ regret bound due to Ha.

This is core online learning and game theory with implications for training dynamics in games.

items.title: WeightLoop: Weight-Space Programming with Experimental Feedback
items.content: arXiv:2611.07319v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Weight-space programming (WSP) shows that language models can reason about and rewrite neural network weights; recursive self-improvement (RSI) motivates feedback-driven improvement. Models guiding experiments receive concrete feedback: completed assays reveal prediction errors and inform what to test next. We introduce WeightLoop, a framework that turns experimental feedback into persistent updates to deployed predictors. GPT-6 Astra inspects a task specification and the model implementation, then writes a bounded, reusable parameter-editing program. As new measurements arrive, the program identifies prediction discrepancies, validates candidate edits using observed outcomes, and writes the selected changes back to the original model. The editor remains fixed while the predictor evolves, enabling repeated updates without further LLM calls or gradient retraining while preserving the original inference interface. In offline replay, targeted edits improve mean ranking utility in seven of eight endpoint-budget settings (all eight versus random edits) and mean final discovery across three sequential tasks. WeightLoop connects WSP with an RSI-inspired improvement loop, making experimental evidence a direct driver of model change and subsequent decisions.

items.title: Unpacking the Compute Efficiency of Strong-to-Weak OPD against GRPO
items.content: arXiv:2611.08453v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) trains a student on its own rollouts under a frozen teacher's per-token supervision. Does this dense signal reduce the training FLOPs needed to reach a target accuracy compared with reinforcement learning? We systematically compare vanilla reverse-KL OPD with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) across task difficulty, student and teacher size, domain, and optimization choices, measuring held-out accuracy against training FLOPs. With an external post-trained teacher, OPD generally loses to GRPO in accuracy per training FLOP at matched settings, even when the teacher is further trained with GRPO, and often suffers response-length inflation. Yet a different teacher changes the picture: when the teacher is the student's own GRPO checkpoint, OPD recovers that checkpoint's accuracy on math with $50\times$ fewer distillation FLOPs than GRPO needs to reach the same accuracy. Following the same teacher setting, we consistently observe this high efficiency with a larger student, on code, and in a second model family. On a single domain, however, the GRPO checkpoint is already the desired model, so distilling it adds to total compute. Across domains, separate GRPO checkpoints hold different capabilities, and no single checkpoint serves every domain. Multi-teacher OPD (DeepSeek-AI, 2026) consolidates per-domain GRPO experts into a single student that matches each expert's accuracy, with the distillation stage costing only 5.2% (on 2 domains) and 8.0% (on 4 domains) of the specialist training FLOPs. Counting specialist training and distillation together, this pipeline reaches joint GRPO's performance on the 2-domain mix with 42.0% fewer total FLOPs.

items.summary: A systematic FLOP-matched comparison of on-policy distillation (reverse-KL) versus GRPO reinforcement learning across task difficulty, model sizes, and domains, measuring held-out accuracy per training FLOP. The surprising finding is that with external post-trained teachers OPD generally underperforms GRPO and inflates response length, though a same-family teacher changes the picture substantially.

items.title: Expanding the Quality-Coverage Frontier with Competitive Flow Matching
items.content: arXiv:2611.07055v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Flow matching (FM) generators often face a quality-coverage tradeoff. Inference-time techniques such as classifier-free guidance raise quality, but at the cost of coverage. We hypothesize this limitation stems from a basic property of the objective: an intermediate noisy image could correspond to many clean images, yet the model can only predict a single velocity, at best averaging over the multiple possibilities. To mitigate this, we introduce competition among predictions during training. We achieve this by augmenting the predictor with a randomly drawn low-dimensional conditioning code $z$. For each training example, we sample $K$ values of $z$ to produce $K$ candidate velocities that compete to explain the target, and apply the loss only to the best-matching candidate. This winner-take-all objective allows different modes to shape different predictions, rather than being averaged into a single compromise. Furthermore, this term naturally enables a new form of guidance, auxiliary conditioning scaling, which complements traditional guidance methods. Together, these two guidance mechanisms show that our method substantially improves the quality-coverage frontier. We validate on ImageNet-256, using two different testbeds, SiT and RAEv2. Given less than 3% of the original SiT pretraining compute for post-training, at the 67% Recall point, our method reduces $\mathrm{FD}_{r,6}$ from 19.22 to 5.91. On RAEv2, at the 70% Recall point, it reduces $\mathrm{FD}_{r,6}$ from 16.83 to 3.18.
items.author: Wenxuan Peng, Richard Zhang, Haitian Zheng, Jaskirat Singh, Tsai-Shien Chen, Eli Shechtman, Bharath Hariharan, Hadar Averbuch-Elor, Zongze Wu

The authors introduce competition among predictions during training by sampling K conditioning codes whose candidate velocities compete to explain each target. This could meaningfully improve generative image models without inference-time guidance tricks.

items.title: WAM-Sim0.1: World Anchored Memory Meets Online RL for Consistent and Realistic Driving Simulation
items.content: arXiv:2611.07939v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Autoregressive driving world models systematically suffer from structural drift, identity drift, and quality decay over long rollout horizons due to transient conditioning signals that lack persistent state. We present WAM-Sim, a driving world model anchored by a persistent hierarchical memory and optimized via online flow-matching RL. WAM-Sim structures persistent context across three temporal and semantic scales: pose-aligned structural tokens encoding persistent road topology, read-only scene tokens supplying geolocated background appearance, and write-once instance tokens preserving individual traffic participant identities across occlusions and chunk boundaries. To restore visual sharpness and physical plausibility degraded by multi-scale conditioning, we introduce an online post-training framework that optimizes self-generated rollouts via flow-matching RL guided by hierarchy-aligned visual rewards and a vision-language model physical judge. The invariant memory empirically confines policy optimization within the anchored context, helping suppress semantic collapse and reward hacking, while online RL systematically enforces physical commonsense and fine-grained visual fidelity. On the nuScenes benchmark, WAM-Sim achieves a superior generation fidelity (FID=3.47, FVD=25.72) and strong downstream perception performance (24.16 mAP, 71.23 road mIoU). On minute-scale rollouts of self-collected data, WAM-Sim substantially mitigates structural and identity drift, preserving high scene similarity and subject identity coherence across extended horizons. Project page: https://fudan-generative-vision.github.io/WAM-Sim.

It further optimizes fidelity via online flow-matching reinforcement learning. Long-horizon consistency is a central open problem for driving simulators and world models.

items.title: Where and Why is Grounded Reasoning Useful?
items.content: arXiv:2611.08485v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Grounded reasoning, where a model outputs text coordinates of relevant locations in chain-of-thought reasoning, is a common strategy for solving complex visual reasoning problems. However, the benefits and limitations of grounded reasoning are understudied. We study where and why grounded reasoning is most useful. To do so, we introduce a chain-of-thought analysis method to measure how much a model uses its outputted grounding in its thinking trace and perform a detailed ablation study of a grounded reasoning training recipe. We find that grounded reasoning improves counting but shows no significant gain over baselines without coordinate grounding across a wide range of spatial reasoning and perception benchmarks. Using several synthetic tasks, we show that grounded reasoning is most useful when a task requires undescribable references, which are visual concepts that are difficult to describe in language. However, we observe that many existing visual reasoning benchmarks are solvable with only describable text references. To close this gap, we introduce BrickVision, a new benchmark that requires undescribable visual references to solve.

items.title: HITCH: Teaching a Vision-Language Model to Operate a Humanoid through a Whole-Body Harness
items.content: arXiv:2611.08039v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Enabling vision-language models (VLMs) to control humanoid robots requires both reliable whole-body interfaces and knowledge of how to use the body that carries over across tasks. We present HITCH (Harness Interfaces To Command Humanoids), a harness in which perception returns the 3D position of any point the VLM selects in its image, and execution turns commands for the pelvis, torso, hands, walking, and gaze into whole-body motion with a learned tracker. We find that both measuring the scene and executing commands accurately raise task success. We then fine-tune a VLM on trajectories in which teacher policies solve five base tasks through HITCH, so that it learns how to operate the humanoid. Without task-specific trajectories, the fine-tuned model completes 51% of SIMPLE episodes and 42.5% of HumanoidArena episodes, and adding five trajectories per SIMPLE task raises its SIMPLE success to 95%. On a real G1, it carries a box and walks to a goal without real training data.

Fine-tuning the VLM on teacher-policy trajectories through HITCH transfers body-operation skills across tasks without task-specific trajectories. This is a compelling recipe for grounding VLMs in whole-body humanoid control.

items.title: Who Should Know What? Empirical Information Design for Multi-Agent LLM Economies
items.content: arXiv:2611.07667v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: The performance of multi-agent LLM systems depends not only on the capabilities of the underlying models but also on information-sharing policies, which govern what information each agent observes and at what level of detail. But does providing AI agents with more detailed information always improve collective outcomes, or can transparency paradoxically degrade efficiency? To investigate this, we introduce empirical information design, an experimental framework that systematically compares disclosure policies across economic markets populated by LLM agents, while holding interaction rules and models fixed. We evaluate ten frontier LLMs in multi-resource trade, bilateral bargaining, and double auctions, using ground-truth utilities to decouple identified opportunities from realized outcomes. We find that finer information disclosure yields highly model-dependent results. In trade, revealing exact valuations rather than ordinal preference rankings reduces realized gains for GPT-6 Sol (from 98% to 91% of maximum) yet increases them for Claude Sonnet 5 (from 72% to 86%). In bargaining, exact information leads Grok 4.7 to produce less balanced agreements, whereas Claude Opus 5.5 divides gains symmetrically. In double auctions, full disclosure inflates price demands, triggering market breakdown and lowering welfare for Gemini 3.1 Pro (97% to 78%), Claude Opus 5.5 (94% to 64%), and Grok 4.7 (97% to 62%). Overall, these results suggest that model selection and information design must be co-optimized, as LLMs vary in how their strategic responses to information impact system objectives.

It finds that more detailed information and transparency can paradoxically degrade collective efficiency, challenging the assumption that more context helps agents. The use of ground-truth utilities to separate information effects from capability effects is a notable methodological contribution.

items.title: Multi-step SWE: Can Coding Agents Keep Building on Their Own Code Over Long Horizons?
items.content: arXiv:2611.07166v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Developers rarely give a coding agent a single request: they ask it to build a component and then to extend, upgrade, and optimize it, each time on code the agent itself wrote. Most benchmarks, however, score one task at a time. We introduce Multi-step SWE, a long-horizon benchmark of 69 software engineering tasks, each a chain of 5-15 dependent steps on a single codebase. Every step is a complete, multi-hour engineering request that starts from the code the agent produced in the preceding steps, so early design decisions and errors carry forward. Across nine frontier models, the strongest model reaches a solve rate of only 18.5%, and 38 of the 69 tasks are not solved by any model. items.title: Beyond Instruction Override: Benchmarking Indirect Prompt Injection with Task-Tampering Attacks
items.content: arXiv:2611.07640v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Indirect prompt-injection (IPI) benchmarks predominantly test planted instructions that redirect a tool-using agent toward an attacker-chosen task. Yet attacker-controlled content can instead tamper with the outcome of the task already in progress. A buyer's dispute evidence can cite a false refund policy to inflate a refund without changing the task. We define IPI by authority rather than instruction-like wording: planted content constitutes an attack when it attempts to influence a decision that its source is not authorized to determine. We introduce a benchmark that makes this boundary explicit: in each of 90 validated cases across three tool-use environments, the user request specifies the source that resolves the targeted decision. Every attack tampers with a decision required by the benign task rather than replacing that task. Each case has attacks with the same harmful outcome that target up to six parts of the agent's decision making: its objective, decision rules, available actions, expected consequences, reading of observations, or beliefs about the current state. Without a defense, attacks on three of the five other targets (decision rules, available actions, and state) have higher mean success than objective attacks across five LLMs. A detection-and-removal defense reduces objective-targeting attacks to 2.4% success but leaves observation- and state-targeting attacks at 9.5% and 12.1%; this gap persists under detection-optimized rewrites. A tool-policy defense still allows 15.4% attack success, close to 17.0% without a defense, because these attacks generally retain expected tools and manipulate values obtained during execution. Evaluations whose attacks redirect the task or target only the agent's objective can therefore overestimate the coverage of these defenses. Code and data are available at https://github.com/amazon-science/task-tampering-prompt-injection.

items.title: Adversarial Multiplicity: Cherry-Picked Models and the Limits of Disclosure
items.content: arXiv:2611.07378v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Predictive multiplicity -- where similarly accurate models disagree on individual predictions -- can be leveraged to optimize secondary metrics (e.g., fairness) without loss in predictive performance. However, exploiting multiplicity opens the opportunity for motivated parties (or coding agents gaming their objectives) to steer predictions toward their own ends, such as in litigation or consumer disputes with automated decision-making tools. In these adversarial multiplicity settings, we distinguish soft manipulation, where parties optimize over innocuous model choices (e.g., hyperparameter tuning, feature engineering), from hard manipulation, where parties directly perturb model parameters. We find a sufficiently flexible model can be manipulated to reverse any individual prediction with minimal change in predictive performance while passing black-box audits, making hard manipulation viable in most regulatory settings. Soft manipulation has smaller effects but can pass white-box audits requiring full access to code and data. Even aggregate estimates can be manipulated: a model's estimated effect of climate change on wildfires can be fully reversed by hard edits and soft search. We find the Reconcile algorithm typically resolves most disagreements between models, but more often in favor of the manipulator when the opposing model is chosen adversarially compared to at random. We map which manipulations can plausibly pass existing regulations and disclosure policies, and recommend mitigations such as pre-registration, proof of model training, sensitivity analyses, multi-metric evaluations, and committing to versioned public models.

items.title: Recursive Sparse Attention: Million-Token Length Extrapolation at Logarithmic Cost
items.content: arXiv:2611.07232v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: At context lengths of about 1M tokens, dense attention is costly in prefill and decoding, and training typically relies on long documents, which become scarcer as the target length increases. Most sparse attention methods score all preceding blocks or tokens, so their selection cost per query is $O(L)$ at context length $L$; hierarchical selection reduces it to $O(\log L)$, but prior trainable hierarchical methods report accuracy only within their training length. We propose RecSA (Recursive Sparse Attention), which builds a tree over the KV cache in which each node summarizes its subtree with one key and one mean-pooled value. The keys come from one pooler per layer, shared by all levels and distilled from dense attention. Each level above the tokens selects at most $k$ candidates, so each query has $O(\log L)$ selection cost and reads $O(\log L)$ entries; the summaries of unselected candidates share one softmax with the exact tokens. Each entry's RoPE position is its index among the candidates of its level, so at any length every relative distance stays within the range seen during training. Initialized from Qwen3-4B and trained on 0.62B tokens at the original model's 32K training length, RecSA outperforms all baselines on RULER at every length from 131K to 2M; at 1M, it scores 60.5, compared with 40.0 for the best baseline, Dense + DCA. With our optimized kernels, RecSA is faster than dense attention in end-to-end prefill and decoding from 64K to 2M; at 524K on one H200 GPU, it accelerates prefill by 3.2x and decoding by 3.8x.

items.title: Social Humanoid: Socially Responsive Human-Humanoid Interaction
items.content: arXiv:2611.08407v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Humanoid robots are typically trained as solitary agents, leaving them unable to coordinate physically with human partners who naturally anticipate and adjust to one another. To bridge this gap, we present Social Humanoid, a hierarchical system that generates and executes socially responsive whole-body motion on a 29-DoF Unitree G1 conditioned on a human partner's motion. Its high-level policy performs flexible sequence modeling of human and humanoid motion through a shared tokenized representation, generating reactive humanoid motion and anticipating the partner's motion when they are occluded, while a low-level whole-body tracking controller executes the generated motion on the robot. To train the system, we introduce a two-phase adaptive retargeting procedure that retargets one interaction partner to the robot while morphing the other partner to preserve contact dynamics, reachability, and relative body scale. We apply this procedure across five motion-capture datasets to produce a new Human-Humanoid Interaction (HHI) benchmark of 260 hours of human-humanoid interactions. Our results demonstrate that Social Humanoid produces coordinated, human-aligned behavior across diverse interaction types in simulation and the real world. Project page: https://von31.github.io/social-humanoid/

items.title: LongBanana: An Expert-Verified Benchmark for Long-Context Multi-Reference Image Synthesis
items.content: arXiv:2611.06856v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: We introduce LongBanana, to our knowledge the first expert-designed and expert-verified benchmark for long-context multi-reference image synthesis in the age of agent-driven image generation. The task requires retrieving dispersed visual evidence, rejecting distractors, binding entities and relations, and composing one coherent final image from multiple references. LongBanana contains 90 carefully designed tasks organized by a 3-by-3 taxonomy; each task includes about 32 reference images, 20 constraints, and 50 evaluation items, yielding 4,670 expert-specified atomic evaluation items in total. Its graph-grounded evaluation design instantiates each task with reference images and an entity-relation graph, then converts node, edge, and whole-graph obligations into checklist items for Content Fidelity, Relational Binding, and Global Constraint Satisfaction. Reviewed expert labels include a 15% double-labeled subset with 89.4% exact agreement and 0.83 quadratic weighted kappa. We further introduce LongBanana-Gen, an agent-harness framework for long-horizon image generation; experiments show that minimal agent harnesses improve over direct generation, while a ReAct-Plan-Exec-Reflect (RPR) workflow yields harness-dependent gains by strengthening evidence grounding and repair. Together, LongBanana provides an auditable testbed for measuring dense visual evidence use and a shared target for developing stronger agent-driven image-generation systems. Code and data are available at the project page: https://long-banana.com/.

items.title: XM4D: 4D Reconstruction through Certifiable Geometric Optimization
items.content: arXiv:2611.07902v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Accurate 4D reconstruction remains challenging: jointly estimating camera motion, scene geometry, and non-rigid deformation entails highly nonconvex optimization, making global optimality difficult to guarantee. We present XM4D, a framework for accurate and efficient 4D reconstruction built upon certifiably globally optimal geometric optimization. By separating the estimation of camera motion from non-rigid deformation, we formulate both stages as structured quadratically constrained quadratic programs (QCQP) that admit semidefinite programming (SDP) relaxations and verifiable global optimality certificates. For camera motion estimation, we lift static point tracks into 3D using foundational depth prediction models and formulate a scaled bundle adjustment problem that jointly estimates camera poses, depth scales, and static landmarks. By analytically eliminating translations and landmarks, we reduce the problem to a QCQP over scaled rotations. For non-rigid reconstruction, we represent dynamic motion using an embedded deformation graph (EDG) and show that its tracking, rigidity, and temporal regularization objectives similarly reduce to a rotation-only QCQP. Both problems admit SDP relaxations that we solve efficiently with a GPU-accelerated Burer-Monteiro solver based on Riemannian optimization. The recovered geometry further initializes dynamic Gaussian splatting for photometric refinement. Extensive experiments across seven benchmarks demonstrate accurate camera motion estimation on both static and dynamic scenes, efficient optimization that scales to thousands of frames, and state-of-the-art novel-view rendering quality.

This brings optimization-theoretic guarantees to a typically nonconvex pipeline.

items.title: Interactive Visual Gym: Evaluating Visual Interaction Models with Simulated Users in Interactive Worlds
items.content: arXiv:2611.08286v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Visual interaction models that support users during ongoing physical tasks require evaluation in closed loop, where assistant responses can change subsequent user behavior and task outcomes. Existing benchmarks largely rely on offline replay and therefore cannot capture these effects. We introduce Interactive Visual Gym, a framework for closed-loop evaluation and training of visual interaction models through joint simulation of executable task environments and human users. We contribute three simulators that recreate everyday tasks and human-aligned action spaces across cooking, household manipulation, and mobile-interface domains, together with a persona-conditioned user simulation harness that collaborates with the assistant while incorporating controlled execution errors and other out-of-plan behaviors. We instantiate the framework as IVG-Bench, a benchmark with 315 interaction scenarios. Evaluating state-of-the-art VLMs as visual interaction models reveals substantial limitations: the best-performing model, Gemini 4 Argon, completes only 53.4% of tasks within the time limit, exhibits significant weaknesses in factual grounding and actionable guidance, and is often too slow to prevent errors when response latency is considered. We verify our evaluation protocol with a human study which finds 78.5% agreement between our interaction-quality metric and participant preferences. We further show that the environments provide useful learning signals: in a proof-of-concept GRPO experiment, closed-loop training improves both task success and interaction quality for Qwen3.5-4B model in our cooking environment.

items.title: Embodied RAG++: Retrieval-Augmented Generation From What Exists to What Works in Embodied Scenes
items.content: arXiv:2611.07517v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: To serve a request in a human environment, a robot system must find an object that satisfies a functional requirement and a robot that can feasibly reach it. Scene graphs record which objects exist and where, but they often omit capabilities documented only in product manuals. Retrieval-augmented generation methods can read such manuals, yet they rarely reason jointly over object capabilities, physical instances, robot states, and dynamic connectivity. We introduce E2W-Bench, the Exists-to-Works Benchmark, which links dynamic hybrid scene graphs with real product manuals to evaluate capability-grounded robot--object assignment under availability, mobility, vertical-reach, and connector constraints. We also present Embodied RAG++, a spatially grounded retrieval framework that scopes retrieval to the manuals linked to candidate objects, caches extracted capabilities per product model, and resolves robot--object feasibility through deterministic spatial reasoning. items.title: EnvOpt: Automated Optimization for Agent Environments
items.content: arXiv:2611.07372v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: An LLM agent's cost and success depend on its model, its harness, and its environment. In addition to the widely studied directions of parameter tuning and harness optimization, we propose the third direction: optimization over stationary environments. Agents are often deployed in rich environments shared by many tasks, such as a company's Slack workspace or a complex collection of data sources, documents or tickets. We call these environments stationary environments. We introduce EnvOpt, a method for automated end-to-end optimization of stationary environments for any given model and harness, using real or synthetic tasks without needing any graders or reference answers. On AutomationBench, EnvOpt reduces the cost of Claude Haiku 4.5 by 72.7% and raises its pass rate by 14.34%. The same environment transfers to Opus 5, cutting its cost by 68.1% with a 1.34% gain. Added on top of Meta-Harness's optimized harness for Haiku 4.5, it lowers cost by a further 83.4% and adds 11.17% accuracy over Meta-Harness alone. Across 5 benchmarks, EnvOpt significantly reduces the cost of agents while improving or maintaining pass rate, and is transferable to different models and different harnesses. We also discuss common successful and rejected environment optimization strategies during automated optimization. More broadly, our results show that how information is represented to an agent shapes both its cost and its success, making the environment worth optimizing in addition to the parameters and the harness.

items.title: TCSExam: Evaluating Frontier LLMs on the Full Range of TCS Research
items.content: arXiv:2611.07962v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Can large language models (LLMs) advance theoretical computer science and resolve its long-standing open conjectures? To study progress toward this goal, we introduce TCSExam, a unified framework and benchmark covering the full range of TCS research. It evaluates theorem proving, solver engineering, and constructions alongside direct attempts to resolve open conjectures, capturing both concrete research accomplishments and progress toward long-standing research goals. TCSExam-Full contains 100 expert-reviewed tasks, with submissions checked by the Lean kernel or an executable task checker. TCSExam-Lite selects 20 tasks, five per track, reducing the number of task attempts by 80% at the same per-attempt budget. We evaluate eight agents on Full and nine on Lite. The TCSExam Index combines all four tracks: GPT-6 Astra leads Full (71.9), and Opus 5.5 leads Lite (72.3). Full and Lite rankings are strongly aligned across eight shared agents (Spearman's $\rho=0.93$), supporting Lite as a compact, discriminative benchmark. The evaluations yield improved solver outputs and mathematical constructions, together with independently verified special cases and bounds from open-conjecture attempts. TCSExam provides an extensible framework with task sources, Docker build recipes, and evaluation tools for reproducible use.
