items.title: Masked diffusion as random sequential adsorption: an exactly solvable model for parallel decoding
items.content: arXiv:2611.07845v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Masked diffusion models generate text by reversing a stochastic masking process. Unlike autoregressive LLMs, which generate text one token at a time, they can reveal many tokens in parallel, at the price of an error, since tokens revealed together are drawn independently. We show that this trade-off maps onto the statistical physics of driven many-particle systems. (i) For any data, the error of parallel generation is the entropy production of the generation process relative to the reversed masking process. (ii) For Markov data, generation is a random sequential adsorption process with labelled gaps, which we solve exactly for any number of steps. (iii) For many steps, the error becomes the dissipation of a slowly driven system: the unmasking schedule plays the role of the driving protocol, the number of steps that of its duration, and the error is set by a thermodynamic metric that we obtain in closed form from the mutual information between tokens. Optimal schedules are geodesics of this metric. The exact solution shows how correlations in the text shape both the error and the quality of the output. The longer the correlations, the more the error concentrates at the start of generation. Schedules that start with small steps then gain more, both in path error and in perplexity, and need fewer steps to reach their asymptotic behaviour.

items.summary: This theoretical paper maps the error of parallel token generation in masked diffusion LLMs onto statistical physics: the error equals the entropy production of the generation process, and for Markov data generation becomes a random sequential adsorption process that is solved exactly. In the many-step limit, the unmasking error corresponds to dissipation of a slowly driven system. This provides the first exactly solvable analytical model for the parallel-decoding accuracy-speed trade-off in diffusion language models.

items.title: Scaling Neural Motor Decoding via Decoupled Behavioral Pretraining
items.content: arXiv:2611.08263v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Recent neural decoding approaches achieve strong performance by training on large collections of paired neural-behavioral recordings, but such datasets are expensive, invasive, and difficult to scale. In contrast, behavioral data is abundant and easy to collect, raising the question of whether neural decoding can benefit from decoupling behavioral and neural representation learning. We introduce BEEMO, a flexible multi-session framework that enables training with arbitrary mixtures of paired neural-behavioral recordings and unpaired behavioral data. A behavior decoder learns movement dynamics directly from behavioral trajectories, while neural activity is incorporated through cross-attention layers when available, allowing behavioral and neural supervision to scale independently. Across multiple intracortical motor datasets and tasks in nonhuman primates, we show that incorporating unpaired behavioral data improves decoding performance, particularly when transferring to new tasks, and that adding even a small amount of behavioral data from the target task further improves transfer. By decoupling neural and behavioral data, we unlock a new dimension for scaling: unpaired behavioral data, which is substantially cheaper and easier to collect than paired neural recordings, can be used directly to improve decoding performance. We further show that behavior-only pretraining, without any neural pretraining, achieves performance comparable to models pretrained on substantially larger neural datasets. Together, our results suggest that scaling behavioral data offers a practical and cost-effective path toward neural decoding models that generalize across subjects and tasks. Code is available at https://github.com/nerdslab/beemo.

Impact is significant for the brain-computer interface subfield but the paradigm of decoupled pretraining is a natural extension of trends elsewhere.

items.title: XStack: A Benchmark for ML Repo Migration
items.content: arXiv:2611.08472v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: ML code should run where researchers choose, not where it was first written. Today, machine learning code mainly lives in two ecosystems, PyTorch on NVIDIA GPUs and JAX on Google TPUs. Migrating repositories between them means building and testing across frameworks and hardware. This migration is (1) a practical need, since it unlocks different hardware for researchers, and (2) a natural benchmark: it involves different frameworks and hardware, covers whole repositories, and is long-horizon and challenging. We introduce XStack, a benchmark that evaluates agents on migrating ML repositories between these two ecosystems. Each agent receives a PyTorch repository and a clean TPU machine and must deliver a JAX repository. Its output passes if it meets our grading criteria, based on the source repository's published result, authenticated and calibrated by us. Migration by agents remains unreliable: Claude Opus 5 passes 75%, GPT-5.6-sol 45%, and every other agent at most 40%. XStack is a step toward freeing ML code from its ecosystem. We release XStack to make progress toward reliable migration across frameworks and hardware measurable.
items.author: Linrong Cai, Taiming Lu, Haozhe Chen, Zhuang Liu
items.summary: XStack is a benchmark evaluating coding agents on migrating entire ML repositories from PyTorch on NVIDIA GPUs to JAX on TPUs, with verifiable pass criteria via building and testing. It offers a practical, long-horizon agentic task spanning frameworks and hardware, unlocking cross-ecosystem portability as both a need and a natural evaluation surface.
items.reasoning: A useful and well-motivated agentic benchmark with clean verification and real practical value for the research community; repo-scale migration is genuinely long-horizon. From a Stanford-affiliated team, though benchmarks in this crowded space often see fast saturation and uneven adoption.

items.title: Structural Conditional Independence Test via Neural Quantile Resolution
items.content: arXiv:2611.07165v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Conditional independence testing is difficult when dependence is weak, localized, or expressed through distributional changes rather than a global mean shift. Existing tests usually return a scalar statistic or p-value, which summarizes evidence against independence but does not describe where the conditional law changes. We propose QRCIT, a quantile-resolution conditional independence test that compares P(X|Z) and P(X|Y,Z) through a quantile deformation learned by a shared model. A lightweight residual quantile-flow model first learns the baseline conditional quantile law and then learns the additional deformation induced by Y, yielding a global predictive-gain statistic with conditional-randomization calibration and an inspectable deformation field over context and quantile level. We also introduce the Structural Dependency Benchmark (SDB), which evaluates dependence structures motivated by real applications, such as context-local, tail-only, sign-reversing, moving-ridge, and mean-neutral patterns. Across synthetic post-nonlinear (PNL) and SDB benchmarks, QRCIT improves detection of structured alternatives, with empirical Type-I behavior evaluated across settings. Higher quantile resolution improves merged-SDB power at moderate sample sizes, while diagnostics restricted to known affected regions improve detection of localized dependence. On Sachs, METABRIC breast cancer, and CCLE/PLX4720, QRCIT provides competitive real-data performance and interpretable deformation patterns. These results support quantile-resolved conditional-law deformation as a practical framework for testing and diagnosing structured conditional dependence.
items.author: Khoa Nguyen, Bao Duong, Thin Nguyen
items.summary: The authors propose QRCIT, a conditional independence test that compares conditional distributions through a quantile deformation learned by a shared residual quantile-flow model. Unlike scalar p-value tests, it localizes where the conditional law changes and provides an inspectable deformation, calibrated via conditional randomization. This handles weak, localized, or distributional (non-mean-shift) dependence that standard tests miss.
items.reasoning: A technically novel contribution to conditional independence testing with interpretability advantages and relevance to causal discovery; impact depends on empirical strength against established kernel-based tests, not fully evident from the abstract.

items.title: Provably Efficient Representation Learning for Low-Rank CMDPs
items.content: arXiv:2611.07295v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: We study representation learning in low-rank Constrained Markov Decision Processes (CMDPs), where both value and reward functions are approximated by a set of unknown representation vectors, and the transition dynamics admit a low-rank factorization. The objective is to maximize expected cumulative rewards while complying with constraints on the expected cumulative utility. To achieve this, we propose \texttt{MFRLC} (Model-Free Representation Learning for Low-Rank CMDP), a model-free algorithm that uses a primal-dual scheme to effectively balance reward regret and constraint violations. To the best of our knowledge, \texttt{MFRLC} is the first representation-learning method for low-rank CMDPs that combines the Least-Squares Value Iteration with Upper Confidence Bound (LSVI-UCB) and primal-dual techniques. \texttt{MFRLC} further enhances value function estimation with bonuses for function approximation and learns the mapping from representations to value functions directly, avoiding explicit estimation of the transition kernel. We prove that, with high probability, \texttt{MFRLC} achieves $\widetilde O(K^{3/4})$ reward regret and cumulative constraint violation over $K$ deployment rounds, independent of the size of the state space. To our knowledge, these are the first sublinear regret and violation guarantees for CMDPs with unknown features.
items.author: Kaixuan Liu, Guojun Xiong, Shengpu Tang, Wanyun Si, Jian Li
items.summary: The paper introduces MFRLC, a model-free primal-dual algorithm for representation learning in low-rank Constrained MDPs, balancing reward regret against constraint violations using least-squares value iteration. The authors claim it is the first representation-learning method for low-rank CMDPs with such guarantees. It advances the theory of safe/constrained reinforcement learning with function approximation.
items.reasoning: Meaningful theoretical contribution to constrained RL with low-rank structure and provable efficiency; the primal-dual combination is technically substantive, though the practical impact of model-free low-rank CMDP methods remains to be shown.

items.title: Binding Paraphrased Instructions to Encountered Objects in sLLM Agents under Partial Observability
items.content: arXiv:2611.07599v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Reliable deployment of LLM agents requires grounding diverse user expressions in their environments. Although RL-finetuned smaller large language model (sLLM) agents rival larger prompted LLMs on embodied tasks, their robustness to instruction paraphrases remains unclear. We introduce ALFWorld-Para to evaluate this robustness under controlled paraphrases, revealing 21-52% declines in success rates (SRs), predominantly driven by object synonyms. Despite retaining knowledge of synonym referents, agents often fail to take the corresponding objects even after observing them, exposing a gap between referential knowledge and object binding. Partial observability further complicates binding, as referents may remain unseen or have already been encountered under different labels. To address this challenge, we propose BINDIntent, a training-free framework that probabilistically binds referring expressions to observed labels using semantic proximity and estimated persistence against unseen candidates. Without additional training or LLM calls, BINDIntent improves synonym-paraphrase success of RL-finetuned sLLMs by 17.5-49.1 percentage points (pp) with only 0.4 ms of CPU overhead per step. It also raises GiGPO-7B's overall SR from 61.8% to 77.4%, surpassing a prompted 24B LLM. Code and benchmark are available at https://github.com/cau-hai-lab/ALFWorld-Para.
items.author: Chanyoung Kim, Harim Song, Byoungchan Ko, Keonyoung Lee, Myungwon Lee, Dahuin Jung
items.summary: The paper introduces ALFWorld-Para, a benchmark showing that RL-finetuned small LLM agents suffer 21-52% success-rate declines when instructions are paraphrased, mostly due to object synonyms. It identifies a gap between referential knowledge and object binding under partial observability, where agents know what a synonym means but fail to act on the corresponding object they have encountered.
items.reasoning: The finding that RL-finetuned agents retain synonym knowledge yet fail to bind it to actions is a crisp, well-motivated diagnosis of an important robustness failure for embodied LLM agents, and the controlled benchmark is a reusable contribution. Scores are limited by the relatively narrow scope of a single simulated environment and the focus on small agent models rather than frontier systems.

items.title: Same Answer, Different Future: Matched Predictions Do Not Imply Matched Belief Updating in Language Models
items.content: arXiv:2611.07913v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Language models can produce similar probabilistic predictions after observing outcomes, reading summaries, receiving instructions, or undergoing activation interventions. Whether these routes induce equivalent belief states remains unclear: agreement in current predictions does not establish how a model will respond to subsequent evidence. We investigate this distinction in a Bernoulli inference task with an analytic Bayesian reference. Across three open-weight language models, we prepare states through four textual routes and two activation-level interventions, measure both next-outcome continuations and explicit probabilistic estimates, and append identical new evidence from each prepared state. We quantify the persistence of the initial belief through its effective evidence weight, the number of new observations it is worth. We find that the format of evidence decides which readouts express its content: outcome sequences primarily affect continuations, whereas summaries and stated rates primarily affect explicit estimates. Moreover, effective weights differ substantially across routes, with summaries receiving weights that scale weakly with their stated observation counts and elicitation questions changing inferred weights by orders of magnitude. In a one-shot steering setting, an intervention that reproduces a natural record's immediate prediction loses most of its effect under subsequent evidence. These results show that agreement in current readouts is insufficient to establish equivalence in belief updating: how a belief is acquired and how it is read jointly determine its subsequent dynamics.
items.author: Weihan Li, Junhao Wu, Xinlei Chen, Tianshi Zheng
items.summary: This study asks whether language models that produce the same probabilistic prediction via different routes—reading outcomes, summaries, instructions, or activation interventions—hold equivalent belief states. Using a Bernoulli inference task with an analytic Bayesian reference across three open-weight models, the authors append identical new evidence to each prepared state and measure how the initial belief persists. The findings show matched predictions do not imply matched belief updating, revealing hidden state differences beneath behavioral agreement.

items.title: From What Is Used to What Is Missing: Rethinking Dynamic Rank in LoRA
items.content: arXiv:2611.07349v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning with LoRA is governed by rank, which controls parameter budget and locally accessible task updates. Existing dynamic-rank methods mainly focus on capacity allocation, leaving unresolved whether the current adaptation space is sufficient for the task. We characterize the first-order information boundary of standard factor gradients, showing that their unobservable subspace coincides with the normal space of the low-rank manifold. Thus, factor gradients alone cannot distinguish under-optimization within the current space from task-relevant directions beyond its first-order reach. This motivates a geometric view of rank evolution, where tangent information optimizes existing degrees of freedom and the normal spectrum quantifies the value of new ones. Under a local quadratic model, we show that leading normal singular directions yield the locally optimal rank expansion, with spectral energy determining its gain. Building on this characterization, we propose GEAR, which turns the tangent--normal decomposition into rank evolution through tangent-space optimization, matrix-free normal-spectrum estimation for rank expansion, and task-induced geometric initialization. Across language and vision benchmarks, GEAR achieves the best average performance in all evaluated settings with substantially fewer trainable parameters. On LLaMA3-8B, it raises the average commonsense score from 86.61 to 88.45 while reducing trainable parameters from 42.0M to 14.4M.
items.author: Peng Xue, Guodong Fan, Guang-Yong Chen, Xing Chen
items.summary: The paper gives a geometric characterization of dynamic rank allocation in LoRA, showing that factor gradients cannot distinguish under-optimization within the current adaptation subspace from task-relevant directions outside it, since the unobservable subspace is the normal space of the low-rank manifold. This motivates rank evolution methods that probe normal-space information to detect missing capacity.
items.reasoning: Insightful theoretical reframing of a practical PEFT question with a concrete implication for designing dynamic-rank LoRA methods; relevant to the widely used LoRA ecosystem, though it remains a focused contribution.

Existing dynamic-rank methods mainly focus on capacity allocation, leaving unresolved whether the current adaptation space is sufficient for the task. We characterize the first-order information boundary of standard factor gradients, showing that their unobservable subspace coincides with the normal space of the low-rank manifold. Thus, factor gradients alone cannot distinguish under-optimization within the current space from task-relevant directions beyond its first-order reach. This motivates a geometric view of rank evolution, where tangent information optimizes existing degrees of freedom and the normal spectrum quantifies the value of new ones. Under a local quadratic model, we show that leading normal singular directions yield the locally optimal rank expansion, with spectral energy determining its gain. Building on this characterization, we propose GEAR, which turns the tangent--normal decomposition into rank evolution through tangent-space optimization, matrix-free normal-spectrum estimation for rank expansion, and task-induced geometric initialization. Across language and vision benchmarks, GEAR achieves the best average performance in all evaluated settings with substantially fewer trainable parameters. On LLaMA3-8B, it raises the average commonsense score from 86.61 to 88.45 while reducing trainable parameters from 42.0M to 14.4M.

items.title: Editing Large Language Models with Geometry-Aware Regularization
items.content: arXiv:2611.06185v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Knowledge editing has become a key technique for updating knowledge in large language models. However, existing methods neglect the geometric structure of the knowledge representation space, leading to two key limitations: they cannot distinguish which pre-trained knowledge should be preferentially preserved (core vs. non-core) nor which new edits are inherently difficult (hard vs. easy). To address this, we propose GEdit, a geometry-aware framework built on a Low-Rank Plus Diagonal (LR+D) factor model that captures the intrinsic low-rank structure of Transformer FFN hidden representations. GEdit features two complementary mechanisms. First, the low-rank regularization applies targeted protection on a low-rank core knowledge subspace. Second, the adaptive regularization dynamically adjusts the regularization strength based on each edit request's editability: relaxing constraints for hard edits to ensure success, and tightening them for easy edits to better preserve pretrained knowledge. Extensive experiments on GPT2-XL, GPT-J, and LLaMA-3-8B under large-scale editing scenarios, including both mini-batch and fully sequential editing settings with up to 10,000 continuous updates, show that GEdit consistently and significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in both editing success and knowledge preservation.

items.title: Before You Continue: Evaluating Time-Sensitive Safety Awareness in Conversational Assistants
items.content: arXiv:2611.06839v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Large language model (LLM) assistants increasingly help users with everyday activities that involve time-dependent constraints. However, users may not mention these constraints in later requests, requiring assistants to recognize and adjust their advice accordingly. To evaluate such capability, we introduce TASC (Temporal Action Safety in Conversation), a benchmark that evaluates whether LLMs apply time-dependent constraints when responding to conversational requests. TASC consists of 3,418 inputs derived from 128 templates, along with a separate set of 33 scenarios designed to compare models' ability to calculate elapsed time with their ability to apply that information. Across 13 models, assistants account for time-dependent constraints in only 30.5% of cases where the proposed action violates a rule, while rarely warning users unnecessarily. More importantly, models fail to apply these constraints in 62.1% of cases despite correctly calculating the elapsed time. Explicitly providing the timing resolves only about half of these failures, revealing a gap between temporal reasoning and its application in conversational advice.

items.title: Who Pays for the Knowledge Models Copy? Model Collapse as Rogers' Paradox
items.content: arXiv:2611.06022v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Generative models trained on the output of earlier models lose knowledge across generations, rare knowledge first. The remedies that work all bring in information from outside the loop, and the theory of model collapse treats that supply as given: a fixed archive, drawn from a fixed distribution. We argue that the supply is the problem, and that cultural evolution has the theory of it. We read model collapse as Rogers' paradox: a population that comes to rely on copying ends up no better off than one that never copied, because copies go stale unless someone keeps learning for themselves. We test the identification in three steps. First, Rogers' model, fitted only to fully synthetic training, predicts to within a few percentage points how much rare knowledge language models, from word trigrams to a pretrained transformer, retain under other mixtures of fresh data. Second, when the world itself changes, a lineage that copies its own past needs more fresh data to keep up the faster the world changes, as Rogers' model says it must and as analyses that assume a fixed target cannot; a lineage that restarts every generation from fixed pretrained weights is largely insulated, because those weights are knowledge that is never copied. Third, we close the loop: when the people who write a model's training data can ask the model instead of finding things out, the supply of fresh data becomes endogenous. At equilibrium, the model is exactly as reliable as it is costly for people to find out for themselves, the population is no better off than without the model, and every increase in the share of model-written text must be paid for by more people learning for themselves. Users who check what they are told and relearn when it is wrong break the paradox. Filters that select plausible text are conformist and accelerate collapse; only checks that carry new information act as critical learning.
items.author: Nam H. Le
items.summary: This theoretical paper reinterprets model collapse through Rogers' paradox from cultural evolution: a population relying on copying gains no benefit unless some members keep learning independently, since copied knowledge goes stale. Fitting Rogers' model to synthetic training predicts model collapse within a few percentage points across a three-step test. It matters by importing a mature evolutionary theory to explain why external data supply, not just copying, determines degradation.

items.title: Householder Motion Embedding: Noise Modulation for Motion-Controllable Video Generation
items.content: arXiv:2611.07294v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Diffusion models for video generation have achieved remarkable success, yet precise motion control under explicit user guidance remains challenging. Recent noise-warping methods introduce temporal correlations by warping the noise according to the user-provided motion signal. However, standard spatial warping generally disrupts the noise's i.i.d. Gaussian structure, requiring distribution correction, such as Jacobian-based correction, but at a substantial computational overhead. We propose Householder Motion Embedding (HME), which encodes the motion signal into the noise through a sequence of Householder reflections that together form an orthogonal transformation applied to each location's channel vector. HME exactly preserves the spatial Gaussian structure within each frame while introducing cross-frame correlations that promote temporally consistent video. HME is agnostic to the network architecture and integrates directly into standard video diffusion fine-tuning pipelines. Experiments on different scenarios show that HME matches or outperforms the state of the art, while achieving a 2.7x speedup over noise warping. These results demonstrate that channel-space Householder transformations offer a principled and efficient alternative to noise warping for motion-controllable video generation.
items.author: Tao Jun Lin, Jinhong Ni, Ruyi Zha, Yifu Wang, Xibin Song, Pan Ji, Hongdong Li
items.summary: The paper proposes encoding user-provided motion into video diffusion noise via Householder reflections forming an orthogonal per-location channel transformation. Unlike standard warping, this exactly preserves the Gaussian noise structure, eliminating costly Jacobian-based distribution correction. This offers an efficient route to motion-controllable video generation.
items.reasoning: Mathematically elegant solution to a known inefficiency in noise-warping methods for motion control, with exact guarantees rather than approximations. Impact is bounded by the niche of noise-warping based motion control, but the technique is clean and broadly reusable.

items.title: Generator-Aligned Reward Modeling with Target-Aware Bounded Optimization for Visual Generation
items.content: arXiv:2611.07648v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Post-training aims to enhance desired attributes in visual generative models while preserving their general generation capabilities. Reward-guided post-training faces two challenges: real training data may mismatch the generator's output distribution, and attribute supervision may be confounded by unrelated content. Unbounded reward maximization can also cause overoptimization and degrade generation quality. We propose a framework combining Generator-Aligned Reward Modeling (GARM) and Target-Aware Bounded Optimization (TABO). GARM mitigates distribution mismatch through generator-support matching and reduces content confounding using content-matched real contrasts, yielding generator-relevant, attribute-focused reward supervision. TABO maps the learned reward to a smooth, upper-bounded function calibrated from real target-positive examples. This transformation is independent of the optimization algorithm and supports both direct reward-gradient and policy-based optimization. We further introduce Target-Aware GRPO (TA-GRPO), an adaptation of Flow-GRPO that combines fixed stage-wise advantage scaling, a generator-to-target curriculum, and timestep-balanced credit assignment for flow-based video optimization. Experiments show that GARM improves target-attribute expression while maintaining competitive generation quality. TABO better balances attribute enhancement and visual quality than unconstrained reward maximization, while TA-GRPO improves target enhancement over vanilla Flow-GRPO and reduces unintended attribute leakage on neutral prompts. These results highlight the importance of generator-aligned reward supervision and controlled, data-calibrated optimization for targeted visual generation.
items.author: Ziqiao Weng, Yuanzhi Liang, Haibing Huang, Weidong Cai, Xuelong Li
items.summary: The paper proposes GARM plus TABO: reward modeling that aligns supervision with the generator's output distribution and reduces content confounding via content-matched real contrasts, combined with bounded optimization to prevent reward overoptimization during post-training of visual generators. It addresses two chronic failure modes of reward-guided post-training. Co-author Xuelong Li adds credibility.
items.reasoning: Tackles well-recognized problems (distribution mismatch, reward hacking) in visual post-training with a two-part framework; timely given the RLHF-for-diffusion trend, though it is one of many concurrent reward-modeling proposals and unique advantages are unclear from the abstract.

items.title: IDPrior: Decoupling Identity Generation from Facial Image Synthesis
items.content: arXiv:2611.07941v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Large-scale identity-labeled face datasets are essential for training modern face recognition models, yet collecting and annotating such data is costly and raises privacy and ethical concerns. Existing synthetic face generation methods typically derive identities from predefined class labels, unconditional image generation, or predefined latent sampling strategies, without explicitly modeling the underlying distribution of facial identities. In this paper, we propose IDPrior, a two-stage framework that decouples identity generation from image synthesis. We first learn a diffusion prior in the embedding space of a pretrained face recognition model to model the distribution of facial identities and generate novel identity embeddings. These embeddings are then used to condition a pretrained identity-conditioned diffusion model (DM), enabling the synthesis of multiple images of the same identity. This modular design provides a scalable approach to identity generation while remaining compatible with existing and future identity-conditioned DMs. Experiments indicate that IDPrior generates diverse and well-separated identities while maintaining a closer correspondence to the distribution of authentic identities. Face recognition models trained on datasets generated using IDPrior-generated identities achieve competitive or improved performance compared with existing synthetic-data-based methods across multiple face verification benchmarks. Code and generated datasets are publicly available at https://github.com/fdbtrs/IDperturb.
items.author: Fadi Boutros, Meri\c{c} Demir\"ors, Darian Toma\v{s}evi\'c, Vitomir \v{S}truc, Naser Damer

This explicitly models the distribution of facial identities, unlike label-derived or unconditional approaches, and addresses privacy and cost issues of large identity-labeled face datasets. It aims to improve training data for face recognition models.
items.reasoning: Decoupling identity modeling from rendering is a conceptually clean approach to synthetic face data, an important problem for both utility and privacy. Face recognition data generation is well-studied, so gains may be incremental, but the identity-space diffusion prior is a sensible and reusable idea.

items.title: Spatiotemporal Dynamics-Aware Industrial Anomaly Detection and Reasoning
items.content: arXiv:2611.08080v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Industrial Anomaly Detection (IAD) is a long-established problem that aims to detect defects in industrial products during manufacturing for quality control. Most existing studies focus on static visual patterns as the basis for detection. However, in real manufacturing environments, many anomalies are dynamics-based, such as irregular movements that cannot be perceived from static cues alone. We observe that even recent Multimodal Large Language Model (MLLM)-based approaches fall short in identifying such dynamic anomalies due to limited temporal modeling capability. To address this, we introduce MUSTARD: MUltimodal SpatioTemporal Anomaly Reasoning and Detection, a framework that equips MLLMs with fine-grained spatiotemporal dynamics awareness for detecting and reasoning about dynamics-based defects. MUSTARD introduces optical-flow-guided keyframe selection and augmented modalities to capture critical motion irregularities through local motion patterns and global dynamic evolution. Its normal pattern-based reasoning pipeline requires only a few normal reference samples as the detection basis, avoiding any model updates. This enables efficient adaptation across various products and provides high decision interpretability. MUSTARD is the first MLLM-based framework for dynamics-based IAD. Experiments demonstrate its superior performance in detecting spatiotemporal anomalies and providing plausible explanations. The code will be made publicly available.

items.title: Reinforcing End-to-End Autonomous Driving Safety via Negative-Aware Planning in a Unified World-Action Model
items.content: arXiv:2611.08111v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: World-action models (WAMs) jointly model future traffic states and driving actions for end-to-end autonomous driving in intelligent transportation systems. However, their action learning remains dominated by expert-trajectory imitation, leaving unsafe alternatives close to expert trajectories insufficiently constrained. To improve WAM robustness in safety-critical scenarios, we propose NegWAM, a safety post-training framework for unified WAMs that learns explicit safety boundaries from near-expert failure trajectories. NegWAM constructs negative trajectories that are geometrically close to the expert trajectory yet carry safety risks, uses them as repulsive anchors to steer predictions away from dangerous behavior, and encodes them as scene-conditioned rider tokens to learn scene--trajectory compatibility. During training, NegWAM jointly optimizes the flow-matching and near-expert negative objectives, while the auxiliary rider branch is discarded at inference, incurring no additional overhead. On NAVSIM v2, NegWAM achieves 40.4 EPDMS on navhard, a 4.1% relative improvement over the strongest compared scorer-free WAM baseline, and achieves 93.3 EPDMS on navtest. These results demonstrate that NegWAM achieves strong performance in safety-critical scenarios while preserving routine-driving performance. Zero-shot closed-loop evaluation on HUGSIM further demonstrates cross-benchmark generalization. The code is available at https://github.com/Zizizi-hao/NegWAM.

items.title: A Unified Fractal Impedance Control Framework
items.content: arXiv:2611.08009v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Physical human--robot interaction requires controllers capable of maintaining intrinsically bounded interactions with the environment. The Fractal Impedance Controller (FIC) has been proven to guarantee these safety characteristics by design. This paper introduces the robotic implementation and experimental validation of its most advanced architecture: the Harmonic-Passive Motion Paradigm (H-PMP), an evolution of the Passive Motion Paradigm designed to mimic human-like interaction. Furthermore, we present a unified framework for FIC deployment, supported by an open-source software suite featuring ROS2, MuJoCo, and physical hardware integrations. Through three experiments conducted on a Kinova Gen3 arm (trajectory tracking, a wall press with sudden loss of contact, and learning-by-demonstration) we compare the H-PMP against earlier FIC architectures. The results demonstrate that the H-PMP achieves a seamless trade-off between admittance and impedance behaviours. This makes it ideal for deployment in unstructured environments, enabling the robot to transition between interaction modes with no computational overhead.
items.author: Adnan Takriti, Mahmoud Sadeq, Quentin Rouxel, Daniele Cafolla, Michael Mistry, Carlo Tiseo
items.summary: This paper presents the robotic implementation and experimental validation of the Harmonic-Passive Motion Paradigm built on the Fractal Impedance Controller, which guarantees bounded, safe physical interaction by design. It also releases an open-source deployment framework integrating ROS2, MuJoCo, and physical hardware, validated on a Kinova Gen3 across tracking and interaction tasks. Intrinsically safe interaction control with open tooling is valuable for pHRI research.

The Fractal Impedance Controller (FIC) has been proven to guarantee these safety characteristics by design. This paper introduces the robotic implementation and experimental validation of its most advanced architecture: the Harmonic-Passive Motion Paradigm (H-PMP), an evolution of the Passive Motion Paradigm designed to mimic human-like interaction. Furthermore, we present a unified framework for FIC deployment, supported by an open-source software suite featuring ROS2, MuJoCo, and physical hardware integrations. Through three experiments conducted on a Kinova Gen3 arm (trajectory tracking, a wall press with sudden loss of contact, and learning-by-demonstration) we compare the H-PMP against earlier FIC architectures. The results demonstrate that the H-PMP achieves a seamless trade-off between admittance and impedance behaviours. This makes it ideal for deployment in unstructured environments, enabling the robot to transition between interaction modes with no computational overhead.

items.title: Near-Minimax Sample Complexity for Multi-Objective Reinforcement Learning under Generative Models
items.content: arXiv:2611.05562v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: In multi-objective reinforcement learning, preferences may be specified only after data collection, requiring one dataset to support a continuum of reward trade-offs. We study finite discounted Markov decision processes with unknown transitions, $S$ states, $A$ actions, and $m$ known reward functions taking values in $[0,1]$, given access to a generative model. The learner must provide an $\varepsilon$-optimal policy for every convex combination of these rewards without further sampling, with a guarantee that holds simultaneously over all preferences and initial states. Writing $H=(1-\gamma)^{-1}$, we establish the constant-confidence minimax sample complexity $\widetilde\Theta\!\left(   \frac{SAH^3}{\varepsilon^2}\min\{S,\log(em)\} \right)$, where the suppressed factors are logarithmic in $S,A,H,\varepsilon^{-1}$ and the dependence on $m$ is explicit. Thus, up to these logarithmic factors, the worst-case statistical cost of supporting all preferences grows logarithmically with the number of objectives and saturates at the number of states. The upper bound uses uniform state--action sampling and empirical planning, with reward rounding in the logarithmic-objective regime. Its analysis chains optimal-value increments over covers of the reward hull. A one-sided Bellman variance bound controls signed value differences under a second transition kernel, preserving the $H^3\varepsilon^{-2}$ dependence. A complementary uniform guarantee for all bounded rewards yields the state-dimension saturation. We establish lower bounds matching up to logarithmic factors through a rare-exit construction with subset rewards and action encoding. These bounds apply to adaptive simulator queries and arbitrary randomized history-dependent output policies, while the upper bounds are attained by deterministic stationary policies.
items.author: Yue Wang
items.summary: This paper establishes the constant-confidence minimax sample complexity for multi-objective RL in finite discounted MDPs with a generative model, where one dataset must support an epsilon-optimal policy for every convex combination of m reward functions. The resulting Theta-tilted bound of SAH^3/eps^2 times min{S, log(em)} matches upper bounds and resolves how the number of objectives enters the complexity.
items.reasoning: A clean theoretical resolution of a well-posed problem in multi-objective RL, with a minimax-matching result that clarifies the (surprisingly mild) dependence on the number of objectives. Rigorous and relevant to preference-conditioned RL, but confined to the generative-model setting and tabular MDPs.

items.title: Efficient Lempel-Ziv Prediction with the Run-Length BWT
items.content:
The Lempel-Ziv parse of Chad Gadya (חד גדיא), right-to-left, drawn as an arc diagram. Generated by Claude Opus 5.5

I have published a new paper on efficient string prediction. It was written during the PIBBSS 2026 summer fellowship, under the mentorship of Vanessa Kosoy.

This research builds on Kosoy's previous work in stringology. Kosoy built a polynomial-time algorithm for predicting repetitive sequences and I have used other algorithmic techniques to further decrease the runtime.

The goal of this post is to explain some of the ideas from Kosoy's paper and how my work builds on them. My writing will be mostly informal; the field of string algorithms has a lot of technical jargon which I will not try to fully explain. I hope to mostly communicate interesting ideas and topics I've bumped into during the research, while linking to external resources for anyone who wishes to learn more.

## The prediction trinity

There are three things we want every good predictor to have:

- Power: can predict general, real-world patterns.

- Efficiency: can run in practice.

- Formal guarantees: we can prove what it can or can't do.

Unfortunately, no framework today satisfies all three properties at once.

Deep learning is powerful and efficient, but lacks a strong framework of formal guarantees. (This might be a problem!)

Solomonoff induction / AIXI are extremely powerful, and have formal guarantees, but can't actually run in practice.

My research is on the third edge: efficient algorithms with formal guarantees, though ones that are still not powerful enough for "actual" intelligence....

items.title: Adapting the Process of Adaptation: Darwinian, Lamarckian, and Agent-Directed Evolution in AI
items.content: arXiv:2611.07048v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Evolution has shaped intelligence for billions of years. Artificial intelligence (AI) now raises a striking possibility: intelligence may begin to direct its own evolution. As AI agents become capable of modifying and evaluating their own behavior, how quickly could they improve, and how can that improvement remain safe? We develop a theoretical framework comparing Darwinian, Lamarckian, and agent-directed evolution following environmental change. Darwinian evolution relies on natural selection, Lamarckian evolution adds inherited learning, and agent-directed evolution allows agents to generate and evaluate behavioral variants and choose how extensively to search. When learning is sufficiently effective, these mechanisms exhibit progressively faster adaptation. Generating more variants accelerates adaptation, while optimal search effort depends on learning ability, problem difficulty, and experimentation costs. However, an agent's ability to direct its improvement does not ensure that improvements are evaluated against the intended objective. When the evaluation target is misspecified, additional search accelerates convergence toward the wrong behavior, even as measured performance improves. In recursive self-improvement, such errors may persist across generations, posing challenges for AI safety. Independent evaluation and oversight must keep pace with autonomous AI development. The central challenge is not simply to accelerate the evolution of intelligence, but to preserve humanity's ability to guide its direction, limit its speed, and intervene when necessary.
items.author: Andrew W. Lo, Chaoyi Zhao
items.summary: The authors build a theoretical framework comparing Darwinian, Lamarckian, and agent-directed evolution in AI agents that can modify and evaluate their own behavior after environmental change. items.reasoning: Timely theoretical framing of self-improving AI through an evolutionary lens, from credible authors (including Andrew Lo at MIT), with direct relevance to safety of recursive self-improvement. Purely theoretical, so empirical grounding is absent.

items.title: Adaptive Semantic Branching: Disagreement-Localized Cross-Trajectory Regeneration for Reasoning Candidate Expansion
items.content: arXiv:2611.07918v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Reasoning trajectories generated for the same problem often arrive at conflicting answers. These disagreements reveal alternative intermediate decisions that can be reused to explore new solutions. We introduce Adaptive Semantic Branching (ASB), a training-free inference procedure that turns cross-trajectory disagreement into targeted candidate generation. ASB first groups independently sampled trajectories by extracted final answer, selects a representative from each group, and aligns their reasoning steps with a monotonic dynamic program. A persistent-divergence objective identifies the point at which initially similar reasoning paths develop different continuations. For each selected directed pair, ASB retains the source trajectory's textual prefix, extracts a short reasoning window from a competing donor trajectory, and generates a fresh solution conditioned on both. A diversity-aware policy allocates up to three additional generations according to the answer-cluster structure. In a 500-problem MATH evaluation with Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, ASB increases oracle candidate coverage from 445/500 (89.0%) with seven initial samples to 455/500 (91.0%), recovering correct candidates for 10 of the 55 initially uncovered problems. The method uses 576 additional generation calls across the evaluation set, averaging 8.152 calls per problem. We provide a precise specification of the branching operator, alignment objective, generation policy, and experimental configuration.
items.author: Jeong-Yoon Kim, Tae-Yoon Lee
items.summary: ASB is a training-free inference procedure that exploits disagreements between independently sampled reasoning trajectories: it groups trajectories by final answer, aligns reasoning steps with a monotonic dynamic program, identifies persistent divergence points, and regenerates targeted candidates from those points. This converts cross-trajectory conflict into efficient candidate expansion for reasoning. It aims to improve inference-time compute efficiency without training.
items.reasoning: The core idea of using trajectory disagreement to localize where reasoning paths diverge and regenerate only there is elegant and fits the active inference-time-scaling research direction. Effectiveness depends on empirical gains over simpler best-of-n and verifier baselines, which the abstract does not establish convincingly.

items.title: More Agents, More Reliable? System-Level Reliability of Multi-Agent LLMs under Operational-Profile Uncertainty
items.content: arXiv:2611.07140v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Teams increasingly build software from cooperating large language model (LLM) agents, often assuming more agents mean more reliability. Yet the usual evidence, average benchmark accuracy, ignores the input mix a deployed system meets and the rule merging the agents' answers. Building on HIP-LLM, a hierarchical imprecise-probability assessment of single LLMs, we propose a framework combining it with a Bayesian network of the system's failure logic for multi-agent systems. Agent failure-probability intervals propagate through this network, where the combining rule can itself fail, into a reliability envelope showing which evidence limits it. In a pipeline extracting regulated chemical-hazard statements, majority voting over three models protected against the weakest but did not clearly exceed the best, and a voter failing on 5\% of demands would largely erase its advantage over the middle model. More agents yield a more defensible reliability claim, not automatically a more reliable system.
items.author: Burkay Tun\c{c}t\"urk, Koorosh Aslansefat, Yiannis Papadopoulos, Bao Nguyen
items.summary: Proposes a framework combining hierarchical imprecise-probability assessment of individual LLMs with a Bayesian network of system failure logic to produce reliability envelopes for multi-agent LLM systems under operational-profile uncertainty. A chemical-hazard extraction case study shows majority voting over three models can produce safety-critical degradation, challenging the assumption that more agents means more reliability.
items.reasoning: Addresses a real and underexplored gap: principled, safety-engineering-grounded reliability analysis for multi-agent LLM systems rather than average benchmark accuracy. The imprecise-probability plus Bayesian network methodology is sound, though the empirical scope is a single pipeline case study.

items.title: Permanent and Transient Representations for Continual Reinforcement Learning
items.content: arXiv:2611.07327v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Continual Reinforcement Learning (CRL) agents struggle to adapt to new situations while retaining prior knowledge, leading to a stability-plasticity trade-off. One approach to solving this problem is by using complementary learning systems: one for slow, long-term learning and another for quick, transient adaptation. Anand & Precup (2023) instantiated this idea using permanent and transient value functions, but used the same features in both systems. Intuitively, long-term learning should rely more on parametric representations for broad generalization, while transient learning would be best served by non-parametric representations for situation-specific adaptation. In this paper, we explore this idea both theoretically and empirically. By introducing a novel non-parametric approximation for estimating the transient value function in complex tasks, we demonstrate that our method enables online learning and outperforms competitive baselines on image-based tasks and Craftax-Classic, underscoring the effectiveness of our system-level decomposition.
items.author: Nishanth Anand, Doina Precup
items.summary: The paper extends complementary learning systems for continual RL by using different representation types for each system: parametric representations for slow long-term learning and non-parametric representations for fast transient adaptation. Anand and Precup provide both theoretical and empirical support for this asymmetry, building on their earlier permanent/transient value function work. It addresses the stability-plasticity trade-off in continual RL.
items.reasoning: Doina Precup's involvement lends strong credibility, and the theoretical-plus-empirical treatment of representation asymmetry in complementary learning systems is a clean conceptual advance. Still a fairly specialized contribution within continual RL rather than a broadly disruptive result.

items.title: IMUDINO: Self-distilled Foundation Model for Inertial Sensing
items.content: arXiv:2611.07437v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: We present IMUDINO, the first foundation model (FM) for inertial sensing to achieve competitive performance across diverse sensing tasks including human activity recognition (HAR), health, motion capture, and odometry. Prior inertial FMs often focus on one subfield of inertial sensing and sometimes underperform state-of-the-art supervised methods (e.g., in HAR), making their scope considerably narrower than FMs for vision and natural language. Moreover, they often require fixed input length and sampling rate, and generalize poorly to unseen sensor locations. To build a general-purpose foundation model for inertial sensing, we adapt the DINO self-supervised learning (SSL) paradigm to inertial data through a set of semantics-preserving motion transformations that simulate variations in motion pattern and sensor setup. For model architecture, we use a plain transformer encoder with frequency-aware positional encoding that natively supports varying input length and sampling rate. This simple setup proved remarkably effective for learning global and dense features generalizable across users, sensor setups, tasks, and, in the case of robot odometry, embodiments. We hope IMUDINO can serve as a backbone for inertial sensing and kickstart the development of general-purpose inertial FMs.
items.author: Zhoutong Ye, Chengwen Zhang, Zixuan Wang, Xufeng Jian, Zhe He, Qingyang Wan, Xutong Wang, Jiaqi Liu, Mingze Sun, Yu Mei, Chun Yu, Yuanchun Shi
items.summary: IMUDINO is presented as the first foundation model for inertial sensing to achieve competitive performance across diverse tasks including human activity recognition, health monitoring, motion capture, and odometry. It adapts the DINO self-supervised paradigm to IMU data using semantics-preserving motion augmentations, and handles variable input lengths, sampling rates, and unseen sensor locations better than prior narrow inertial models. This narrows the gap between inertial sensing and vision/language foundation models.
items.reasoning: Genuinely useful generalization contribution in an underserved modality, with a clear SSL adaptation and broad task coverage. The DINO-to-IMU transfer is more adaptation than architectural novelty, and hardware-sensing research typically has a smaller immediate audience, but multimodal and embodied AI relevance is growing.

items.title: GraspBench: Execution-Aware Cross-Robot Evaluation of 6-DoF Grasp Generation in MuJoCo
items.content: arXiv:2611.07651v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Modern 6-DoF grasp generators are often evaluated using grasp scores, dataset-level metrics, or single-robot demonstrations, yet proposal quality alone does not determine whether a grasp is executable by a particular robot. We present GraspBench, a controlled MuJoCo protocol for evaluating complete grasp-generation pipelines after robot-specific inverse-kinematics filtering, motion planning, and fixed approach-close-lift execution. GraspBench evaluates six configured pipelines across four robot embodiments, five diagnostic objects, and a structured tabletop pose grid, yielding 540 scenarios per method and 3,240 method-scenario evaluations in total. Missing outputs are conservatively counted as failures, and success follows the binary lift criterion produced by each method's execution runner. GraspGen achieves the highest overall success rate (73.1%), followed by EconomicGrasp (63.5%), while robot- and object-conditioned analyses reveal substantial variation across embodiments and object geometries. GPG produces the largest native candidate sets but achieves 44.3% success, indicating that proposal volume alone does not guarantee robot-executable grasps. Cluster-aware paired intervals support the principal method differences while not estimating repeated-execution uncertainty. The results characterize complete configured pipelines on fixed scenarios rather than intrinsic model quality or stochastic repeatability, showing that grasping performance depends jointly on the generator, robot embodiment, scene, and execution protocol.

items.title: THG-Omni: Traceable Human-Centric Graph Supervision for Video Reasoning
items.content: arXiv:2611.07836v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Omni-modal models can answer questions about video, but their predictions rarely show which participant, event, or interval supports an answer. Moreover, answer-level supervision alone does not teach a model to interpret structured video evidence. To systematically mitigate this issue, we present THG-Omni, a human-centric graph-supervision framework that links Segment Anything Model~3 participant tracks with temporally grounded Qwen3-VL annotations. Candidate semantic claims are checked against the source video and available audio before they are used to construct training questions, while track geometry provides explicit spatial and temporal supervision. The resulting questions teach an omni-modal reasoning model to interpret participant attributes, actions, affect, interactions, and their timing from a structured graph. At inference, THG-Omni uses a predicted graph constructed from the evaluation video. Experiments on IntentBench show consistent improvements over the unadapted backbone across social reasoning, emotion understanding, and deception perception. On NExT-QA, THG-Omni achieves 89.54\% accuracy with the matched graph, compared with 85.10\% without graph input. Further validation experiments show that compact graph input achieves 78.22\% accuracy, compared with 78.02\% using the full graph and 77.58\% without graph input. A complementary diagnostic demonstrates that the predicted graph preserves evidence useful for answering questions even without the source video and audio. Together, these findings show that THG-Omni improves human-centric video reasoning while grounding its evidence in identifiable participants and events. Our codes are available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/review-n94hhfcwp5666/
items.author: Jisheng Dang, Kai Wei, Ronghao Lin, Bimei Wang, Hong Peng, Wei-Shi Zheng, Bin Hu, Qi Tian, Tat-Seng Chua
items.summary: THG-Omni constructs traceable human-centric graph supervision for omni-modal video reasoning by linking SAM 3 participant tracks with temporally grounded Qwen3-VL annotations, verifying candidate claims against source video and audio before use. This teaches models to cite which participant, event, and interval supports an answer, addressing the traceability gap in video question answering. It matters for trustworthy multimodal reasoning with structured evidence supervision.
items.reasoning: A substantial data-and-supervision contribution from a strong author group (including Qi Tian and Tat-Seng Chua) addressing an important interpretability problem in video reasoning; leveraging existing SAM 3 and Qwen3-VL rather than novel modeling slightly limits architectural novelty.

items.content_html: arXiv:2611.07836v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Omni-modal models can answer questions about video, but their predictions rarely show which participant, event, or interval supports an answer. Moreover, answer-level supervision alone does not teach a model to interpret structured video evidence. To systematically mitigate this issue, we present THG-Omni, a human-centric graph-supervision framework that links Segment Anything Model~3 participant tracks with temporally grounded Qwen3-VL annotations. Candidate semantic claims are checked against the source video and available audio before they are used to construct training questions, while track geometry provides explicit spatial and temporal supervision. The resulting questions teach an omni-modal reasoning model to interpret participant attributes, actions, affect, interactions, and their timing from a structured graph. At inference, THG-Omni uses a predicted graph constructed from the evaluation video. Experiments on IntentBench show consistent improvements over the unadapted backbone across social reasoning, emotion understanding, and deception perception. On NExT-QA, THG-Omni achieves 89.54\% accuracy with the matched graph, compared with 85.10\% without graph input. Further validation experiments show that compact graph input achieves 78.22\% accuracy, compared with 78.02\% using the full graph and 77.58\% without graph input. A complementary diagnostic demonstrates that the predicted graph preserves evidence useful for answering questions even without the source video and audio. Together, these findings show that THG-Omni improves human-centric video reasoning while grounding its evidence in identifiable participants and events. Our codes are available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/review-n94hhfcwp5666/

items.title: Machine Learning for Live-Birth Prediction After IVF/ICSI From Structured Clinical Data: A Systematic Review, Meta-Analysis, and Critical Appraisal
items.content: arXiv:2611.07124v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Machine-learning models predicting live birth after in vitro fertilisation (IVF) or intracytoplasmic sperm injection (ICSI) from routine clinical data report performance from near chance to near perfect. We systematically reviewed these models under PRISMA 2020, searching OpenAlex, Scopus and Web of Science to 22 October 2026, appraised them with PROBAST+AI and TRIPOD+AI, and pooled their discrimination with random-effects meta-analysis on the logit scale. We define what fixes the meaning of a model's output (decision point, endpoint, unit of analysis, data source) and map the 48 included studies by model family, decision point and validation design. Models evaluated only internally pooled to an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.814, against 0.756 (95% prediction interval 0.546-0.889) for models evaluated on a later period or another centre, and 0.764 for studies not at high risk of bias; neither difference was significant, and heterogeneity was extreme. Models whose decision point was not stated pooled to 0.910, the only significant moderator in meta-regression. Against logistic regression fitted to the same data, the best machine-learning model gained a pooled 0.056 AUC (95% CI 0.017-0.090). Of 48 studies, 47 were at high or unclear risk of bias, only four assessed the calibration slope, and no model has evidence of clinical impact. The certainty of the pooled evidence is low to very low; the gains that survive validation came from staging predictions to decision points and local calibration, not deeper architectures. We provide a TRIPOD+AI-mapped checklist, a benchmark specification and a research agenda.
items.author: Abdul Raheem Shahzad, Muhammad Zaheer Khan, Umar Ajaib, Asad Ur Rehman, Juan Deng, Ming Zhang
items.summary: A systematic review and meta-analysis of 48 studies using machine learning to predict live birth after IVF/ICSI from structured clinical data, appraised with PRISMA 2020, PROBAST+AI, and TRIPOD+AI standards. The authors pool discrimination metrics and define standardized semantics for model outputs, decision points, and validation designs. It exposes wide performance variability and likely methodological weaknesses in this clinical ML literature.
items.reasoning: Rigorous, standards-based appraisal of a clinically important application area; meta-analyses of this kind are highly useful for steering the field, though as a review it introduces no new methods.

items.title: Loopback Transformer: Towards a Unified View of Residual Looped Transformers
items.content: arXiv:2611.07226v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Looped Transformers reduce parameter count by repeatedly applying shared blocks, but parameter sharing alone does not determine how the results of repeated computation are reused. We take the depth-memory view of residual connections and analyze which representation is stored after each block application and how later reads weight it. A full block output contains both its input and its new update, so weighting that output also reweights the history already carried by the input. Reading individual updates instead, with the shared stack's input kept on a separate path, gives separate controls over input strength, total update weight, and allocation across updates. The Loopback Transformer implements these controls: geometric decay sets the total update weight and supplies a recency prior, and attention learns how to allocate that weight. On ClimbMix, Loopback reaches lower validation loss than standard Transformer baselines with 40-75% of their Transformer parameters (excluding token embeddings and the output head) at reference scales from 191M to 3B, with training tokens and executed depth matched. It also has higher mean accuracy over thirteen downstream tasks at 1.4B and 3B. At 191M, 374M, and 778M, it has the lowest validation loss and the highest thirteen-task mean among the standard Transformer and seven looped residual designs.
items.author: Xuan Ouyang, Zefan Cai, Chenlong Zhang, Cheng Luo, Ke Wan, Junjie Hu
items.summary: The Loopback Transformer analyzes residual looped transformers through a depth-memory lens, separating how repeated computation results are stored and re-read. By keeping the shared stack's input on a separate path and reading individual updates with geometric decay, it gains independent control over input strength, total update weight, and allocation across updates. This offers both a conceptual unification and a parameter-efficient architecture variant.
items.reasoning: Provides a clean conceptual framework for residual looped transformers plus a concrete architecture; relevant to parameter-efficient recurrent-depth models, though looped transformers remain a minority approach and empirical strength is unclear.

items.title: AtlasULP: Domain-aware Universal Link Prediction via Relation Atlas
items.content: arXiv:2611.07347v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Link prediction (LP) is a widely applied task in graph learning. Conventional LP approaches typically follow a dataset-specific paradigm, requiring independent training for each graph and incurring high computational and maintenance costs in large-scale applications. Motivated by these limitations, recent work explores Universal Link Prediction (ULP), aiming to enable training-free inference on arbitrary unseen graphs. However, existing methods primarily rely on subgraph sampling strategies to construct universal representations, which are unable to capture higher-order information due to the exponential growth of higher-order neighborhoods. As a result, they often under-perform on graphs where long-range signals are essential, such as biological networks. Moreover, their prediction models are typically domain-agnostic and lack the ability to adapt to different graph domains, leading to limited generalization. To address these challenges, we propose an Atlas-based Universal Link Prediction framework (AtlasULP), which introduces the relation atlas to capture structural associations between node pairs from both global and local perspectives, enabling a comprehensive characterization of connectivity signals across diverse graph domains. Building upon this representation, we develop a domain-guided prompting ULP model, which generates domain-aware prompt tokens from contextual structures and performs prompt-guided in-context prediction for adaptive link inference. Extensive experiments demonstrate that AtlasULP consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods across diverse graph domains.
items.author: Yujing Liu, Yixin Liu, Yu Zheng, Lianhua Chi, Alan Wee-Chung Liew, Heng Tao Shen, Shirui Pan
items.summary: AtlasULP addresses universal link prediction, enabling training-free inference on unseen graphs, by replacing subgraph sampling with a relation atlas that captures higher-order structural information without exponential neighborhood growth. This improves performance on graphs where long-range signals matter, such as biological networks. It reduces the cost of per-graph model training at scale.
items.reasoning: A sensible advance over sampling-based universal link prediction with good motivation from cross-domain generalization; the higher-order representation is the key novelty but impact is confined to the graph-learning community.

items.title: EnergyBench: a live, gate-aligned benchmark of day-ahead forecasts for European power markets
items.content: arXiv:2611.07784v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Energy forecasting models are usually compared on backtests and fixed public datasets. Backtests can use data that did not yet exist when the forecast would have been made, and a fixed test set, reused across studies and possibly contained in the pretraining data of foundation models, invites overfitting to the benchmark. EnergyBench evaluates every entry live instead. Each day at 11:30 CET/CEST, thirty minutes before the day-ahead (SDAC) gate closes, every model forecasts the next day's price, wind and solar generation and load on the 15-minute grid for six bidding zones (BE, NL, FR, DE-LU, DK1, DK2). Unlike existing live benchmarks, EnergyBench runs the models itself, on one information set that it freezes at the cut-off and publishes, including three numerical weather prediction models, so that foundation models can be compared with and without the same weather covariates under the actual market deadline. Errors are pooled per series against a seasonal-naive baseline, and models are ranked by a Bradley-Terry rating on the Elo scale with a day-bootstrap interval. The field spans baselines, linear and gradient-boosted models on the frozen weather, eighteen time-series foundation models from eleven families, ensembles, and the grid operators' own forecasts. Over the first thirty-two live days, the covariates reduced the error of each of the ten foundation models run with and without them by 37-51% on matched races (64-73% on wind, 48-61% on solar). Used zero-shot, these models match or outperform a LightGBM model trained on the same covariates. Model size, from 3M to 331M parameters, has a much smaller effect, and median ensembles of the covariate models rank highest. The grid operators' pre-gate forecasts remain ahead on wind and solar, where the best single foundation models have 16-22% more error; on load the gap is 4-6%, within the intervals.
items.author: Evgenii Genov, Ander Martinez Alonso, Christoph Bergmeir
items.summary: EnergyBench evaluates day-ahead energy forecasting models live rather than on backtests: each day at 11:30 CET, thirty minutes before the day-ahead market gate closes, participating models forecast next-day price, wind, solar, and load across six European bidding zones on a 15-minute grid. Unlike existing live benchmarks, it runs the models itself on a frozen, published information set, eliminating look-ahead leakage and benchmark overfitting. This addresses fundamental flaws in how energy forecasting is usually compared.
items.reasoning: Methodologically rigorous live-benchmark design with real-world operational relevance for energy markets; impact is domain-specific but the anti-leakage design is exemplary.

items.title: A Proxy-Based Method for Measuring Racial Disparities in~Text-to-Image~Generators
items.content: arXiv:2611.07132v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: We present an automated method for auditing text-to-image generators for representational bias against ground-truth demographic benchmarks. Our approach adapts the racial proxy variables used in U.S. antidiscrimination law to provide a fine-grained comparative analysis of variations in racial representation in generated images. We classify each generated image by race and then compare the model's distribution to publicly available demographic benchmark data to identify patterns of over- and under-representation. We also measure skin tone using CIELAB values and calculate cosine similarity amongst groups of images in order to capture biases that don't show up in demographic comparisons such as differences in image quality across races and skin tones. We report on experiments testing three models (Imagen 4 Fast, Stable Diffusion 3.5 Large Turbo, and Flux Schnell) using three categories of proxies (geographic, occupational, and surname) and 50 variants within each category. We find notable variation across the models as well as by proxy category. For example, Imagen 4 Fast overrepresents white classified images more than the other models tested and produces images with lighter, more homogeneous skin tones. Imagen 4 Fast also had the largest representational disparity for Black demographics among surname and geographical prompts. Stable Diffusion 3.5 Large Turbo produces results that overall diverge most from census data but yield the most diverse range of skin tones. Our method yields a generalizable and legally-grounded auditing tool that surfaces detailed information about model outputs without relying on implicit normative definitions of fairness.

It additionally measures skin tone via CIELAB values and image-group similarity to capture quality and homogeneity biases beyond demographic counts.
items.reasoning: Well-grounded fairness auditing methodology with a thoughtful legal framing and multi-signal measurement (demographics, skin tone, image quality). Impactful for AI accountability, though auditing approaches in this space are numerous.

items.title: TACT-KV: Tri-Axis Cosine Transform for Compressing Volumetric KV Caches in Medical VLMs
items.content: arXiv:2611.07593v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) applied to 3D medical scans face a structural memory wall. A single CT or MRI volume produces tens of thousands of vision tokens, and the resulting key-value (KV) cache scales linearly with both batch and context. Existing KV compression methods operate on the cache's feature or token statistics, or apply 1D and 2D transforms, leaving the three-axis spatial structure in the cache unexploited. We propose TACT-KV (Tri-Axis Cosine Transform), a calibration-free KV compression method that exploits strong spatial correlations in visual KV states along all three anatomical axes of 3D scans. This correlation concentrates the KV cache energy under a frequency-domain transform. TACT-KV applies a separable 3D discrete cosine transform to the KV cache, allocates a per-layer bit budget across frequency bins via reverse water-filling (more bits to high-energy components), and quantizes each bin with a fixed scalar codebook. We derive a close-form relation: the distortion reduction from adaptive bit allocation is dominated by the spectral concentration of the transformed cache. Across six medical VLMs and two 3D CT benchmarks, TACT-KV achieves the lowest 1-bit prediction-flip rate on eleven of twelve model and dataset pairs in our main comparison. The same advantage reproduces on four general-purpose VLMs evaluated on video tasks, indicating that the benefit of exploiting three-axis structure generalizes beyond medical imaging. At equal high-bandwidth memory (HBM), TACT-KV scales the decoding batch size on a single GPU by up to $8\times$.

items.title: Unifying Central Flow, Rod Flow, and the Edge Coupling
items.content: arXiv:2611.08358v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: At the edge of stability, the iterates of gradient descent oscillate along the sharp directions of the Hessian. This poses a significant challenge for continuous-time models as the usual continuous-time approximation -- the gradient flow -- admits no oscillations. Several continuous-time models have been proposed to capture the behavior at the edge of stability, among them central flow and rod flow. Although both models can be interpreted as performing a coarse-graining in time, the connection between them remains poorly understood. Here we show that both flows can be derived from a third object, the edge coupling: a functional on consecutive iterates whose critical points are the fixed points and period-two orbits of gradient descent. It is revealed that the two flows correspond to coarse-grainings at different time scales. Rod flow coarse-grains over only the fastest time scale, while central flow coarse-grains over both the fast and intermediate time scales. Furthermore, using the edge coupling, we derive rod flows and central flows for momentum methods such as heavy ball and Adam. We verify the derived flows experimentally on representative neural network architectures, where they track the discrete iterates throughout all phases of training -- including the transition from the stable regime to the edge of stability.
items.author: Eric Regis, Sinho Chewi
items.summary: This theory paper unifies continuous-time models of gradient descent at the edge of stability, showing that central flow and rod flow can both be derived from a common object called the edge coupling, a functional on consecutive iterates whose critical points capture fixed points and period-two orbits. This clarifies how oscillatory training dynamics, which gradient flow cannot capture, should be modeled. It matters for the theoretical understanding of why deep networks train stably despite sharp curvature.
items.reasoning: A clean theoretical unification from credible authors (Chewi is an established optimization theorist), advancing the edge-of-stability literature. The contribution is foundational rather than immediately practical, so applied impact is indirect, but the conceptual clarity is significant for optimization theory.

items.title: Adapting Qwen3 to Tajik from 0.6B to 8B: Lower Text Loss Did Not Mean Better Understanding
items.content: arXiv:2611.06062v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Small LoRA adapters trained on Tajik news and books lowered Qwen3's Tajik text loss at every size we tried, from 0.6B to 8B, by 0.60 to 1.45 nats per token, but none of them improved Tajik reading comprehension where it can be measured. On Belebele the 1.7B and 8B adapters left accuracy unchanged and the 4B adapter lowered it by 3.7 points; at 0.6B the score rose by 4.2 points but sits near chance and coincides with a change in which answer letter the model prefers, so we do not read it as understanding. At 8B, continued pretraining on about 375 million tokens of raw Tajik text was followed by a Belebele gain of 9.9 points. After a further supervised fine-tuning stage, our main model, e3, is 11.4 points above Qwen3-8B on Belebele; its English MMLU changed by -1.2 points, and a loss larger than 3.3 points is excluded. The same heavy recipe applied to Qwen3-0.6B-Base brought its text loss close to that of the 8B model after books-only pretraining, while its multiple-choice answers stayed near chance and its English MMLU fell by 7.6 points. We report 15 trained models and their 5 starting models from June to October 2025, scored in 2026 on one harness with paired intervals, and we report what went wrong: lost training records, a thinking-mode dataset with almost no reasoning in it, later branches whose training data was never documented, and a 4-bit release that contains no transformer layers.
items.author: Tohir Saidzoda, Madina Abdusalomzoda, Nasimjon Rajabov, Akhrorkhon Ikromov, Komron Giyosiev, Abubakr Abdullozoda, Amin Jalilov, Jonibek Kishvarov, Rahmonali Sharipov, Mariyamkhon Shodyeva
items.summary: A systematic study adapting Qwen3 models (0.6B to 8B) to Tajik with LoRA adapters, showing reduced Tajik text loss did not improve reading comprehension on Belebele, while continued pretraining plus supervised fine-tuning yielded an 11.4-point gain. It demonstrates that loss reduction from cheap adapters is a misleading proxy for capability.
