items.title: CardioLM: A multilingual suite of small language models for the cardiology domain
items.content: arXiv:2611.07940v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Background: Cardiovascular care generates large volumes of clinical free-text documentation in local languages. However, clinical natural language processing (NLP) resources remain concentrated in English, and no existing benchmark is cardiology-specific, multilingual, and broad in entity coverage.   Methods: We present two contributions. The first is CardioCCC, a corpus of 508 cardiology case reports originally published in Spanish and extended to Czech, Dutch, English, Italian, Romanian, and Swedish through machine translation, annotation projection, and clinician review, with annotations covering diseases, symptoms, procedures, and medications. The second is CardioLM, comprising CardioBERTa, a set of language-specific encoders obtained by continued pretraining on cardiology and biomedical corpora, and CardioNER, a set of named entity recognition (NER) models fine-tuned on CardioCCC.   Results: Cardiology-specific pretraining reduced pseudo-perplexity by up to a factor of eight, yet changed strict span-level F1 by at most 0.04, with benefits concentrated in languages whose backbones lacked biomedical coverage. The jointly trained multilingual XLM-RoBERTa-large models achieved the best strict F1 in nearly every language and entity type, exceeding the strongest monolingual system by up to 0.13 F1. A large share of residual errors concerned boundary detection: relaxed matching recovered 0.10-0.23 F1 for disease, procedure, and symptom, but only 0.01-0.07 for medication. Clinicians rated CardioNER well above a rule- and dictionary-based baseline, with the mean rating across entity types rising from 26% to 73%.   Conclusions: Specialty-specific pretraining is not the decisive factor for downstream entity recognition, whereas multilingual joint training yields the strongest results in nearly all settings and a simpler deployment path for multi-country clinical information extraction.

items.title: FedReason: Large Language Models as Weight-Space Meta-Aggregators for Heterogeneous Federated Learning
items.content: arXiv:2611.08383v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Federated learning servers combine client models with a fixed aggregation rule, and each rule in common use is designed for one kind of heterogeneity. We study whether a large language model (LLM) that inspects the client models can choose the rule itself, without any training on the server. In FedReason, the LLM is called every ten rounds. It analyses the weights by running code in a restricted server-side sandbox, sees only the printed results, may score a few candidates on a 500-image proxy set, and submits a short Python aggregation program. The server applies the program until the next call and falls back to FedAvg whenever its output is invalid. Full weight tensors never leave the server. We evaluated FedReason with Claude Opus 5.5 on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 with ResNet-18 under Dirichlet label skew, width-heterogeneous sub-models and Byzantine clients, in 168 runs against 14 baselines. Across 12 paired label-skew runs it beat FedAvg by 1.26 percentage points on average (10 wins), and a control that spends the same per-round proxy budget on choosing among standard rules by 1.08 points. It was the strongest server-side rule on CIFAR-100 but did not beat SCAFFOLD, which changes client training. With three of ten clients malicious, it excluded all sign-flipping clients from the first round and stayed about one point below FLTrust without training a root model. Without proxy feedback, accuracy fell from 73.8% to 38.8% in one seed. A 60-round run cost 0.79 USD in API fees on average.

items.title: SteelAgent: LLM-Orchestrated, Physics-Informed Steel Property Prediction with Audited Generalization and Calibrated Uncertainty
items.content: arXiv:2611.06953v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Steel property models can perform well on random test splits even when they extrapolate poorly to unfamiliar alloys. SteelAgent couples metallurgical descriptors and machine-learning models with a language-model interface for property prediction, uncertainty reporting and inverse design. We examine how the choice of held-out unit changes the conclusions drawn from SteelBench tensile-strength evaluations. For gradient boosting, pooled out-of-fold $R^2$ fell from 0.859 on a random split to 0.113 when steel families were held out. Empirical coverage of nominal 90% prediction intervals ranged from 91.0% under random splitting to 37.6% on held-out sources. The effect of physics-derived features depended on the evaluation. They increased gradient-boosting $R^2$ by 0.2534 in a 17-family holdout analysis and decreased it by 0.358 in a separate four-grade laboratory analysis. We report group-level errors and a synthetic regression experiment illustrating how calibration can deteriorate on held-out groups. These results motivate reporting the evaluation population alongside a property estimate or compliance score.

items.title: Robust Stream Classification using Time Neutralising Decision Trees
items.content: arXiv:2611.06991v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Data Streams are characterised as a potentially infinite source of data subject to non-stationarity. This non-stationarity, also called Concept Drift, often results in deployed predictive models having to be perpetually retrained as the underlying data generating process of the stream changes over time. Drift Detectors are a class of methods used to identify these changes, triggering these retraining procedures. Historically, Stream Learning has operated under the assumption that instances are only seen once, and cannot be stored for later use. Contemporary work relaxes this assumption, yet drift detection and simple resetting procedures are still ubiquitous.   Building on related work which has shown that traditional Batch Learning algorithms often outperform Stream Learning algorithms when instances can be stored, we introduce Time Neutralising Trees (TNT), a Decision Tree architecture that enables robust stream classification in settings with Concept Drift. During training, TNT will filter out ("neutralise") old training samples that are no longer relevant given the current context of the stream. If those instances become relevant again, TNT will then re-include them. We evaluate TNT, and related algorithms on 24 real and semi-real classification data streams from the USP DS repository. Results show strong evidence that TNT achieves best-in-class performance on a wide-range of data streams with varying concept drift types.
items.author: Brandon Gower-Winter, Georg Krempl
items.summary: The authors propose time-neutralising decision trees for data stream classification, addressing concept drift without relying on the usual detect-and-retrain paradigm. The approach builds on prior work showing batch learners can handle stored stream instances, offering robustness to non-stationarity by construction. This could reduce the operational cost of perpetually retraining deployed stream models.
items.reasoning: Addresses a practical and persistent problem in stream learning with a clean algorithmic idea, but decision-tree-based stream methods have limited reach relative to modern deep learning, and the abstract suggests incremental rather than foundational progress.

Building on related work which has shown that traditional Batch Learning algorithms often outperform Stream Learning algorithms when instances can be stored, we introduce Time Neutralising Trees (TNT), a Decision Tree architecture that enables robust stream classification in settings with Concept Drift. During training, TNT will filter out ("neutralise") old training samples that are no longer relevant given the current context of the stream. If those instances become relevant again, TNT will then re-include them. We evaluate TNT, and related algorithms on 24 real and semi-real classification data streams from the USP DS repository. Results show strong evidence that TNT achieves best-in-class performance on a wide-range of data streams with varying concept drift types.

items.title: Teaching Agents the "Principle", Not the "Reward"
items.content: arXiv:2611.07130v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Reinforcement learning has achieved strong performance in many tasks by letting agents learn from nothing more than a reward signal. However, in more complex tasks, agents still struggle to learn good, generalizable policies, even with carefully designed rewards and abundant samples. We argue that this difficulty stems from the reward decoding burden: designers encode their knowledge of the desired behavior into rewards and penalties, and agents must infer this knowledge from long sequences of noisy scalars. To address this burden, we propose prescriptive policy learning (PPL), which directly teaches agents higher-level knowledge about the tasks, termed principles of behavior, such as how to maintain balance, how to accumulate energy, and how to land smoothly. Through appropriately selected key quantities and references, PPL can directly indicate at every step whether the agent follows the principles and to what extent. Our experiments show that agents can learn good, generalizable policies without any reward. Taught only simple heuristic principles, PPL agents outperform reward-based methods with far fewer samples. Their policies also transfer directly to harder settings and keep performing well, demonstrating their strong generalization ability. In summary, PPL provides a new approach in which rough knowledge of the desired behavior is enough for agents to learn good, generalizable policies, even when the system dynamics cannot be accurately modeled.

items.title: RLGPA: A Reinforcement Learning-Guided Granularity Planning Attack for Decision-Based Sparse Adversarial Examples
items.content: arXiv:2611.07512v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Decision-based sparse attacks must reduce perturbation support using only the victim's predicted label. The best restoration strategy varies as support contracts: coarse removal works early, while tail states need finer, history-aware tests. We propose RLGPA, an online reinforcement learning method that schedules support-reduction executors and their granularity under a hard query budget. A masked Dueling Double DQN selects among seven stable policy--scale actions; each action produces support-relative restoration groups that are rebuilt after every macro decision. A feasibility-preserving executor commits only adversarial restorations and feeds support gain and query cost back to the planner. Under the matched top-1-label oracle, RLGPA reaches 61\% targeted ASR at sparsity 0.01 on CIFAR-10 (vs. 25\% SparseEvo, 0\% Pointwise), and 75.5\%/73.0\% on ResNet50/ViT at sparsity 0.005 (vs. 29.0\%/15.5\%). A fixed-probe test reduces median \(L_0\) from 165 to 23 after 40 images without any update. State-blind and state-shuffled controls degrade significantly, confirming that the learned policy uses attack state; the main gains come from state-conditioned executor scheduling and dynamic repartition. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/Acui001/RLGPA.git.
items.author: Chao Zhou, Shenghua He, Jiaxin Mo, Qiangguo Yu, Fengchuang Xing
items.summary: RLGPA uses online reinforcement learning (a masked Dueling Double DQN) to schedule support-reduction strategies at varying granularities for decision-based sparse adversarial attacks under a hard query budget, switching from coarse to history-aware fine moves as perturbation support contracts. The method improves attack efficiency against label-only oracles. It is relevant primarily as an adversarial robustness stress test.
items.reasoning: Technically competent application of RL to orchestrate adversarial attack strategies; the granularity-planning idea is somewhat novel, but the contribution is an attack method of mostly niche robustness-research interest.

items.title: Non-Parametric Mutual Information Estimation with Vine Copulas
items.content: arXiv:2611.07693v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: We introduce VINE: a non-parametric mutual information (MI) estimator based on simplified D-vine copulas. Approximating the joint density with a simplified D-vine allows the density ratio to simplify to a product of pair copulas, which we can estimate non-parametrically. This structural simplification yields VINE, a flexible and computationally efficient MI estimator. We compare VINE against SotA neural MI estimators on a range of datasets, both under settings where the simplified D-vine assumption holds and where it is violated, demonstrating competitive accuracy at a lower computational cost for low- to medium-dimensional datasets.

items.title: Towards Multiscale Molecular Representation Learning through Geometry-Based Fragmentation for Polymer Property Prediction
items.content: arXiv:2611.07998v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: It is well established that molecular substructures can contribute unequally to chemical and physical properties, with specific motifs or side chains often playing dominant roles. Fragment-based representations have therefore emerged as an effective strategy for incorporating chemically meaningful inductive biases, as exemplified by molecular fingerprints and fragment-based attention mechanisms. However, many existing fragmentation-based machine learning methods rely on predefined chemical rules, which may yield suboptimal fragmentation for previously unseen or chemically unfamiliar structures and often overlook the importance of multiscale molecular representations. To address these limitations, we formulate molecular fragmentation as a radius-constrained optimization problem inspired by the k-center formulation, where the number of clusters is not fixed a priori but emerges from the specified radius, and propose a geometry-based fragmentation method that partitions arbitrary molecular or material structures using largely geometric information, without relying on predefined chemical fragmentation rules. The method provides flexible control over fragment size, enabling the construction of multiscale fragment representations for scale-adaptive modeling. Building on this framework, we develop a geometric fragment-based attention mechanism that integrates multiscale structural information and incorporate it into a multimodal machine learning model combining p-SMILES representations with three-dimensional (3D) conformational information. Experiments on a benchmark polymer dataset show that incorporating 3D conformational information improves prediction accuracy for several properties over models based exclusively on p-SMILES representations. Explainable artificial intelligence analyses further provide insights into the physical relevance of the learned representations.

items.title: Detecting Weather Fronts from Satellite Observations: What Does Reanalysis Add?
items.content: arXiv:2611.08148v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Weather fronts are transition regions between air masses with contrasting thermodynamic properties and are associated with mid-latitude precipitation and severe weather. We investigate machine learning (ML) methods for detecting weather fronts and quantify the contribution of reanalysis data to performance. We compare two configurations of the same ML model for pixel-wise frontal classification over the North Atlantic and Europe: (1) using only geostationary infrared satellite observations, and (2) additionally using 28 ERA5 reanalysis fields. The satellite-only model achieves a neighbourhood critical success index at a 150 km tolerance (CSI@150) of $0.402$, which lies within the range of agreement between analyses from different meteorological services. The satellite$+$ERA5 model achieves $0.575$, an improvement of $0.173$. Our analysis shows that low-level winds are the least predictable from the satellite representation ($R^2 = 0.23$, compared with $0.88$ for temperature), while removing winds or moisture causes the largest decreases in detection performance.

It is a careful application study with meteorological grounding relevant to operational forecasting.

items.title: Geometric Relevance Is Not Sufficient: Evaluating Focused Post-Training Supervision in Diffusion Docking
items.content: arXiv:2611.08249v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Diffusion-based molecular docking requires learning a corrective score field across a broad corruption distribution, yet individual pose errors can differ substantially in their structural consequences. This creates a post-training conflict between preserving broad score-field coverage and concentrating supervision on corrections that appear more relevant to docking geometry. Using DiffDock, a fixed-budget study compares broad continuation with torsional supervision focused on Cartesian consequence or conditional target consistency, and with a broad/focused mixture. Evaluation separates fixed score fidelity, generated-pose quality, best-of-10 sampling capacity, and confidence-selected Top-1 docking performance. At <5 Angstrom, broad continuation had the highest mean Top-1 success among trained policies, and focused or mixed supervision showed no consistent advantage under the tested budget. The starting model had better fixed score fidelity, whereas the evaluated broad-continuation model had higher mean Top-1 success with the same aggregate best-of-10 recovery. Focusing supervision on structurally consequential or more consistently specified corrections did not consistently improve returned-pose success over broad continuation.

Findings indicate that concentrating supervision on geometrically relevant corrections does not necessarily improve docking outcomes. The work provides useful guidance on post-training data selection for generative scientific models.

items.title: Module-Aware Optimization for Graph Neural Networks
items.content: arXiv:2611.08379v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Different optimizers impose different geometries on parameter updates. Adaptive methods such as Adam and AdamW use coordinate-wise updates, while matrix-aware optimizers such as Muon utilize weight-matrix structure through orthogonalized updates. For Graph Neural Networks (GNNs), however, the effective geometry of its weight matrices is shaped not only by its learned channel-mixing weights, but also by the graph-propagated representations it acts on. Thus, even if an update is well normalized as a matrix, its effect on the layer output can be amplified when applied to graph-propagated features. To address this gap, we introduce GraphMuon, a graph-aware optimizer that adapts Muon's matrix updates to the covariance structure of graph-propagated layer inputs. GraphMuon performs orthogonalization in a metric defined by these propagated representations and normalizes step sizes according to the update's induced effect on the layer representation. We show that theoretically, vanilla Muon can suffer from graph-induced update amplification, while our GraphMuon can mitigate this effect. As such, our GraphMuon yields a graph-metric analogue of Muon's polar update step. Empirically, GraphMuon achieves $1.32\times$-$2.42\times$ validation-loss time-to-target speedups over AdamW on three large-scale OGB benchmarks. Across 15 dataset-architecture configurations spanning node classification, inductive graph classification, and graph regression, it achieves lower time-to-target in 13 cases, while maintaining competitive or superior predictive performance. Code is available at https://github.com/guy-hadad/GraphMuon.
items.author: Guy Hadad, Haggai Roitman, Moshe Eliasof, Bracha Shapira
items.summary: GraphMuon adapts the Muon matrix-aware optimizer to graph neural networks by accounting for the covariance structure of graph-propagated features, which shape the effective geometry of weight-matrix updates beyond learned channel-mixing weights. The observation that well-normalized matrix updates can be amplified by graph propagation motivates the graph-aware correction. It extends the growing literature on module-aware optimizers.
items.reasoning: Timely extension of Muon-style optimization to GNNs with a clear geometric motivation, but likely incremental relative to the original optimizer line and dependent on breadth of empirical gains.

items.title: Approximating the Euclidean Ball by Polytopes: Surprising Rates in High Dimensions
items.content: arXiv:2610.34651v2 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: We provide sharp estimates on the number of vertices needed to approximate the Euclidean unit ball $B_d\subset\mathbb R^d$ with relative symmetric-difference volume error at most $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$. We show that the minimum vertex budget $N_\varepsilon(d)$ satisfies $$\log N_\varepsilon(d)\asymp d\log\left(1+\frac1{\varepsilon\sqrt d}\right).$$ In particular, $\exp(O(\sqrt d/\varepsilon))$ vertices suffice for every $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$ and all sufficiently large $d$. We also prove that achieving a fixed error $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$ requires at least $\Omega\bigl((\tfrac{1+\varepsilon}{2\sqrt\varepsilon})^{d-1}\bigr)$ facets, an exponential number in $d$. We extend our vertex approximation result to Gaussian symmetric-difference error, and give a positive answer to the question of De, Nadimpalli, and Servedio about subexponential vertex complexity for approximating Euclidean balls.   We also disprove a Macbeath-type extremality principle for unrestricted vertex approximation. Whereas the ball uniformly maximizes the inscribed approximation error among all convex bodies (Macbeath, 1951), we show that approximating the hypercube $[-1,1]^d$ to relative error $\varepsilon$, with $\delta:=1-\varepsilon$, requires $N\ge\frac{\delta}{2}\exp(\Omega(\delta^2d/\log^2(2/\delta)))$ vertices whenever $d\ge16\log(2/\delta)$. Thus, when $d$ is large, the cube is harder to approximate than the ball in this sense.   Finally, we determine the sharp dimensional order of the classical Laguerre-Delone triangulation number, showing that $\mathrm{ldel}_{d-1}=\Theta(d^{-1/2})$ as $d\to\infty$. This improves both the upper bound of Ludwig, Sch\"utt, and Werner and the lower bound of B\"or\"oczky by a factor of order $\sqrt d$. By classical asymptotic approximation theorems (Ludwig, 1999), this improvement applies to every convex body in $\mathbb R^d$ with $C^2$ boundary and positive Gaussian curvature.

items.title: Bayesian Tensor Train Kernel Machines with Automatic Model Complexity Inference
items.content: arXiv:2611.07129v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Tensor Network (TN) kernel machines accelerate supervised learning by using low-rank TNs to reduce computation and memory. However, most TN-based methods are deterministic with manually tuned ranks and feature dimensions, while the existing Bayesian TN kernel machine is restricted to the CANDECOMP/PARAFAC decomposition (CPD), whose single rank is shared by all modes. We extend this framework to the tensor train (TT) and propose Bayesian Tensor Train Kernel Machines (BTT-KM), whose hierarchical ARD-type priors on the TT cores infer the TT ranks and feature dimensions from data. Since each TT core is coupled to the others only through its neighbors, its closed-form posterior update requires propagating the contributions of all other cores along the chain. Mean-field variational inference yields a Bayesian alternating least squares algorithm with the same computational complexity as its deterministic counterpart and a closed-form predictive distribution. A synthetic experiment illustrates that BTT-KM recovers the true TT ranks and feature dimensions from an over-parameterized initialization.

items.summary: This work extends Bayesian tensor-network kernel machines from the CP decomposition to the tensor train format, using hierarchical ARD-type priors on TT cores to automatically infer ranks and feature dimensions from data. The neighbor coupling of TT cores requires careful posterior propagation, yielding a scalable supervised learning method without manual complexity tuning.
items.reasoning: Technically solid extension with practical appeal (automatic rank inference), but tensor-network kernel machines remain a niche area relative to deep learning; moderate novelty and impact.

items.title: Using Transformers to Generate 3-Manifold Triangulations
items.content: arXiv:2611.07514v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Using dehydration signatures as an encoding, we train GPT-2-style transformers to generate triangulations of 3-dimensional manifolds. Our main runs each use approximately 3 exaFLOPs, spanning a 200 million parameter model trained on 60 million sphere triangulations to an 11 million parameter model trained on 1.1 billion sphere triangulations. The optimal model has 10 blocks, width 640 and generates dehydration signatures of closed manifolds of various topological types at a rate of 6.9%, 82% of which are spheres. To investigate how our method scales, we use the technique of IsoFLOP curves on 15-tetrahedron triangulations of the 3-sphere, over a compute range of 6 to 3000 petaFLOPs, and observe neural scaling behaviour. We extract a parameter scaling exponent of $\alpha = 0.49$ ($[0.48, 0.50]$ stat, $\pm 0.02$ syst), and an optimal ratio of 234 tokens per parameter for training. In addition, we present a number of smaller experiments, including evidence that transformers are able to learn to count degree-one edges near-perfectly, but get progressively worse when counting edges with higher degrees.
items.author: Daniel Bruwel, Ashvni Narayanan, Jonathan Spreer
items.summary: The authors train GPT-2-style transformers to generate triangulations of 3-manifolds using dehydration-signature encodings, spanning roughly 3 exaFLOPs of training compute and models from 11M to 200M parameters. items.reasoning: An interesting application of language-model-style training to pure mathematics (low-dimensional topology) with a genuine scaling-law analysis, which is rare outside standard domains. The low valid-generation rate and specialized topic limit broader impact.

items.title: Transformer-Based Trajectory Prescription for sEMG-Optimizing Robot-Mediated Rehabilitation
items.content: arXiv:2611.08295v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Robot-mediated rehabilitation has the potential to deliver high-intensity, individualized therapy, but existing systems (which have not consistently improved outcomes) typically prescribe kinematic trajectories rather than explicitly targeting the neuromotor activations thought to support recovery. To address this gap, and ultimately enable activation-optimizing rehabilitation robot behavior, we present a personalizable transformer-based model mapping individuals' muscle activations (as measured via surface electromyography) to prescribed contact force trajectories when interacting with an end-effector rehabilitation robot. The model uses a transformer encoder-decoder leveraging rotary positional embeddings (RoPE) to generate a latent representation of trajectory-relevant and user-specific neuromotor factors, and augments trajectory prediction with flow matching to produce a distribution over plausible prescriptions biased toward the training distribution. Using data from 16 healthy participants completing 15 isometric trajectory tracking tasks, we evaluate generalization across held-out tasks and users, as well as the feasibility of user-specific fine-tuning within a therapy-session timescale. The model achieves mean trajectory prediction errors of <8% on held out tasks and users, with effectively instantaneous deterministic inference and sub-second sampling of trajectory distributions. An initial test using the model during live rehabilitation tasks demonstrates that, on average, participants reach the target neuromotor activations with just 15% error accumulated throughout the task. These results provide a proof of concept for data-driven, activation-targeted trajectory prescription in robot-mediated rehabilitation and establish a foundation for future validation in clinical populations. Data and code have been open-sourced as part of the OpenRobotRehab project on SimTK.

items.title: Matching the Training-Time Weight Rule in Inference-Time Expert Deactivation
items.content: arXiv:2611.05804v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Expert deactivation at inference time changes both token routing and expert weights, and its effect on performance depends on how these changes are implemented. We compare removal, freezing, remaining-expert renormalization, and unnormalized re-routing on identical disabled sets across five instruction-tuned checkpoints from four model families, with a base OLMoE checkpoint as an additional comparison. We develop a weight-sum model that relates the loss of expert contributions and changes in branch scale to the weight rule used during training. With half of the experts deactivated according to activation-based rankings, remaining-expert renormalization yields the highest perplexity in models trained with raw router probabilities, whereas unnormalized re-routing yields the highest perplexity in models trained with normalized weights. Perplexity ranges from 1.4 to 73 times the intact baseline when the training rule is retained, and from 14 to 28,740 times the baseline under a rule mismatch. Task outcomes vary across evaluation types: on OLMoE, GSM8K strict-match accuracy falls to zero under all four implementations. Extending the model to changes in the number of active experts yields a further prediction, supported by the OLMoE experiments: the perplexity penalty from additional renormalization increases as fewer experts are activated.
items.author: Hao Cheng (Zhejiang Gongshang University), Zhiyu Yang (Chang'an University), Bo Ma (Zhejiang Gongshang University), Hanzhang Jia (University of Sussex)
items.summary: This paper analyzes inference-time expert deactivation in mixture-of-experts models, comparing removal, freezing, renormalization, and unnormalized re-routing across five checkpoints from four model families plus OLMoE, and develops a weight-sum model tying performance loss to the weight rule used during training. With half the experts deactivated, the best weight rule depends on whether models were trained with raw router probabilities. It provides actionable guidance for MoE compression and editing.
items.reasoning: A useful empirical and analytical contribution to a practically relevant topic (MoE sparsification at inference), with a clean comparative design across model families and a simple predictive model. The scope is narrow and the findings are specific to deactivation settings, but the training-time/inference-time consistency insight is valuable.

items.title: Information-Matched Auditing of Conversational Emotion-Shift Forecasting: A Leakage-Safe Evaluation Protocol
items.content: arXiv:2611.05895v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Comparisons in conversational emotion-shift forecasting are easily distorted when a learned model receives rich features but its transition baseline is given a noisy or unavailable current-emotion label, when hyperparameter budgets differ, or when target-turn information enters the representation. We present an information-matched, leakage-safe auditing protocol that closes these gaps with an explicit commitment point, executable causality tests, equal four-configuration validation searches, and seed-dialogue-aware inference. Applying it to six causal model families on four text corpora and two feature-source sensitivity configurations shows that a deployable train-only current-emotion classifier feeding the transition baseline yields a different verdict than an oracle diagnostic where both sides receive gold current emotion. Under the deployable condition, learned models improve over the predicted-label baseline on all four primary corpora; DailyDialog gains are large and survive a 72-comparison Holm correction (best ROC-AUC gain = +0.167, adjusted p=.0144). Under matched gold information, the baseline remains competitive on IEMOCAP and stronger on MELD, while every model retains a large DailyDialog advantage. We additionally report precision-recall AUC, calibration, a strictly utterance-local feature control, same-person self-shift forecasting, and a future-access dose-response test. An eight-item leakage checklist accompanies the protocol. Code, raw seed predictions, and reporting artifacts are available from the corresponding author upon request.
items.author: Bin Wen, Dai-Qiao Zhang, Tien-Ping Tan
items.summary: Presents an information-matched, leakage-safe auditing protocol for conversational emotion-shift forecasting that controls for feature asymmetry, hyperparameter budgets, and target-turn information leakage. Applied to six causal model families on four corpora, it shows apparently large reported gains can shrink or disappear under fair comparisons.
items.reasoning: Methodologically careful and relevant to reproducibility in emotion modeling, but its impact is mostly confined to the conversational emotion forecasting subfield where evaluation distortions are identified.

items.title: AssameseLM-E2B: An Open-Weight Assamese Language Model for Efficient Consumer-Grade Deployment
items.content: arXiv:2611.06170v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: While Large Language Models (LLMs) excel in high-resource languages, their performance often degrades in low-resource languages due to tokenization inefficiencies, generative instability, and linguistic interference. This paper presents AssameseLM-E2B and its instruction-tuned variant, AssameseLM-E2B-it, a 2-billion-parameter model adapted specifically for low resource Assamese language. Built upon the Gemma-4 architecture, the model incorporates an expanded byte-level BPE vocabulary to reduce tokenization overhead by nearly 500% compared with multilingual 2B--3B baselines. We employ a parameter-efficient Continual Pre-Training (CPT) pipeline with Hybrid LoRA, followed by Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) on a balanced, multi-domain dataset to enhance instruction-following and Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) capabilities.   Evaluation demonstrates a Bits-per-Byte (BPB) score of 0.7488 on FLORES-200, alongside an overall RAG score of 96.7% and 100% refusal accuracy on adversarial unanswerable prompts. Comparative analysis reveals significant limitations in general-purpose baselines, including receptive-productive decoupling, generative degradation on Romanized Assamese, and unintended Bengali script assimilation. These results demonstrate the potential of parameter-efficient adaptation for developing capable, locally deployable language models for low-resource languages under constrained computational resources.

It targets consumer-grade deployment efficiency.

items.title: Balancing hierarchical representation and quantization: A performance trade-off in text embeddings
items.content: arXiv:2611.06859v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Hierarchical text embedding models offer variable-length representations, while quantization reduces numerical precision; both aim to improve computational efficiency. This work is an empirical benchmark study of how these two orthogonal, already-established techniques interact. We evaluate 38 tasks from the Massive Text Embedding Benchmark (MTEB) using four transformer-based embedding models, covering 1D and 2D hierarchical representations combined with 32-bit, 8-bit, and binary quantization, for 168 configurations per task. We report each efficiency dimension separately: theoretical per-vector storage and end-to-end evaluation time. Under a Friedman test with Nemenyi post-hoc analysis, int8 quantization is statistically indistinguishable from float32 for pair classification and re-ranking and costs at most 1.5 percentage points overall, whereas binary quantization is significantly worse across every task category. Halving the embedding dimension once is not statistically detectable above $m=16$; two successive halvings always are. Combining an 8x dimensionality reduction with int8 yields a 32x reduction in per-vector storage at 94.4% of baseline effectiveness. Because evaluation times were measured once, we treat them as indicative: we find no evidence that quantization speeds up evaluation, whereas sampling from intermediate layers shortens it substantially. Retrieval degrades far faster than every other category, so we report findings per task category.
items.author: Kai Ponel, Marco Polignano, Erasmo Purificato, Aylin Julia Temizkan, Marco Levantesi, Giovanni Semeraro, Ernesto William De Luca
items.summary: An empirical benchmark of how hierarchical (variable-length) embedding representations interact with quantization, evaluating 168 configurations per task across 38 MTEB tasks and four transformer embedding models. Using Friedman tests with Nemenyi post-hoc analysis, it finds int8 quantization statistically indistinguishable from full precision, reporting storage and end-to-end time separately.
items.reasoning: A solid, statistically careful empirical study with practical guidance for embedding deployment efficiency, but it combines established techniques rather than introducing new methods, and findings (int8 is fine) largely confirm practitioner intuition.

items.title: Text-Only Domain Adaptation for Low-Resource Medical ASR: Shallow Fusion and Density Ratio Rescoring for Hausa
items.content: arXiv:2611.05744v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Automatic speech recognition (ASR) systems often struggle with specialised medical vocabulary, especially in low-resource languages where domain-specific speech data are scarce. We investigate text-only domain adaptation for Hausa medical ASR using the fixed MMS-1B-FL102 acoustic model and two decoding-time language-model fusion methods: Shallow Fusion (SF) and the Density Ratio Approach (DRA). A 4-gram KenLM trained on 19,421 Hausa health sentences serves as the medical target model, while a 75,372-sentence general-domain model provides the source prior for DRA. Evaluation uses 250 recordings of 25 physician-reviewed prompts from 10 speakers across six northern Nigerian states. Under prompt-disjoint five-fold cross-validation, SF and DRA reduce WER from 29.56% to 23.55% and 23.33%, respectively. Both significantly outperform greedy decoding (p < 0.001), while their difference is not significant (p = 0.423). However, general-LM-only SF achieves 23.96% WER, indicating that the medical LM's additional improvement over a general LM is modest. Medical Term Error Rate also improves under fusion, but does not establish a distinct medical-domain advantage. These findings demonstrate that lightweight, text-only language-model fusion can improve Hausa medical ASR without additional domain-specific speech collection.
items.author: Oche David Ankeli, Hassan Adelani Luqman, Theodora Ngozi Egbunike, Joshua Gottschalk, Bonaventure F. P. Dossou

Evaluation uses 250 physician-reviewed recordings from six northern Nigerian states under prompt-disjoint cross-validation. It matters as a low-cost recipe for improving specialized ASR where domain speech data is unavailable.

items.title: Perceptual Distortion for Overfitted Video Coding: Sliced Matching in Space, Error Alignment in Time
items.content: arXiv:2611.07148v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Recent works in neural video coding have increasingly been trading off perceptual quality against reconstruction fidelity at a fixed bitrate. Wasserstein Distortion (WD) offers a principled approach to balancing these objectives by relaxing spatial correspondences in feature matching, enabling lightweight overfitted image codecs to compete with computationally intensive generative decoders. Extending vanilla WD to video, however, presents two challenges: its independent Gaussian approximation limits the expressiveness of feature distribution matching, while unconstrained texture resampling across frames introduces temporal inconsistencies. We address these challenges by distinguishing between the correspondences that can be relaxed and those that must be preserved. Spatially, we introduce a local sliced Wasserstein distortion (SWD) that matches empirical feature distributions through one-dimensional optimal transport, capturing cross-channel dependencies without enforcing exact spatial alignment. Temporally, we employ a novel flow residual that constrains coding errors along motion trajectories, preserving temporal consistency without imposing additional reconstruction fidelity constraints. Evaluated on UVG and HEVC Class B with the overfitted codec COOL-CHIC, our framework achieves BD-rate reductions of 9.2% in DISTS and 3.0% in LPIPS relative to frame-wise WD, averaged over test sequences, while lowering tOF by 10.2% at matched rate.
items.author: Tianyi Yang, Ge Gao, Fan Zhang, David Bull
items.summary: This work extends Wasserstein Distortion to neural video coding, addressing its limited expressiveness from independent Gaussian approximations and temporal inconsistency from unconstrained texture resampling. The method uses sliced matching in space and error alignment in time to balance perceptual quality and fidelity at fixed bitrate. It enables lightweight overfitted codecs to compete with heavy generative decoders.
items.reasoning: Solid extension of a principled compression metric to video with sensible design choices, from a credible Bristol video coding group (Bull, Zhang). However, the topic is specialized and overfitted codecs have limited generality.

items.title: Degree-Equalized View-Graph Selection under Tight Pair Budgets
items.content: arXiv:2611.07498v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Fully matching all image pairs in Structure-from-Motion is quadratic in the number of images, so practical pipelines pass a budgeted subset to the final matching and reconstruction backend. One-shot selectors score candidates with image retrieval, cheap geometric probes, or a learned prior and finalize B pairs before full matching. Their priorities do not account for the degree already allocated to each image, which can concentrate edges on a few images. Across nine large 1DSfM internet photo collections at B=2N, the coverage top-B selector leaves 54% of covered images with realized degree at most two. Reconstruction can then fail even when the selected graph is nearly connected and almost fully verified. Our training-free greedy rule, Degree-Equalized Allocation (DEAL), exponentially downweights pairs whose endpoints are already well covered. On these collections, DEAL improves the one-shot selector built on the same prior (from 0.776 to 0.929) and matches the mean registered-image ratio of an SfM-supervised edge prior under the shared backend (0.929 vs 0.930), without training. On the largely saturated 38-scene standard benchmark suite, DEAL gives the highest mean among the evaluated training-free selectors (0.875 vs 0.858 one-shot).
items.author: Minhyeok Im, Jongseong Brad Choi
items.summary: The paper shows that one-shot view-graph selectors in Structure-from-Motion can concentrate matching edges on few images, causing reconstruction failure even on nearly connected verified graphs, and proposes a training-free greedy degree-equalizing selection rule. At B=2N on nine 1DSfM collections it substantially improves degree coverage. A focused but useful improvement to SfM pipelines.
items.reasoning: Identifies a real failure mode in budgeted SfM matching with a simple effective fix, but the scope is narrow classical 3D reconstruction plumbing. Training-free simplicity is a plus.

On these collections, DEAL improves the one-shot selector built on the same prior (from 0.776 to 0.929) and matches the mean registered-image ratio of an SfM-supervised edge prior under the shared backend (0.929 vs 0.930), without training. On the largely saturated 38-scene standard benchmark suite, DEAL gives the highest mean among the evaluated training-free selectors (0.875 vs 0.858 one-shot).

items.title: Egocentric Action Recognition with Objects and Vision-Language Affordances
items.content: arXiv:2611.07673v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Action recognition, and more specifically egocentric action recognition, is a core task in computer vision, with applications such as monitoring the daily life activities of elderly people and task assistance. Recent methods rely on visual modalities such as RGB video or depth. However, in egocentric video, an action is largely defined by its objects, which these methods rarely model. We propose a method that combines a frozen SlowFast video expert with an attention-based object expert by late fusion. Each object is represented with its affordances, that is, what can be done with it, generated zero-shot by a vision-language model. Since datasets such as MECCANO annotate only the objects involved in each action, evaluating with these boxes tells the model which objects are active. We therefore train on annotated boxes and evaluate the method with detections from the official active-object detector, and with annotated boxes as an upper bound. Without affordances, our fusion reaches 68.4% Top-1 with annotated boxes but 49.0% with detections. About half of this drop comes from non-active detections. To remove them, the same vision-language model generates an interaction affordance that decides whether a hand is manipulating each detected object. On MECCANO, objects raise the Top-1 of the video expert from 44.9% to 49.0%, and the two affordances raise it to 49.9%, above SlowFast and object-aware RGB baselines. Code will be released upon acceptance.

items.title: Rain Beyond Streaks: Cascaded Realistic Rain and Wet Surface Synthesis via Scene Priors
items.content: arXiv:2611.07793v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Realistic rain synthesis is a persistent challenge for vision systems operating in adverse weather. Existing methods primarily focus on generating rain streaks, often neglecting consequent surface effects such as reflections and puddles, which are critical for perceptual realism and robustness of downstream vision tasks. We introduce CascadeRS, a rain synthesis framework that leverages depth and segmentation priors to render scene-consistent rain and surface effects. In addition to rain streaks, CascadeRS produces reflections and puddles aligned with scene semantics through a physics-inspired zero-shot, controllable generative pipeline. It produces photorealistic rainy urban scenes, with high perceptual realism, which we validate qualitatively with an extensive user study and quantitatively. We produce the Cityscapes-CascadeRS dataset, to study downstream task performance under real rainy conditions. Our results establish CascadeRS as a scalable and realistic rain-generation framework for evaluating and enhancing the robustness of vision in adverse rainy weather. Code and dataset are available via https://github.com/nis-research/CascadeRainSynthesis

Validation covers perceptual realism qualitatively and quantitatively.

items.title: ATHAAR: A Medieval Scientific Arabic Manuscript Dataset for Handwritten Text Recognition
items.content: arXiv:2611.08091v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Despite recent progress in handwritten text recognition, medieval Arabic scientific manuscripts remain an open challenge for current vision-language models (VLMs) due to cursive ligatures, variable diacritization, and more importantly the lack of training data. This paper aims to address this gap, by proposing the first annotation guidelines dedicated to the transcription of scientific Arabic manuscripts inspired by textual criticism, a well-established approach to historical text editing. We then propose, ATHAAR, a new dataset manually annotated following this guideline. Unlike previous resources in the field, ATHAAR varies both witnesses of the same text, calligraphic styles, and content to deal with texts but also numerals. Relying on state-of-the-art VLMs, we finally design a set of experiments to study models transfer across scripts, chapters, and treatises. Our findings highlight the limitations of current systems when faced with the specificities of ancient scientific texts.

items.title: Adaptive Low-Light Enhancement for Road Anomaly Detection: A Multi-Architecture Benchmark and Edge Deployment Study
items.content: arXiv:2611.08393v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Road anomaly detection systems on autonomous vehicles must function reliably under degraded visual conditions including darkness, rain, and Harmattan dust haze. This paper benchmarks four object detection architectures, YOLOv8n, YOLOv12n, RT-DETR, and Faster R-CNN, under physically grounded lighting and weather degradation, and shows that uniform application of the SCI low-light enhancement network is actively harmful at dusk-level lighting (-16.1% to -30.7% mAP@50). We propose a lightweight, training-free luminance-adaptive router that selects between no enhancement, moderate SCI, and denoising plus strong SCI based on per-frame Rec. 601 luminance, recovering most of the dusk penalty while preserving low-light gains, and we validate the full pipeline on NVIDIA Jetson Nano edge hardware.

items.title: FFMT: Frequency-Factorized Multi-Rate Tokenization for Music-to-Dance Generation
items.content: arXiv:2611.07384v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Dance motion combines slowly varying body configurations with rapid local movements. We investigate how explicit temporal-frequency decomposition can guide the temporal resolution and codebook capacity of discrete motion representations. We introduce frequency-factorized motion tokenization (FFMT), which separates root-relative motion into a low-frequency choreographic scaffold and a complementary high-frequency residual. FFMT uses a lower token rate and a smaller codebook for the low-frequency component, and a higher token rate and a larger codebook for the high-frequency residual. This representation further induces a plan-then-articulate autoregressive factorization: low-frequency tokens establish coarse choreography, while high-frequency tokens realize local motion details conditioned on the generated plan and music. Experiments on AIST++ and FineDance show strong distributional fidelity while preserving realistic diversity and music--motion synchronization. Ablations consistently support frequency factorization, asymmetric temporal allocation, and low-to-high conditioning.

items.summary: FFMT decomposes dance motion into a low-frequency choreographic scaffold and a high-frequency residual, tokenizing each at different rates with differently sized codebooks. This representation enables a plan-then-articulate autoregressive factorization where coarse choreography is established first, then refined with rapid local movements.
items.reasoning: A clean, principled representation-design contribution for motion generation; frequency-factorized multi-rate tokenization could generalize to other sequential generation tasks, though the application domain is niche.

items.title: Dynamic Watermarking and Action-Conditioned Latent Dynamics for Secure Vision-Based Controllers
items.content: arXiv:2611.07403v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Replay attacks are difficult to detect in vision-based control systems because previously recorded observations can remain plausible while the physical system follows a different trajectory. This paper develops an adaptive dynamic-watermarking framework for detecting replay attacks against vision-based controllers. A private Gaussian watermark is added to the nominal control input, and a control input-conditioned latent dynamics network (LDN) predicts the corresponding evolution in a compact latent space learned from image observations. Attack evidence is obtained from the discrepancy between the predicted latent response and the latent representation of the received image observation. A reinforcement learning policy adjusts the watermark covariance using the latent state and detector confidence, thereby balancing attack detectability, watermark energy, and control distortion. A Lagrangian penalty on task-specific safety costs is included during training to limit the adverse effect of the excitation. The framework is evaluated on a vision-guided UR5 manipulation task in which the robot reaches a target while avoiding a moving human arm under nominal and replay-attacked observations.

A reinforcement learning policy adjusts watermark strength adaptively.

items.title: Dual-Arm Tabletop Rearrangement with Movable Stacking and Gap-Aware Push Transfers
items.content: arXiv:2611.07726v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Object rearrangement in cluttered tabletop scenes is challenging, especially in wide workspaces where dual-arm systems improve coverage and efficiency. Limited free space often necessitates buffering, while objects near or across the shared reachability region of the manipulators must be transferred under careful coordination to avoid inter-arm collisions. Conventional inter-arm transfer typically relies on a fixed handoff configuration, which constrains where and how objects are exchanged, enforces spatiotemporal synchronization of the arms, and reduces flexibility in dense layouts. This paper presents a dual-arm rearrangement framework that combines movable stacking with Gap-Aware Push Transfer for asynchronous cross-boundary exchange. The method scans the shared boundary to identify collision-free transfer gaps, places an object near a selected crossing point, and then pushes it into the receiving workspace without requiring simultaneous interaction between the two arms. A joint Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS)-based planner coordinates both manipulators while reasoning over buffering and transfer decisions, and execution cost is used after planning to assess the resulting plan. Experiments show that the proposed method shortens joint execution sequences and becomes increasingly advantageous over a fixed handoff baseline as scene density increases, achieving lower execution cost in denser scenes while remaining competitive in lighter ones.

This improves flexibility and coverage in dense, wide workspaces. It is a solid contribution to multi-arm manipulation planning.

items.title: Generalized Hyperrectangular Prediction Sets in Multivariate Conformal Prediction
items.content: arXiv:2611.05543v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: In multivariate conformal prediction, many nonconformity scores yield prediction sets with complex geometry (e.g., ellipsoids or density level sets) that are difficult to interpret and visualize. Hyperrectangles offer a practical alternative by providing one interval per output. We extend this notion to Cartesian products of arbitrary one-dimensional sets, which we call generalized hyperrectangles. We introduce a rectangularization framework that turns any continuous multivariate nonconformity score, or conditional density, into one yielding generalized hyperrectangular prediction sets with finite-sample coverage. We establish key geometric properties of our rectangularization framework and provide useful intuitions on generalized hyperrectangles. We further establish a representation theorem showing that a broad class of hyperrectangular conformal methods based on max-aggregated coordinate-wise scores can be interpreted as rectangularizations of implicit conditional densities. Through synthetic and real-world experiments, we quantify the efficiency cost of rectangularization, while highlighting its benefits, especially for practical applications of uncertainty quantification.

The technique is somewhat incremental, but the framework's generality (applicable to any continuous nonconformity score) gives it broad applicability.

items.title: Towards Efficient Whole Page Ranking with One-Pass Inference
items.content: arXiv:2611.05542v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Whole-page ranking jointly optimizes advertisements and organic content to balance business outcomes and user engagement under complex layout and business constraints. Existing non-autoregressive (NAR) approaches enable efficient page generation but typically score candidate items independently of previously selected items, limiting their ability to capture order-dependent interactions. Autoregressive (AR) methods address this limitation through sequential conditioning, but incur substantial inference overhead that challenges large-scale deployment. Bridging this quality-efficiency gap remains a challenge in industrial whole-page ranking.   We propose Multi-Item Scoring (MIS), a prefix-aware NAR-style framework that incorporates sequential context into efficient multi-item scoring. MIS integrates global candidate interactions, localized prefix conditioning, and position-aware scoring within a shared representation architecture. By computing reusable representations once per request and performing lightweight prefix-conditioned scoring during constrained beam search, MIS captures important sequential dependencies without repeated full-model inference.   Experiments on KuaiRand-1K and RL4RS demonstrate that MIS approaches the generation quality of an autoregressive CGA baseline while achieving 4.07x and 3.54x faster CPU decoding, respectively. In a randomized evaluation on a large-scale social-video platform, MIS improves the realization metric by 0.104% and watch time by 0.058%, while reducing ranking-service CPU consumption by 9.73%. These results demonstrate that prefix-aware multi-item scoring can narrow the quality gap between NAR and AR generation while retaining the efficiency required for industrial scalability.

It bridges the quality gap between autoregressive methods and the efficiency of NAR approaches under layout and business constraints for ads and organic content.

The technique is a targeted engineering innovation rather than a broadly generalizable research advance, and evaluation details in the abstract are limited.

items.title: Regularization vs. Convolution in Kernel-Based Hypothesis Testing
items.content: arXiv:2611.06778v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: The maximum mean discrepancy (MMD) test is a popular nonparametric test on general domains. Two lines of work have studied its optimality through structurally different approaches. The first, a convolution approach on $\mathbb{R}^d$, uses translation-invariant kernels with a shrinking bandwidth and is minimax optimal over Sobolev balls under $L^2$-separation; the second, a regularization approach on general measurable spaces, uses spectral regularization of the kernel covariance operator and is minimax optimal over Hellinger- and $\chi^2$-separated alternatives. In this paper, we study the regularization approach over Sobolev balls under $L^2$-separation, which reveals the connection between the two approaches. We show that, with a translation-invariant kernel on $\mathbb{R}^d$, both are ways of meeting a single condition on the kernel's spectral density: the spectral regularized discrepancy captures the $L^2$-separation $\Delta$ of a Sobolev alternative of smoothness $s$ as soon as the regularization parameter $\lambda$ is below the spectral density on frequencies up to $\Delta^{-1/(2s)}$. A kernel with a shrinking bandwidth $h$ meets this condition with $\lambda \asymp h^d$, and under this coupling the constant regularizer, which gives the MMD test itself, attains the Sobolev minimax rate. This explains, from a spectral perspective, the need for a shrinking bandwidth in the convolution approach. With a non-constant spectral regularizer, our analysis requires the bandwidth to shrink only when the spectral density decays faster than any polynomial, as for the Gaussian kernel. Thus, for Mat\'ern and Laplace kernels, a fixed bandwidth with $\lambda \to 0$ attains the Sobolev minimax rate. Finally, an adaptive test over a grid of bandwidths and regularization parameters is minimax optimal, up to a $\log\log$ factor, over both classes without prior knowledge of the smoothness.

items.summary: The authors unify two previously separate lines of work on MMD test optimality - the convolution approach with shrinking bandwidths on R^d and the spectral regularization approach on general spaces - by analyzing the regularization approach over Sobolev balls under L2-separation. They reveal an explicit connection between the two approaches.
items.reasoning: A rigorous unification result in kernel two-sample testing theory that clarifies the relationship between established techniques. Valuable for the nonparametric testing community but mathematically specialized with limited broader reach.

items.content_html: arXiv:2611.06778v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The maximum mean discrepancy (MMD) test is a popular nonparametric test on general domains. Two lines of work have studied its optimality through structurally different approaches. The first, a convolution approach on $\mathbb{R}^d$, uses translation-invariant kernels with a shrinking bandwidth and is minimax optimal over Sobolev balls under $L^2$-separation; the second, a regularization approach on general measurable spaces, uses spectral regularization of the kernel covariance operator and is minimax optimal over Hellinger- and $\chi^2$-separated alternatives. In this paper, we study the regularization approach over Sobolev balls under $L^2$-separation, which reveals the connection between the two approaches. We show that, with a translation-invariant kernel on $\mathbb{R}^d$, both are ways of meeting a single condition on the kernel's spectral density: the spectral regularized discrepancy captures the $L^2$-separation $\Delta$ of a Sobolev alternative of smoothness $s$ as soon as the regularization parameter $\lambda$ is below the spectral density on frequencies up to $\Delta^{-1/(2s)}$. A kernel with a shrinking bandwidth $h$ meets this condition with $\lambda \asymp h^d$, and under this coupling the constant regularizer, which gives the MMD test itself, attains the Sobolev minimax rate. This explains, from a spectral perspective, the need for a shrinking bandwidth in the convolution approach. With a non-constant spectral regularizer, our analysis requires the bandwidth to shrink only when the spectral density decays faster than any polynomial, as for the Gaussian kernel. Thus, for Mat\'ern and Laplace kernels, a fixed bandwidth with $\lambda \to 0$ attains the Sobolev minimax rate. Finally, an adaptive test over a grid of bandwidths and regularization parameters is minimax optimal, up to a $\log\log$ factor, over both classes without prior knowledge of the smoothness.

items.title: Persistent Retrieval for Conversational Agents: A Study of Retrieval Efficiency
items.content: arXiv:2611.07899v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Conversational agents can retrieve information directly or delegate retrieval to a subagent. This design choice affects how retrieval history is maintained, what context each model call receives, and what information must be re-retrieved in follow-up questions. We compare three designs: skill-based retrieval in the main agent, a non-persistent retrieval subagent that generates a findings response, and our persistent retrieval subagent, which maintains retrieval history across turns and returns retrieved evidence directly to the main agent. Our approach also allows the main agent to request corrections from the same subagent.   We evaluate the three designs on enterprise questions posed independently, within shared conversations, and as dependent follow-ups. Across five multi-turn settings, our approach uses 43.3% fewer recorded agent-model tokens and incurs 45.0% lower estimated API cost than skill-based retrieval, while reducing average response time by 9.1%. Compared with non-persistent retrieval, it reduces response time by 15.6 seconds per question, while using 65.1% more tokens and incurring 29.1% higher estimated API cost.   Our approach shifts the retrieval subagent from producing synthesized responses to maintaining retrieval state and supplying evidence that the main agent can directly evaluate and use for answer generation.
items.author: Karthik Ravula, Sathwik Kowtha, Rishabh Verma, Kala Mehak Jain, Gunjit Mittal
items.summary: The paper compares three retrieval architectures for conversational agents: skill-based retrieval in the main agent, a non-persistent retrieval subagent, and a persistent retrieval subagent that maintains retrieval history across turns and returns evidence directly. The persistent design also lets the main agent request corrections from the same subagent. It evaluates the designs on independent, shared-conversation, and dependent enterprise questions to measure efficiency effects.
items.reasoning: A useful empirical systems study for practitioners designing multi-turn agent architectures, with a clear design-space framing. However, the scope is enterprise Q&A, the contribution is architectural comparison rather than a new method, and the generalization beyond the tested workload is unclear.

items.title: Batch-Conditioned Semantic Anchors for Robust Transductive Adaptation of Vision--Language Models
items.content: arXiv:2611.06993v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Transductive adaptation improves vision-language models at test time by refining predictions on an unlabeled batch, but current methods face a key trade-off. Aggressive approaches exploit batch structure but can drift when batches are sparse, have prior shift, or cover little of the label space. Conservative methods better preserve CLIP text semantics, but fixed semantic references can under-adapt even when the batch provides strong corrective evidence. We propose JPTA (Joint Prior and Transport Adaptation), a prior-aware framework that casts transductive VLM adaptation as batch-conditioned semantic reference estimation. Instead of treating CLIP text prototypes as fixed priors or freely replaceable, JPTA views them as semantic references that shift toward image-side batch structure only under calibrated evidence. It estimates batch priors and soft image-side prototypes to form transported semantic references whose impact is scaled by batch reliability. Across standard benchmarks, low effective-class regimes, all-class evaluation, and online streams, JPTA consistently outperforms TransCLIP and StatA, with the largest gains on sparse and prior-shifted batches. Anchor-drift, active-support, and absent-class-mass diagnostics show that JPTA fixes effective-class mismatch without unconstrained transductive drift, indicating that robust transductive VLM adaptation should recalibrate semantic references using reliable batch evidence rather than choose between unrestricted transduction and fixed prototypes. Code is available at https://github.com/MR-Sherif/JPTA.git.
items.author: Mohammed Rahman Sherif Khan Mohammad, Ardhendu Behera, Sandip Pradhan, Swagat Kumar, Amr Ahmed
items.summary: Proposes JPTA, a prior-aware framework for transductive test-time adaptation of vision-language models that treats CLIP text prototypes as semantic references to be estimated per batch rather than fixed priors or freely replaceable. This addresses the trade-off between exploiting batch structure and preserving text semantics under sparse batches, prior shift, and partial label-space coverage.
items.reasoning: A sensible and well-motivated contribution to test-time adaptation of CLIP-style models, with a clear framing of the drift-versus-under-adaptation trade-off. The contribution is incremental within a crowded adaptation literature, and evaluation details in the abstract do not suggest breakthroughs.

items.title: Energy-Aware Open-Vocabulary Detection Scheduling for Low-Power Robotic Autonomy
items.content: arXiv:2611.07663v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Open-vocabulary object detection (OVD) lets robots search for run-time object queries, but fixed-rate inference spends embedded compute on low-value frames during idle motion, map revisits, or stable viewpoints. This paper presents an energy-aware OVD scheduler for low-power mobile robots. The scheduler uses odometry, map change, and detector confidence to switch among low-, mid-, and high-power YOLO-World-S modes on a Jetson Orin Nano. We evaluate the energy-quality trade-off on an AgileX LIMO using 40 real navigation trials: two target objects, five placements per target-policy pair, and four perception policies. Across bottle and cup trials, the scheduler records 8/10 mission success compared with 7/10 for each fixed-rate baseline, while reducing mean Jetson input power (a Jetson-side power-draw metric) by 5.2% relative to an 8 Hz high-rate baseline and lowering achieved OVD call rate by 34.0%. It does not minimize mission-window Jetson input energy because longer missions can erase instantaneous power savings. A separate 60 s stationary microbenchmark isolates the perception workload: the scheduler lowers mean power from 8.045 W to 7.301 W and energy from 484.7 J to 438.1 J relative to the 8 Hz baseline. These results support robot-state-aware OVD scheduling as a promising power-management mechanism with competitive task reliability, while showing that mission-window Jetson input energy must be read together with task progress and runtime.
items.author: Abdul Basit, Muhammad Shafique
items.summary: The paper presents a scheduler that switches among low-, mid-, and high-power YOLO-World-S modes on a Jetson Orin Nano using odometry, map change, and detector confidence, reducing wasted inference on low-value frames during robot navigation. Real trials on an AgileX LIMO show slightly better mission success than fixed-rate baselines with reduced energy use.
items.reasoning: A practical systems contribution for energy-efficient perception on embedded robots with real hardware trials, but engineering-oriented with modest gains (8/10 versus 7/10 success) and limited generalizability beyond the tested setup.

items.title: ZeroRAG: Adaptive Semantic Peer Routing for Decentralized Retrieval-Augmented Generation
items.content: arXiv:2611.07928v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is a standard approach to enhance the reliability of large language model (LLM) outputs by retrieving documents relevant to a query and supplying them in the LLM prompt. Today's RAG systems collect, index, and serve these documents from centralized stores. In practice, however, documents are owned by organizations, devices, and individuals who cannot or will not surrender custody of them to a central party, e.g., because of privacy, copyright or regulatory compliance. Existing modern decentralized retrieval techniques either reintroduce a coordinating authority, or rely on a global data structure that requires continuous network-wide coordination (e.g., DHTs). We present ZeroRAG, a decentralized routing layer for document retrieval in RAG that performs semantic query routing across an overlay of peers with- out global data structures or centralized orchestration. Documents remain with the peers that own them, and each peer keeps only lightweight local state: a bounded set of neighbor advertisements and a cache of recently routed queries. Using these, ZeroRAG steers each query through a best-first walk that progressively rewires the overlay toward semantically relevant neighbors, so recall improves over time as the network self-organizes. We evaluate ZeroRAG using three real-world workloads and two decentralized baselines. We find that ZeroRAG outperforms baselines in terms of recall and required network messages, approaches the recall and LLM answer accuracy of a centralized document store, self-heals after catastrophic peer failures, and scales to 100 000 peers.
items.author: Petru Neague, Quinten Stokkink, Martijn de Vos, Rafael Pires, Mathis Randl, Anne-Marie Kermarrec, Johan Pouwelse
items.summary: ZeroRAG enables retrieval-augmented generation without centralized document stores, routing queries through peer networks for parties who cannot surrender document custody due to privacy, copyright, or regulatory constraints. It avoids both coordinating authorities and global data structures like DHTs via adaptive semantic peer routing. This addresses a real deployment constraint for RAG in privacy-sensitive and federated settings.
items.reasoning: A well-motivated systems contribution from an experienced distributed-systems group (TU Delft / INSA lineage); decentralized retrieval is niche but increasingly relevant to sovereign AI and privacy constraints, though adoption barriers are significant.

items.title: Estimating Spectrum-Free Information Bounds for Generative Surrogates Beyond Conditional Collapse
items.content: arXiv:2611.07826v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Conditional generative surrogates in high-energy physics, such as models that predict reconstructed jets from partons, are often evaluated on $1\text{D}$ marginal divergences among other metrics. Taken alone these metrics can reward conditional collapse. On a CMS simulation benchmark, a sampler that ignores the conditioner beats a trained Mixture Density Network (MDN) on all four target marginals under both KL and Wasserstein-1, and cannot be stably separated from a Conditional Flow Matching (CFM) model on two of the four. We instead score the models with the Continuous Ranked Probability Skill Score (CRPSS) from forecast verification, taking the exact marginal as the reference. We show how global skill depends on the evaluation spectrum, and we also report it within bins of a conditioning variable, where that dependence largely goes away. We then introduce a data-driven $k$-Nearest-Neighbor ($k$-NN) extrapolation that estimates the best CRPS the conditioning information allows. Both models agree with this estimate on all four targets, which suggests that current architectures have reached the information available in the conditioner, at least as far as these per-target scores can tell.
items.author: Chaitanya Dumbre, Sourabh Dube
items.summary: The paper shows that common 1D marginal divergence metrics can reward conditional collapse in generative surrogates for high-energy physics, demonstrating on a CMS benchmark that an unconditional sampler beats a trained mixture density network on all marginals. The authors propose using the Continuous Ranked Probability Skill Score against the exact marginal as a more informative evaluation.
items.reasoning: Identifies a concrete and consequential evaluation flaw for conditional generative models in scientific applications and imports a well-justified alternative metric from forecast verification. Impact is largely confined to surrogate modeling evaluation practice, but the demonstration is convincing.

items.title: SHORE: Stability-Hybrid On-Policy Reinforcement Learning for Online Bin Packing
items.content: arXiv:2611.08364v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Online 3D bin packing with a processing buffer requires choosing which box to pack, its orientation, and its placement while keeping the stack stable under unknown future arrivals. A collapse ends the episode and forfeits the remaining volume. Existing methods use geometric rules or hard stability masks, limiting how risk can influence the joint choice of box, orientation, and placement. We propose Stability-Hybrid On-Policy Reinforcement Learning (SHORE), which combines a learned stability probability of a placement with an on-policy estimate of its return conditional on stability. A 3D U-Net learns stability from executed outcomes and simulated alternatives, revealing outcomes of actions underrepresented in early rollouts. A discrete on-policy actor--critic uses stability predictions in both its action values and policy prior, with gates that limit the effect of an untrained or changing model. In deployment, SHORE does not require additional search or simulation overhead. In Isaac Gym, SHORE reaches 73\% space utilization by 0.4M environment steps, while the same learner without stability modeling reaches that level at about 1M. On the expanded 60-box set, SHORE achieves 0.734 space utilization versus 0.588 for the GOPT state-of-the-art baseline, with a higher placement-failure frequency (1.03\% vs. 0.63\%), trading more risk for greater packed volume. The results show faster learning and higher utilization on the more demanding realistic box arrival set. Ablations suggest that simulated alternatives provide useful early supervision, while executed outcomes alone sustain later performance. We also demonstrate the method on a real robot to verify the simplicity of integrating the method to real bin packing pipelines.
items.author: Chang Shi, Ann Majewicz Fey
items.summary: SHORE combines a learned stability probability, trained by a 3D U-Net from executed and simulated packing outcomes, with an on-policy estimate of return conditional on stability for online 3D bin packing with a processing buffer. This hybrid replaces hard stability masks and lets risk influence joint choices of box, orientation, and placement. It matters for physically grounded sequential decision-making where failures terminate episodes.
items.reasoning: A competent RL application with a sensible hybrid design that addresses a concrete physical failure mode. The contribution is incremental relative to broader on-policy RL and learned-safety-critic literature, and the setting is fairly specialized, though the stability-hybrid idea could transfer to other risk-sensitive manipulation tasks.

items.title: Selective, Risk-Controlled Emotion Forecasting in Conversation: From a Persistence Barrier to Departure Detection with Conformal Guarantees
items.content: arXiv:2611.05896v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Forecasting emotion in conversation is increasingly framed as predicting the next emotional state's value. We show this targets a hard quantity in a state-observed testbed and propose a learnable, deployable reformulation instead. On valence-arousal-dominance trajectories from a dyadic corpus, repeating a speaker's own previous state sets a persistence baseline that no frozen-encoder correction meaningfully improves upon and a state-space filter exceeds; the floor requires the historical state to be observed, since an estimated anchor collapses persistence below a direct forecaster. What survives is the timing of a departure from persistence, learnable on three of four corpora and near chance on the highest-base-rate corpus, a negative result we report. We recast the task as selective departure forecasting: a lead-time-weighted metric with a leakage protocol, and commitment policies whose best choice switches with the departure rate. A dialogue-level conformal risk control bounds the expected loss of committed predictions, meeting the target in all twelve configurations tested, though the guarantee is bought through abstention, with coverage and alarm recall falling sharply on the hardest corpus. One tested language model's confidence fails as a ranking signal where another succeeds, a model-dependent failure not yet attributable to family versus scale. Code and result logs are available from the corresponding author upon request.
items.author: Bin Wen, Dai-Qiao Zhang, Tien-Ping Tan
items.summary: Shows that next-emotion-value forecasting in conversation is dominated by a persistence baseline, and reformulates the task as detecting departures from persistence with conformal risk guarantees. The paper reports an honest negative result: departure timing is learnable on only three of four corpora and near chance on the highest-base-rate corpus.
items.reasoning: A candid negative-result paper with a principled task reformulation and conformal guarantees, valuable for tempering overclaims in emotion forecasting, though the empirical footprint is small and domain-specific.
