items.title: CMDiff: Left Atrial Scar Segmentation from 3D LGE MRI Using Conditional Mask Diffusion Model: A Feasibility Study
items.content: arXiv:2611.07814v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Late gadolinium enhancement (LGE) cardiac MRI enables non-invasive assessment of left atrial (LA) scar, an imaging marker associated with atrial fibrillation ablation outcome. However, automatic scar segmentation is hindered by low contrast, the thin atrial wall, scarce labels, and extreme class imbalance. Conditional diffusion offers iterative mask generation, but its suitability for sparse 3D LA scar segmentation remains unclear. To address this gap, we propose Conditional Mask Diffusion (CMDiff), which predicts clean masks using a dynamic-encoder-conditioned 3D sinusoidal UNet. We compared CMDiff with a deterministic baseline on identical cases in five-fold cross-validation of 60 scar-labelled public LASCARQS subjects, with 48 training and 12 held-out cases per fold. CMDiff achieved a scar DSC of 0.47 $\pm$ 0.08, HD95 of 12.89 $\pm$ 6.39 mm, and ASD of 1.91 $\pm$ 0.96 mm, compared with deterministic baseline values of 0.51 $\pm$ 0.08, 10.86 $\pm$ 5.39 mm, and 1.58 $\pm$ 1.03 mm, respectively. Under the same implementation, clean-mask prediction performed substantially better than the noise-prediction configuration evaluated in this study. Thus, CMDiff was technically feasible but did not improve segmentation performance: DSC was lower, and both HD95 and ASD were higher. Direct mask diffusion therefore provides an analytical alternative, but not a competitive performance advance for this task. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/jizhang02/CMDiff.
items.author: Jing Zhang, Bastien Bergere, Jonas Leite, Emilie Bollache, Mika\"el Laredo, Alban Redheuil, Nadjia Kachenoura
items.summary: CMDiff applies conditional diffusion to segment left atrial scar in 3D LGE cardiac MRI, using a dynamic-encoder-conditioned 3D sinusoidal UNet, and is evaluated against a deterministic baseline in five-fold cross-validation on 60 LASCARQS subjects. Scar segmentation is clinically meaningful for predicting atrial fibrillation ablation outcomes but is hampered by low contrast and extreme class imbalance. The paper positions itself explicitly as a feasibility study.
items.reasoning: Clinically relevant application of conditional diffusion to a hard segmentation problem, but the small cohort (60 subjects), feasibility framing, and comparison to only a deterministic baseline limit the strength of conclusions at this stage.

items.title: Edge-Assisted Crowdsensing for Explainable Cyclist Safety Perception
items.content: arXiv:2611.08441v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Cyclist fatality rates remain high despite policy support for active travel, and autonomous vehicles add complexity to mixed traffic. Neither crash statistics nor multi-model detection pipelines scale to continuous monitoring of perceived safety along a route. We present an edge-assisted crowdsensing system: handlebar cameras supply street-level frames, a vision-language model (VLM) turns each frame into structured traffic attributes through a single prompt, and an explainable boosting machine (EBM) combines them with OpenStreetMap road infrastructure and on-bike kinematics to predict a crowdsourced 1-9 safety score. Extraction belongs at the network edge: the fastest self-hosted model needs 2.49 s per frame and scoring takes 0.4 ms on a CPU. On 1,362 annotated frames from two London routes, the EBM regressor reaches 72.2 percent binary accuracy and a mean absolute error of 1.011 under five-fold cross-validation. It is within one accuracy point of black-box ensembles. Its per-feature shape functions give exact attribution: physical lane separation is worth +0.97 rating points, a painted lane +0.70 and a construction site -0.65. Planners can therefore price an infrastructure change in rating points, and the results enter cost-benefit analysis directly. We also report inter-annotator agreement (alpha = 0.4695), an attribute audit, and a sensitivity analysis linking attribute error to accuracy. With re-encoding, a 20 s sampling interval serves 1,000 riders at 54 Mbit/s at a cost of 1.4 accuracy points, making continuous monitoring practical.

items.title: Wedge-Jamming Mechanism for String Configuration
items.content: arXiv:2611.07748v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Variable stiffness mechanisms that achieve both flexibility and rigidity are important technologies for robotic systems. Recently, wire-based jamming mechanisms have attracted significant attention. In the wire-based jamming mechanisms, modules are chained by a wire, and the overall stiffness is controlled by changing the friction between the modules through wire tension. These mechanisms have been widely studied due to their simple structure and controllability. However, conventional wire-based jamming mechanisms mainly focus on holding torque along the joint axis, and the resistance against disturbances in other directions has not been sufficiently explored. In this study, we propose a wedge-jamming mechanism that introduces wedge-shaped contact surfaces into the modules of wire-based jamming structures. By changing the wedge angle, the holding characteristics against disturbances in different directions can be adjusted. Experimental results show that an out-wedge configuration improves resistance to vertical disturbances, while an in-wedge configuration enhances resistance to torsional disturbances. These results demonstrate that the anisotropic holding performance of wire-based jamming mechanisms depend on wedge geometry.
items.author: Taro Tako, Takanori Jin, Hiroshi Kaminaga, Taisuke Kobayashi
items.summary: The authors propose a wedge-jamming mechanism for wire-based variable stiffness structures, adding wedge-shaped contacts to resist disturbances in directions beyond the joint-axis holding torque that conventional jamming mechanisms address. Variable stiffness with both flexibility and rigidity is a key enabler for soft and safe robotic systems. This extends the design space of jamming-based variable stiffness mechanisms.
items.reasoning: A credible mechanical-design contribution with clear motivation, but it is a niche hardware mechanism whose broader impact depends on adoption in variable-stiffness robot platforms.

items.title: Risk-Sensitive Non-Parametric and Kernel Bandits
items.content: arXiv:2611.06489v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: We study non-parametric bandits in which arms are evaluated using Cumulative Prospect Theory (CPT) rather than expected reward. We consider continuous action spaces with arm-dependent noise and propose Non-Parametric CPT Bandits ($\mathtt{NPCB}$), an optimistic algorithm that decouples mean estimation from CPT-based decision-making. We prove CPT regret of order $\widetilde{\mathcal O}\bigl(\sqrt{T\,\dim_E(\mathcal F,T^{-2})\,\log N(\mathcal F,T^{-2},\|\cdot\|_\infty)}\bigr)$, where $\dim_E$ is the Eluder dimension of the function class $\mathcal F$, $T$ is the time horizon, and $N$ is its covering number in the sup norm. This matches the order-wise regret of classical non-parametric bandits, showing that CPT risk sensitivity incurs no additional order-wise regret cost. We extend $\mathtt{NPCB}$ to unknown noise CDFs, retaining the known-CDF mean-learning term and adding a CDF-learning cost governed by a distributional Eluder dimension. We also study Kernel-CPT bandits and obtain information-gain-based regret bounds for a broad range of kernels, matching the corresponding risk-neutral kernel rates up to logarithmic factors.

items.title: Fundamental Limits of Coherent Imaging in The Presence of Atmospheric Turbulence
items.content: arXiv:2611.06784v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: We study the fundamental limits of jointly estimating the signal amplitude and the atmospheric phase distortion in complex-valued multi-look coherent imaging, where the measurements are corrupted by multiplicative speckle and additive Gaussian noise, all looks share a known Gaussian sensing matrix, and both parameters belong to structured classes. By analyzing a constrained maximum likelihood estimator, we establish an upper bound on the joint minimax risk that holds uniformly over the admissible parameter classes, while oracle reductions and Fano-type arguments yield worst-case lower bounds over the admissible parameter classes. These results quantify the effects of structural complexity, signal and measurement dimensions, the number of looks, and the noise level, and establish matching minimax rates in several settings, with a remaining gap for phase estimation at low noise when the measurement dimension exceeds the signal dimension. We also construct a two-stage estimator for signal recovery under arbitrary diagonal sign distortions in the real-valued analogue. Under additional conditions, it recovers the signs up to a global sign with high probability and yields a uniform signal risk bound without a distortion-complexity term. Numerical experiments illustrate the dependence of the joint, signal, and phase errors on the model parameters and provide further support for the theoretical analysis.

The results quantify how structural complexity, dimensions, and number of looks affect fundamental estimation limits.

items.title: SD-LoRA: Training-Time Structural Distillation into LoRA for Few-Shot Vision-Language Adaptation
items.content: arXiv:2611.07063v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Few-shot adaptation of vision-language models must balance two competing goals: learning fine-grained visual distinctions from very limited supervision and preserving the efficiency that makes frozen CLIP-like models attractive for deployment. Existing lightweight adaptation methods, including prompt tuning, LoRA, and cache-based adapters, typically supervise global image embeddings and therefore underuse token-level structure. Conversely, structure-aware methods exploit local evidence but often introduce additional inference-time computation. We propose SD-LoRA, a structural distillation framework that uses token-level graph reasoning only during training and transfers its effects into a lightweight LoRA-adapted CLIP model. During training, a heterogeneous graph teacher models patch-patch, global-local, and visual-text relations over high-resolution ViT tokens. Rather than retaining this graph at test time, SD-LoRA transfers its structural bias into the shared CLIP-LoRA backbone through implicit distillation and Prototype Predictive Alignment, which aligns graph-conditioned representations with support-derived class prototypes. At inference, the graph teacher is discarded; prediction requires only a single CLIP-LoRA forward pass and a cache-based classifier. Across 11 few-shot benchmarks, SD-LoRA improves over a strong CLIP-LoRA baseline by 2.4/1.8/3.0/2.4/2.0 percentage points in the 1/2/4/8/16-shot settings, respectively, without additional graph computation at test time. Results on base-to-novel generalization, cross-dataset transfer, out-of-distribution robustness, and calibration further show that training-time structural supervision improves both accuracy and transfer reliability. Code is available at https://github.com/MR-Sherif/SD-LoRA.git.

items.title: Task-Calibrated Random Features via Influence-Based Error Cancellation
items.content: arXiv:2611.07209v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Random features approximate kernel integrals by Monte Carlo, yet only selected frequency-sampling errors affect a downstream task. We propose Task-Calibrated Random Features (TCRF), which balance frequency moments constructed from task-specific influence using weights shared across kernel entries. Closed-form weights coincide with classical minimum-distance calibration; the contribution is a reusable, task-derived calibration space. We show that first-order variance equals the residual variance after projection onto this space. For kernel ridge regression, complete cancellation yields a non-Gaussian second-order limit. For kernel Stein discrepancy, a subset identity and disjoint-block variance decomposition eliminate the linear component of pilot noise. Positive exponential-tilting weights preserve the positive-semidefinite feature representation and support higher feasible calibration ranks. Paired experiments show improved approximation to exact kernel ridge regression at larger frequency budgets and to the exact empirical Stein discrepancy under a fixed alternative, even after accounting for a frequency-equivalent pilot budget. Gains are smaller with cross-validated ridge, landmark pilots require conservative rank selection, and near the Stein null allocating the pilot budget to additional ordinary frequencies is preferable.

items.title: Patch Attention Wisely: Understanding Patch Length in Attention-Based Forecasting
items.content: arXiv:2611.08160v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Attention-based time series forecasters commonly group consecutive observations into patches. Patch length is known to have a substantial impact on forecasting performance, yet its selection remains largely empirical. We develop a theoretical framework that explains why patch length matters for forecasting accuracy and provides a principled basis for its selection. For linear state-space models, we derive an exact factorization of the forecasting coefficient matrix that separates forecast dynamics from filtering dynamics. We show that dominance of a single forecast component at long horizons does not generally imply a rank-one representation. This explains why longer horizons alone need not reduce representational complexity. We combine the factorization with estimation bounds to develop a patch-selection criterion that balances representation and estimation errors under temporal dependence. Our analysis establishes conditions under which balanced patching is justified and clarifies how predictive structure, head count, training sample size, and long-run dependence enter the selection criterion.

items.title: Trust Responsive Runtime Authorization for Agentic AI with Empirical Characterization of Policy Behavior and Parameter Sensitivity
items.content: arXiv:2611.06996v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: The policy that converts runtime estimates of an autonomous agent's condition into operational authority is rarely specified or measured. We empirically characterize the Trust Responsive Authorization Policy (TRAP), which maps an Authorization Readiness Score (ARS), a weighted combination of runtime trust, operational stability, and contextual risk, onto discrete authorization levels through an asymmetric rule: escalation requires consecutive observations above a band edge plus a margin, while a sharp drop in readiness restricts authority at once. On one matched set of 100 Monte Carlo traces, we compare TRAP with static, trust-only, risk-only, and symmetric policies. Under abrupt degradation, TRAP restricts at onset and re-escalates sooner after recovery than the symmetric policy, with the highest and, descriptively, least variable stability among the adaptive policies, although more of its post-recovery escalations occur below the selected trust threshold. Paired bootstrap intervals exclude zero for the remaining differences. In one-factor sweeps, recovery time rises with the escalation margin and run length, shifts with the score weights, and is unchanged by the restriction threshold. In an exploratory post-freeze experiment, when the same degradation is spread over 5-20 intervals, TRAP restricts only on the 4 traces that retain a single-interval drop above that threshold; averaged over all 100 traces, it holds authority above what readiness supports for 15.9-18.9 of the 20 degradation intervals, against 0.8 under abrupt degradation and about 10 for the symmetric policy. Its restriction advantage therefore depends on degradation being abrupt. All reported values are traceable to the publicly available, versioned research release.

items.title: Redacting Personal Data: A Speed and Accuracy Comparison of Regex, Presidio and Hybrid Designs
items.content: arXiv:2611.07633v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Many enterprise projects now pass free text to large language models (LLMs), and that text often contains personally identifiable information (PII) such as names, phone numbers, email addresses, home addresses and dates of birth. Once a prompt is sent, this data is copied into provider systems, application logs and observability traces. Redacting PII before the call is an obvious control, yet teams seldom have numbers on what it costs in latency or what it lets through. This paper compares four redaction designs that any LLM pipeline can adopt: a pure regular-expression (regex) redactor, Microsoft Presidio running on a spaCy model, a hybrid in which Presidio finds only person names while regex handles structured identifiers, and a fast hybrid that calls spaCy's named-entity component directly. All four share a known-entity rule, which removes the person the system already knows it is handling, and a consistent placeholder scheme, so the LLM can still tell one person from another after redaction. We evaluate the designs on a sample workflow, which we call ProfileAssist, that turns resumes into structured profiles, using 100 synthetic resumes (523 characters on average, with 900 PII values and 600 business terms that must survive). Regex ran at a 0.20 ms median but caught only 88.9% of PII, because it cannot find names that are not known in advance, such as the references listed in a resume. Presidio, hybrid and fast hybrid each caught 100% of PII and kept 100% of business terms, at median latencies of 37.59 ms, 30.23 ms and 13.48 ms. Measured against a 9,120 ms median LLM call, even the slowest option adds only 0.41% to the request. We therefore recommend the fast hybrid as a default for LLM pipelines that handle personal data, with regex kept as a safety net rather than as the only control.

items.summary: The authors compare four practical PII-redaction designs for LLM pipelines: pure regex, Microsoft Presidio with spaCy, a hybrid where Presidio handles names and regex handles structured identifiers, and a fast hybrid variant. The paper quantifies the latency and recall trade-offs that teams usually lack data on when redacting prompts before they are sent to model providers. It provides actionable engineering guidance for privacy-preserving LLM deployment.

Presidio, hybrid and fast hybrid each caught 100% of PII and kept 100% of business terms, at median latencies of 37.59 ms, 30.23 ms and 13.48 ms. Measured against a 9,120 ms median LLM call, even the slowest option adds only 0.41% to the request. We therefore recommend the fast hybrid as a default for LLM pipelines that handle personal data, with regex kept as a safety net rather than as the only control.

items.title: SMART: State-based Multi Agent Reasoning Traces for Verification-oriented Problem-Solving
items.content: arXiv:2611.08196v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Complex problems with limited context, such as claims, require a means to obtain additional knowledge necessary for solution reasoning. We propose a multi-agent framework, SMART, to obtain knowledge through capturing the implicit state of participating entities in a problem context. SMART curates the state knowledge as diverse, complementary and solution-salient premises using a variety of LLMs and a structured role-based prompt strategy. Using knowledge from these real-world verified curated premises, SMART's knowledge guided solution reasoning improves validation performance up to 20% on complex scientific claims spanning 3 datasets. We show that grounding premises in real-world knowledge is necessary and improves performance up to 5%.

items.title: A minimal dynamical model of human-AI cognitive coevolution
items.content: arXiv:2611.06928v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: The rapid deployment of generative AI raises the question of whether pervasive cognitive offloading drives a measurable, potentially irreversible decline in unassisted human reasoning. We examine this question with a phenomenological dynamical model based on the Cattell-Horn-Carroll distinction between fluid intelligence ($G_f$) and crystallized intelligence ($G_c$). Starting from the discrete-time Bivariate Latent Change Score formalism used in cognitive-aging research, we derive its continuous-time linear counterpart and introduce a fast third variable representing composite machine-intelligence capability. The machine variable enters the human subsystem through Hill-function modifications of the self-feedback and cross-coupling coefficients. We emphasize that our phenomenological model captures both the positive and negative effects of AI on human cognition. By formalizing the qualitative concepts of positive and negative impacts, we introduce definitions for AI-induced cognitive decline and AI-induced cognitive augmentation. A singular-perturbation reduction, justified via Tikhonov's theorem, collapses the resulting three-dimensional system onto a two-dimensional slow manifold. On this manifold we locate two bifurcations of the equilibrium. In one parameter regime, weakening the contribution of fluid reasoning to crystallized knowledge produces a saddle-node bifurcation that eliminates the stable positive equilibrium. In another, reversing the contribution of crystallized knowledge to fluid reasoning creates opposing feedback; increasing fluid self-feedback then reduces damping and produces a supercritical Hopf bifurcation with a stable periodic orbit. We discuss limitations and future directions, interpret our results as a phenomenological account of a coupled socio-technical system, and state the conditions under which each dynamical regime applies.

items.summary: Builds a phenomenological dynamical model, based on fluid vs. crystallized intelligence from cognitive-aging research, to study whether pervasive cognitive offloading onto generative AI could cause lasting declines in unassisted human reasoning. The model couples human intelligence variables to a machine-intelligence variable via Hill functions, providing a formal framework for a widely debated societal question.
items.reasoning: Tackles a timely and important question about human-AI cognitive coevolution with an interesting transfer of longitudinal cognitive modeling tools. However, it is a phenomenological model with assumptions that are hard to validate empirically, limiting its evidential weight; conceptual contribution rather than new capability.

items.title: Depth or Description? When a One-Step Latent Score Replaces Lookahead in Proactive Information Acquisition
items.content: arXiv:2611.07155v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: A proactive agent must decide what to ask before it acts. Exact lookahead values combinations of questions but is expensive and leans on a fitted model; a one-step score is cheap but can miss them. Our main finding: the need for depth often lies in how the hidden cause is described. A one-step score on the label can be blind to an interaction among answers. A score on a suitable latent cause is not, and where that latent encodes the decision it replaces most of depth at a fraction of the search. Described differently, the same problem can defeat the score while exact values do not move, so keep the latent small and check it against exact values. Probabilities learned from one language model's answers do not carry to another unless planning allows for both; those read from tokens are worth only a few labels.
items.author: Biswa Sengupta
items.summary: Analyzes when a cheap one-step score can replace expensive lookahead in proactive agents deciding what to ask before acting, finding that the need for depth often depends on how hidden causes are described. A score computed on a suitable latent representation can substitute for most of the search depth, while the same problem can defeat a label-level score, with cross-model transfer caveats.
items.reasoning: An interesting conceptual result connecting representation choice to planning depth in proactive agents, with practical implications for efficient agent design. However, it is a single-author analysis piece with limited empirical breadth shown in the abstract, and the framing is somewhat abstract.

items.title: Selective Retrieval Routing for Multi-Violation Knowledge Graph Repair
items.content: arXiv:2611.07342v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Knowledge graphs often contain missing or inconsistent facts that undermine the applications built on them. Schema validation detects such violations but does not identify which of several valid repairs recovers the intended graph. External corpora can supply the evidence needed to identify the intended repair, but retrieving from them is costly and not always successful. We propose a framework for selective retrieval in iterative graph repair. An LLM repair agent explores and edits the graph, while a router controls its access to a researcher agent that retrieves external evidence. We extend a violation-injection framework to generate cases with multiple compatible violations and known reference repairs. The agent's repair outcomes on these cases provide supervision for training the deployment-specific router. On two building-automation datasets, researcher access improves repairs for some violations and degrades them for others, with effects differing across deployments. The router uses fewer repair-time tokens than always enabling access in all six evaluation suites. It achieves higher repair $F_1$ than always disabling access in five of six suites.
items.author: Tung-Wei Lin, Gabe Fierro, Han Li, Tianzhen Hong, Pierluigi Nuzzo, Alberto Sangiovanni-Vinentelli
items.summary: The paper proposes a framework for iterative knowledge graph repair in which an LLM repair agent edits the graph while a router selectively controls access to a retrieval agent that gathers external evidence, cutting retrieval costs. The authors extend a violation-injection framework to generate cases with multiple compatible violations and known reference repairs for evaluation. This addresses when external retrieval is worth its cost during graph repair.
items.reasoning: A sensible agent-orchestration contribution combining LLMs, knowledge graphs, and cost-aware retrieval routing, with a careful evaluation methodology. The application niche is relatively narrow and the academic team is mid-tier, so impact is likely moderate rather than field-shaping.

items.title: Echoes of Error: Residual-Directional Local Rollout Consistency for Timeseries Forecasting
items.content: arXiv:2611.07473v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: In time-series forecasting, rollout errors are not merely one-step fitting discrepancies: once fed back into the evolving state, they can perturb future predictions. We formalize this effect through local rollout consistency, which compares the next prediction produced under teacher forcing with that produced under free running. In principle, this consistency can be enforced directly by tracking the residual-induced perturbation of the next state. In practice, however, the residual-to-state alignment operator is often difficult to design when the input state and output block have different dimensions, heterogeneous components, or architecture-dependent layouts. We therefore use a first-order local surrogate that penalizes the Jacobian-vector product of the predictor along the actual feedback perturbation, suppressing precisely the directions through which self-generated errors remain visible to future predictions. We further give the same loss a geometric interpretation near a predictive manifold: by controlling residual-induced directions that probe the normal bundle, the objective yields theoretical conditions under which free-running trajectories remain inside a stability tube around the manifold. Experiments on time series forecasting tasks support this view, showing that the proposed regularization improves predictive accuracy. More broadly, our results suggest a training principle for time-series forecasters and sequential predictors: a model should not only make small one-step errors, but also learn not to let its own errors echo into the future. Code is available at https://github.com/Wangzzzzzzzz/Echoes-Of-Error.
items.author: Zheng Wang, Kaixuan Zhang, Xiaonan Lu, Wanfang Chen
items.summary: Formalizes how rollout errors in time-series forecasting compound when fed back into the evolving state, introducing local rollout consistency that compares predictions under teacher forcing versus free running. Because the residual-to-state alignment operator is hard to design across architectures, the authors derive a first-order surrogate penalizing Jacobian-vector products in the residual direction. This yields a training regularizer aimed at reducing compounding rollout error.
items.reasoning: A technically sound and well-motivated regularizer for a well-known problem (compounding rollout error), but the scope is an incremental training technique within time-series forecasting rather than a broad advance. Novelty is moderate and empirical evidence is only sketched in the abstract.

items.title: Neural Image Compression with Internal-External Prior Fusion and Alignment
items.content: arXiv:2611.07644v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Existing context models for learned image com- pression rely primarily on internal priors from the current image, overlooking common patterns and typical textures shared across natural images. To address this limitation, we propose an Internal-External Prior Fusion-Alignment (IE-PFA) context model built upon quadtree spatial-channel joint modeling, where a learnable dictionary shared by the encoder and decoder serves as an external prior. Specifically, an RWKV-based Spatial- Channel Prior Fusion (RSCPF) module efficiently fuses inter- nal and external priors along spatial and channel dimensions with linear complexity, while a training-only Self-Distilled Prior Alignment (SDPA) mechanism aligns them without inference overhead. Moreover, our model supports variable-rate coding over 64 quality levels within a single network and is accelerated by custom CUDA operators. Experiments on seven benchmarks demonstrate state-of-the-art rate-distortion performance, achiev- ing an average BD-Rate saving of 21.65% over VTM-22.0-Intra, with only 29.9M parameters and the fastest coding speed among advanced neural codecs (61 ms encoding and 52 ms decoding). Code is available at https://github.com/stcnjtech/DCVC-X-Intra.

items.reasoning: A competent architecture contribution to learned image compression with sensible efficiency choices (RWKV, training-only alignment), but in a specialized subfield with incremental novelty over existing context models.

items.title: Network Effect Decomposition for Causal Effect Estimation under Network Interference
items.content: arXiv:2611.07879v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Estimating causal effects from observational network data requires accounting for both individual treatment and neighborhood exposure. Existing outcome models commonly incorporate these intervention variables into a joint predictor and estimate causal effects through prediction contrasts, leaving the corresponding response components implicit. We propose the $\underline{N}$etwork $\underline{E}$ffect $\underline{D}$ecomposition $\underline{Net}$work (NEDNet), which parameterizes the conditional outcome response as a query-invariant pre-treatment baseline plus separate treatment- and exposure-response pathways. Path-specific neighborhood contextualization supplies local pre-treatment information to the two pathways. We characterize the fitted response through a unique reference-normalized decomposition, which is equivalent to a zero mixed treatment--exposure contrast. Experiments on semi-synthetic benchmarks derived from BlogCatalog and Flickr show that NEDNet achieves the lowest PEHE among the compared methods for individual, peer, and total effects across homogeneous and covariate-heterogeneous response settings.
items.author: Zhirong Huang, Wenzhen Zhang, Guangquan Lu, Boyan Chen, Debo Cheng, Shichao Zhang
items.summary: NEDNet is a neural architecture for causal effect estimation under network interference that decomposes outcome response into a query-invariant pre-treatment baseline plus separate treatment- and exposure-response pathways, with path-specific neighborhood contextualization. This addresses the common flaw of joint predictors that leave response components implicit in network data. It advances causal inference methodology for interconnected observational data.
items.reasoning: A principled methodological contribution to causal ML under interference, a genuinely hard and important problem, but targeted at a specialist audience and its impact depends on empirical validation beyond the abstract's characterization of fitting behavior.

items.title: tok: a textual concrete syntax of BPMN and DMN for humans and AI agents
items.content: arXiv:2611.07945v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: tok is a plain-text notation for Business Process Model and Notation (BPMN) 2.0.2 process models and Decision Model and Notation (DMN) 1.5 decisions. One engine checks a tok document against both standards, compiles the document to XML with an automatic diagram, and serves language-model applications through the Model Context Protocol. The paper classifies the notation as an alternative concrete syntax of the BPMN and DMN metamodels and reports one study. A tok model takes 2.2 times fewer tokens than the smallest BPMN XML of 893 files exported by 37 tools and 7.7 times fewer than the files as exported. The checker signals 98.2% of 1,411 injected faults, against 85.8% for the XML Schema with bpmnlint. Four language models new to tok write valid tok from a one-page reference for 85.7 to 100% of 87 process descriptions from two datasets and valid BPMN XML for every description, and the strongest model writes tok with 25% and 19% fewer tokens than BPMN XML. As agents with a lean skill and one checker tool, the models write valid tok for 97.6 to 100% of the descriptions, the strongest model spends 21% and 14% fewer tokens on tok than on BPMN XML, and a skill which sends the model to read the reference through a tool costs 1.7 to 2.8 times the tokens of the lean skill. Of 47 event logs simulated from public models, 44 fit their source models, and tok imports every model discovered from the logs.

This is a practical bridge between formal business-process standards and LLM agents.

items.title: DART: Domain-Agnostic Residual Transfer for Generalist Anomaly Detection
items.content: arXiv:2611.08271v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Generalist Anomaly Detection (GAD) aims to detect anomalies in unseen domains using only a few reference samples. Recent normal-abnormal guided methods improve this setting by exploiting abnormal references, but their residuals often mix transferable anomaly cues with domain-specific appearance factors such as texture, geometry, and acquisition conditions. This residual domain entanglement limits cross-domain transfer and may produce spurious activations on novel domains. We propose DART, a plug-in framework for normal-abnormal guided GAD that learns to separate residuals into anomaly-relevant and domain-specific components. DART combines a Residual Disentanglement Module, which preserves anomaly-discriminative information while suppressing domain information, with Cross-Domain Meta-Training, which forms episodes across source domains to make the separation effective. The method is architecture-agnostic and can be inserted between residual computation and the detection head of existing GAD pipelines. Experiments on MVTec AD, VisA, and BraTS show consistent improvements over multiple base methods, with the largest gains under stronger domain shifts. https://github.com/aqeeelmirza/DART

items.summary: DART is a plug-in framework for few-shot generalist anomaly detection that disentangles residuals from normal-abnormal reference comparisons into anomaly-relevant and domain-specific components, suppressing spurious activations on unseen domains. It combines a Residual Disentanglement Module with domain-invariant filtering to improve cross-domain transfer.
items.reasoning: A reasonable architectural contribution to a growing anomaly detection subfield, addressing a clearly articulated problem (residual domain entanglement). However, plug-in refinements to existing normal-abnormal guided methods typically yield incremental benchmark gains rather than conceptual advances.

items.title: Backbone-Informed Adaptation after EEG Pretraining: A Capacity-Controlled Study
items.content: arXiv:2611.07192v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) foundation models learn representations that combine information across channels and time. This structure motivates adapters that model the same relationships during downstream learning. However, it is not clear whether such a design outperforms other candidate adapters. Moreover, in order to arrive at a fair comparison between candidate adapters, we also need to consider their trainable parameters. Here, we ask whether a backbone-informed (native) adapter makes better use of a given capacity by comparing it against a token-wise multilayer perceptron control that transforms each feature vector independently. We approximately match their trainable parameter counts and keep the pretrained encoder fixed. Across two EEG foundation models and tasks covering emotion recognition, sleep staging, and EEG event classification, the native adapter shows no consistent advantage. For one backbone, differences between the designs are small relative to variation across runs. For the other, the token-wise control performs better on emotion recognition and EEG event classification. On sleep staging, the native adapter's advantage over the token-wise control is reduced when we also train the component that processes sequences of EEG segments. The relative performance of the two adapters depends on the backbone, task, and downstream training protocol. These findings motivate evaluating backbone-informed adapters against capacity-matched alternatives.
items.author: Mingyang Jiang, Yamin Li, Fan Ma, Daniel Moyer, Hua Xu, Catie Chang
items.summary: This study asks whether adapters that mirror the channel-time structure of EEG foundation models outperform simpler token-wise MLP adapters, under controlled and approximately matched parameter counts with frozen encoders. It is a careful capacity-controlled comparison across two settings. The result informs adapter design for EEG and possibly other structured-modality foundation models.

items.content_html: arXiv:2611.07192v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) foundation models learn representations that combine information across channels and time. This structure motivates adapters that model the same relationships during downstream learning. However, it is not clear whether such a design outperforms other candidate adapters. Moreover, in order to arrive at a fair comparison between candidate adapters, we also need to consider their trainable parameters. Here, we ask whether a backbone-informed (native) adapter makes better use of a given capacity by comparing it against a token-wise multilayer perceptron control that transforms each feature vector independently. We approximately match their trainable parameter counts and keep the pretrained encoder fixed. Across two EEG foundation models and tasks covering emotion recognition, sleep staging, and EEG event classification, the native adapter shows no consistent advantage. For one backbone, differences between the designs are small relative to variation across runs. For the other, the token-wise control performs better on emotion recognition and EEG event classification. On sleep staging, the native adapter's advantage over the token-wise control is reduced when we also train the component that processes sequences of EEG segments. The relative performance of the two adapters depends on the backbone, task, and downstream training protocol. These findings motivate evaluating backbone-informed adapters against capacity-matched alternatives.

items.title: Two-stage residual learning for calibrated uncertainty in solar irradiance forecasts
items.content: arXiv:2611.07444v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Accurate forecasting of renewable generation requires not only point predictions but also reliable estimates of the uncertainty attached to them, particularly at extended horizons. Machine learning models are increasingly used to predict solar output, but they typically report a single value and capture the associated uncertainty poorly. The standard remedy is to train a model to predict the parameters of an assumed probability distribution directly. Here we develop an alternative two-stage method, motivated by synthetic solar signal generation, in which the forecast error is modeled separately from the expected irradiance. A first long short-term memory (LSTM) network predicts the expected global horizontal irradiance, and a second network models the distribution of the forecast error, which is added back to the mean to give both the forecast and its uncertainty. Using historical weather data from the National Solar Radiation Database and a probability integral transform evaluation, we show that explicitly modeling the error brings the predicted standard deviation markedly closer to the historical value, reducing the deviation between the two by 34.6 percent for a standalone LSTM and by 56.5 percent when the LSTM is coupled to Gaussian process regression, the most reliable of the configurations tested. Because the method models the total forecast error directly, it captures the full predictive uncertainty that matters for decisions, rather than only the model contribution that dropout-based approaches estimate.

items.reasoning: Practical contribution to uncertainty quantification in renewable forecasting with a clean alternative to parametric density prediction, but the technique is a modest variation on residual and distributional regression ideas.

items.title: Understanding Data Influence in Transportation Networks: A Physics-Constrained Influence-Function Framework
items.content: arXiv:2611.07526v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Understanding how individual training observations influence model predictions is important for developing reliable and interpretable data-driven transportation systems. Existing influence-function methods, however, are primarily formulated for unconstrained learning and do not explicitly account for physical constraints that couple different components of a transportation network. Under such constraints, perturbing a training observation can affect model parameters and predictions only through physically feasible directions, potentially changing how its influence propagates across the network. This paper develops a hard physics-informed influence-function framework for constrained learning, in which training-data influence is characterized within the physically feasible space defined by network constraints. The analytical results reveal how physical constraints alter the magnitude, direction, and spatial distribution of training-sample influence relative to conventional influence measures. Using traffic prediction under flow-conservation constraints as a case study, we show that influential observations identified by the proposed framework differ systematically from those identified by classical influence functions. Through orthogonal decomposition, we quantitatively characterize how much of a perturbation in the training data is propagated through the network via the flow-conservation constraints and how much is removed by the constraint projection. The proposed influence framework provides a physically consistent approach for evaluating training-data influence in constrained transportation learning problems, with potential applications to data diagnostics, sensor evaluation, and targeted data collection.

items.title: Comparing Classification and Feature Learning by Analyzing Their Loss Functions in Normalized Spaces with Different Scale Factors
items.content: arXiv:2611.07741v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Classification and feature learning are two closely interrelated fundamental tasks. Feature learning in supervised settings is typically achieved by training classification models, under the common assumption that higher classification accuracy implies better feature quality. In this paper, we first point out that classification accuracy reflects the sample-wise local properties of a model on a dataset, whereas feature learning aims to learn features with good dataset-level global properties, such as intra-class compactness and inter-class separability. From the first principle of feature learning, we redesign the binary cross-entropy (BCE) loss, a counterpart of the cross-entropy (CE) loss used in classification. Then, in normalized feature space, we analyze the minima of the BCE and CE losses and show that both can lead to neural collapse, where sample features from different classes become maximally compact and maximally separated. More importantly, by investigating the convergence behaviors of the two losses as the scale factor $\gamma$ varies in the normalized space, we reveal how classification accuracy and feature quality change differently across spaces of different sizes. Under a fixed training strategy, a very large $\gamma$ achieves perfect classification accuracy but slows convergence toward the ideal feature geometry, whereas a very small $\gamma$ makes classification highly sensitive to small perturbations. A moderate $\gamma$ is therefore necessary for simultaneously achieving reliable classification and well-structured features. Extensive experiments validate these findings and demonstrate that BCE loss exhibits advantages in long-tail and open-set recognitions, as it better aligns with the global requirements of feature learning.

items.title: GTAFL: Addressing Test-Agnostic Long-Tailed Federated Learning in Medical Image
items.content: arXiv:2611.08021v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: In healthcare, protecting patient privacy is crucial due to the sensitivity of medical data and its extensive accessibility. Federated Learning (FL) offers a decentralized and privacy-preserving training paradigm, making it an ideal solution for healthcare applications. A critical challenge in healthcare is that real-world medical data often exhibits long-tailed distributions in local and global views. Existing methods addressing long-tailed FL problem typically assume that the model will be evaluated on uniform test data distribution. However, practical test data in healthcare systems is often agnostic and unpredictable, leading to potential model failures in real-world scenarios. In this paper, we introduce a novel task termed Test-Agnostic Long-Tailed Federated Learning and propose GTAFL, a comprehensive framework to address this challenge. During the training stage, GTAFL employs adaptive re-sampling, expert classifier retraining, and self-supervised learning to correct biased classifiers and distorted feature spaces caused by long-tailed training distributions. During the inference stage, an ensemble mechanism combines retrained expert classifiers to handle test data with unknown distributions. Extensive experiments on CIFAR10 and two medical datasets manifest that our framework outperforms other state-of-the-art methods. The code is available at https://github.com/cgy-lavine/GTAFL

items.summary: The paper introduces Test-Agnostic Long-Tailed Federated Learning (GTAFL), addressing the realistic healthcare scenario where federated medical data is long-tailed in local and global views while test distributions are unpredictable. Existing long-tailed FL methods typically assume uniform test distributions, which fails in practice. The proposed approach targets privacy-preserving decentralized training robust to agnostic test shifts.
items.reasoning: Well-motivated problem formulation combining two real challenges in medical FL, but the abstract suggests incremental combination of known techniques rather than a fundamental advance.

items.title: ToroFit: Fitting Wedge Sums of Tori to High-Dimensional Data
items.content: arXiv:2611.06990v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Data arising in scientific applications often exhibits complex nonlinear structure. Identifying and parameterizing said nonlinearities can enable better modeling, enhance predictive analysis, data interpolation, denoising, and anomaly detection. In this paper, we develop theoretical and computational methods to detect and parametrize Euclidean point cloud data lying near a wedge sum of tori. Specifically, we use persistent cohomology and cup products to identify the distinct toroidal components, and on each component, we optimize over low-energy multivariate trigonometric polynomials for best data fit. The ensuing optimization problem reduces to generalized ridge regression, which can be solved efficiently via standard techniques. We demonstrate the utility of the proposed framework in both synthetic and real datasets, including interpolation of low frame-rate recurrent videos, attractor recovery in quasiperiodic dynamical systems, and the parametrization of gene-space cycle data for parasites and humans.

items.title: EDGAR: Efficient Diffusion-Driven Gaussian Avatar Refinement via Synthetic Failure
items.content: arXiv:2611.07909v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Recent advances in Gaussian splatting have enabled efficient and photorealistic head avatar reconstruction, yet monocular video-based or image-based methods still suffer from under-constrained geometry and texture, leading to artifacts such as blurring, stretching, and temporal instability. We present EDGAR (Efficient Diffusion-Driven Gaussian Avatar Refinement), a conditional diffusion framework designed to enhance the quality of Gaussian avatars by correcting artifacts while preserving identity fidelity. To train EDGAR, we construct EDGAR-SET, a hybrid triplet dataset composed of real-captured and synthetic-rendered samples, which simulates realistic Gaussian avatar failure cases by pairing degraded renderings with ground-truth and reference images. EDGAR refines degraded frames through a fusion block that injects identity features extracted by the self-supervised Sapiens model into a one-step diffusion backbone, enabling effective artifact removal without sacrificing efficiency. Our EDGAR model incorporates a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architecture to address diverse degradation types and severity levels. The refined multi-view renderings are subsequently used as pseudo-targets to optimize a single underlying Gaussian avatar, so that the final avatar can be rendered without applying EDGAR to every output frame. Experiments on three different Gaussian avatar reconstruction methods, each evaluated under three different settings, show improvements in both perceptual and reconstruction measures over the raw outputs and an SDEdit-style refinement baseline. In addition, cross-view evaluation demonstrates improved calibrated consistency, while tests under large yaw and open-mouth expressions verify robustness under extreme settings. These results collectively indicate a useful operating regime for recoverable appearance artifacts. The code is available at https://kwanyun.github.io/edgar/

items.title: Regret Bounds for Profit Maximization in Bilateral Trade: Learning the Best Posted-Price Mechanism
items.content: arXiv:2611.08173v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Bilateral trade models the task of intermediating between two strategic agents, a seller and a buyer, willing to trade a good for which they hold private valuations. We study this problem from the perspective of a profit-maximizing broker in a regret minimization framework. At each time step, a new seller and buyer arrive and the broker proposes a trading price to each agent. The trade happens if both agents accept, and the profit of the broker is the difference between the price received from the buyer and the one paid to the seller. At the end of each interaction, the learner only observes whether the trade occurred, and its goal is to achieve sublinear regret relative to the best fixed pair of prices in hindsight.   We start by investigating the adversarial version of the problem, where buyer and seller valuations are generated by an adversary. In this setting, we construct a polynomial-time learning algorithm with a $\tilde O(T^{\frac 23})$ regret rate, which is nearly tight even if the valuations are drawn i.i.d. from independent distributions, thus matching the rate for one-sided pricing. Our adversarial algorithm combines a localized estimation procedure with an information-based minimax construction.   We then consider valuations drawn i.i.d. from independent distributions satisfying the monotone-hazard-rate (MHR) property and provide a learning algorithm with nearly tight $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{T})$ regret. The algorithm combines localized estimation with a stochastic convex bandit routine applied to the negative logarithm of expected profit. Finally, we complement this result by showing a separation between MHR and regular distributions, proving that the minimax regret rate in the latter setting is $\tilde \Theta(T^{\frac 35})$. This last result contrasts with the $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{T})$ regret bound that can be obtained for one-sided pricing with regular distributions.

items.title: Human-like cross-language generalisation in deep neural speaker embeddings and its acoustic foundations
items.content: arXiv:2611.05384v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Generalisability is a central question for deep neural networks, including the cross-language generalisation of speaker embeddings. This study examined whether deep neural speaker embeddings generalise across languages and how such generalisation relates to human perception and acoustic structure. Using Cantonese--English bilingual speech presented in within- and cross-language conditions, we derived similarity from 18 state-of-the-art models and compared it with human ratings and acoustic features using linear mixed models and representational similarity analysis. Embeddings exhibited cross-language generalisation that broadly paralleled human behaviour, reflecting accurate identity discrimination and sensitivity to language switching. This generalisation relied on largely shared acoustic cues with language-sensitive weighting, mirroring human patterns. Together, these findings provide converging evidence for human--machine alignment in cross-language voice similarity processing.

Embeddings showed cross-language generalization broadly paralleling human behavior, reflecting identity discrimination and sensitivity to language switching. This connects machine speaker representations to human auditory perception and their acoustic underpinnings.

items.title: ProcessPrefBench: Evaluating Cross-Task Transfer of Individual Process Preferences from Naturalistic Human-AI Interaction
items.content: arXiv:2611.06065v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: In natural human-AI dialogue, users' corrections, requests, and self-descriptions carry reusable signals about how they want work to be done. These signals reveal individual process preferences, user-specific standards for evidence, depth, analytical focus, procedure, and delivery. We ask whether a preference revealed in one dialogue can shape an assistant's later answer when the task does not restate it. ProcessPrefBench uses three months of natural dialogues from two knowledge workers to build 66 source-target cases separately judged for source evidence and target applicability. Sources are preselected, so the benchmark tests application rather than retrieval. We test three models with target-only, full-history, and distilled-preference prompts. Target-specific 0-2 rubrics score preference realization, and a task gate flags severe failures. Compared with target-only prompting, full-history and imperative distilled-preference prompting raise preference realization by 0.204 and 0.244 points on the 0-2 scale, respectively, with no reliable advantage from distillation. Fabricated-evidence failures rise from 5.8% under target-only prompting to 10.1% under full-history and 10.4% under imperative prompting. ProcessPrefBench highlights a tension in learning from dialogue, where drawing on prior interactions can improve preference realization yet also invite fabricated evidence. We hope it helps build assistants that honor a user's process preferences without sacrificing factual reliability.
items.author: Yiwen Yang, Guanming Liu
items.summary: Introduces ProcessPrefBench, built from three months of natural dialogues between two knowledge workers and an assistant, testing whether a user's process preference revealed in one conversation transfers to later, unrelated tasks. It evaluates three models under target-only, full-history, and distilled-preference conditions on 66 curated source-target cases.
items.reasoning: A novel question at the intersection of personalization and instruction-following, but the benchmark is very small (66 cases, two users), limiting statistical power and generalizability.

items.content_html: arXiv:2611.06065v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In natural human-AI dialogue, users' corrections, requests, and self-descriptions carry reusable signals about how they want work to be done. These signals reveal individual process preferences, user-specific standards for evidence, depth, analytical focus, procedure, and delivery. We ask whether a preference revealed in one dialogue can shape an assistant's later answer when the task does not restate it. ProcessPrefBench uses three months of natural dialogues from two knowledge workers to build 66 source-target cases separately judged for source evidence and target applicability. Sources are preselected, so the benchmark tests application rather than retrieval. We test three models with target-only, full-history, and distilled-preference prompts. Target-specific 0-2 rubrics score preference realization, and a task gate flags severe failures. Compared with target-only prompting, full-history and imperative distilled-preference prompting raise preference realization by 0.204 and 0.244 points on the 0-2 scale, respectively, with no reliable advantage from distillation. Fabricated-evidence failures rise from 5.8% under target-only prompting to 10.1% under full-history and 10.4% under imperative prompting. ProcessPrefBench highlights a tension in learning from dialogue, where drawing on prior interactions can improve preference realization yet also invite fabricated evidence. We hope it helps build assistants that honor a user's process preferences without sacrificing factual reliability.

items.title: Template Gap Reconstruction for Shell Output Simulation with Small Language Models
items.content: arXiv:2611.06731v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Small language models offer a compact basis for shell simulation without executing submitted commands, but full-output decoding requires them to predict recurring utility structure alongside content that varies across executions. We introduce template gap reconstruction (TGR), which supplies reusable output literals interspersed with sentinels to be interleaved with autoregressively generated gaps. A template selector chooses which template to be reconstructed, with the empty template retaining full-output decoding. We construct a template bank from 18.7 million outputs collected across heterogeneous execution environments and train a template selector and five reconstruction models initialized from various small language model checkpoints on a target environment excluded from bank construction. Evaluation demonstrates that TGR improves output edit similarity (O-ES) over full-output decoding (FOD) when the optimal template covers more than 25\% of the template, while performing similarly for lower-coverage outputs. Additionally, TGR outperforms FOD for shorter gap sequences, with O-ES values of 0.964 and 0.812, respectively, while maintaining similar performance for longer sequences. TGR reduces the number of tokens generated by 26.3--38.3\% across used tokenizer families. These results support using a reusable output structure as a practical design choice for small shell simulators, improving response fidelity and shortening generation targets while keeping template selection and residual prediction central to response quality.

items.title: Self-Supervised Diffusion Models for Handwritten Signature Verification via Ruin Reconstruction
items.content: arXiv:2611.07810v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Handwritten signature verification (HSV) is a critical biometric technique in legal and forensic authentication, whose efficacy hinges on the discriminability of signature representations. Current HSV methods predominantly adopt supervised learning to enhance representation quality, leaving self-supervised learning largely unexplored. We propose \emph{SigDiffuser}, a diffusion-based self-supervised framework for signature representation and verification. At its core, \emph{SigDiffuser} introduces a novel pretext task termed \emph{Reconstruction from Ruins (RFR)}, which deliberately ``ruins'' signatures through severe crumpling, obliterating their structural integrity and writing styles. A visual encoder is employed to capture crucial handwriting patterns from intact signature regions, guiding the denoiser to reconstruct the ``ruined'' portions and learning meaningful representations. Additionally, we introduce a \emph{pyramidal feature aggregation module (PFAM)} to bridge the visual encoder and denoiser, enhancing representation quality via hierarchical aggregation and modulation. Extensive experiments on multilingual signature datasets demonstrate that \emph{SigDiffuser} significantly outperforms both state-of-the-art SSL methods and HSV models. We further show that increasing the crumpling severity on signatures effectively improves representation quality. Notably, our work demonstrates that extreme destruction, coupled with self-supervised diffusion models, can yield superior signature representation compared to traditional mild deformations, paving new avenues for HSV and other biometric domains. Code will be publicly available.

items.title: Describe Your Facial Expressions by Linking Image Encoders and Large Language Models
items.content: arXiv:2611.08138v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: This paper presents a novel task of describing human facial expressions of a facial image in natural language, which captures the nuances of facial actions and emotional states beyond traditional emotion categories or facial action units (AUs). To achieve the facial expression captioning model, we propose a three-stage training framework that trains a vision-to-language model using synthesized image-text pairs and the BLIP-2 pre-training techniques. To overcome the challenge of missing training image-text pairs for facial expression captioning, we propose a strategy that involves synthesizing and combining captions using GPT-3.5 and existing annotations on either emotion categories or AUs. Experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of our method in generating captions that describe details of facial actions and emotions, as well as the inferential relationship between them, even when those emotions are not present in the training data. It is also demonstrated that the vision-to-language task enhances the performance of the intermediate visual features on both AU detection and emotion classification tasks.

items.title: An Empirical Study of Reinforcement Learning for Keypoint Positioning of Deformable Linear Objects
items.content: arXiv:2611.07261v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Deformable linear object (DLO) manipulation is challenging because high-dimensional configurations, nonlinear contact dynamics, and diverse material and geometric properties produce a broad range of object responses that are both difficult to model and data-intensive to learn. This work studies reinforcement learning for planar manipulation of a one-end-grasped DLO, focusing on training efficiency, observation design, robustness, and zero-shot sim-to-real transfer. We compare three Proximal Policy Optimization training stacks and find that the GPU-parallel MuJoCo Playground stack enables faster convergence and more consistent performance than CPU-based alternatives under the same wall-clock budget. Relative keypoint observations and an asymmetric actor-critic formulation further improve learning efficiency. Policies trained with observation noise, delay, domain randomization, and disturbances achieve simulation success rates of 96.4% for single-point tracking, 98.0% for disturbance recovery, and 88.8% for two-point tracking. Using markerless RGB-D keypoint estimation, the policies transfer without real-world fine-tuning, succeeding in 9/10, 10/10, and 8/10 physical trials, respectively.

items.summary: This empirical study compares three PPO training stacks for planar manipulation of grasped deformable linear objects, finding GPU-parallel MuJoCo Playground enables faster convergence than CPU alternatives under equal wall-clock budgets. It also examines observation design, asymmetric actor-critic setups, robustness, and zero-shot sim-to-real transfer.
items.reasoning: Practical empirical guidance for sim-to-real DLO manipulation with a useful finding about GPU-parallel training stacks; solid methodology but bounded novelty and narrow task domain.

items.title: Flexible Piezoelectric Tactile Sensing System for Intelligent Object Recognition
items.content: arXiv:2611.07779v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Tactile sensing provides information about object properties that can improve robotic grasping and manipulation. However, accurate object recognition during the early stages of grasping remains challenging, particularly under strict real-time constraints. This study presents a flexible, distributed piezoelectric tactile sensing system for early-stage object recognition. The system was experimentally evaluated using six everyday objects and three recognition approaches: feature-based classification using support vector machines (SVMs), raw-signal classification using 1D convolutional neural networks (1D-CNNs) and convolutional recurrent neural networks (C-RNNs), and spatiotemporal heatmap classification using a 2D-CNN. The effects of sensor count and temporal window size on recognition accuracy and real-time feasibility were systematically investigated. Increasing the number of sensing elements improved recognition performance across all approaches. The best-performing method, based on spatiotemporal heatmaps and a 2D-CNN, achieved F1-scores of 0.9796, 0.9846, and 0.9903 using 16, 24, and 32 sensors, respectively. The optimal configuration, comprising 32 sensors and a 100-ms temporal window (50 samples), was deployed on an embedded edge platform, achieving an end-to-end recognition latency of approximately 101 ms from contact onset and an energy consumption of 63.8 microjoules per inference. These results demonstrate the potential of distributed piezoelectric tactile sensing for accurate, energy-efficient, and real-time object recognition during robotic grasping.

items.title: Distributed Geometric Optimization and Control of Rigid Differential-Drive Formations from Relative-Position Measurements
items.content: arXiv:2611.07163v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Distance based formation control fixes the shape of a robot team but leaves its position and orientation unconstrained. We regulate all three for differential drive robots that have only one absolute position anchor, absolute headings, body frame relative position measurements, and communication with their neighbors. We derive a two layer estimation control scheme directly from optimization. The first half of the result is a set of graph-proximal estimators that reconstruct the centroid, the anchor vector, and the centered coordinates. Exact proximal updates reach consensus in finitely many steps, and a finite number of primal dual iterations leaves a bounded reconstruction error. The controller combines proximal centroid and orientation steps with distance gradient shape regulation, and a finite rotation removes the orientation drift caused by the shape step. A discrete Lyapunov analysis gives local exponential convergence once the estimators have converged. We validate the method in ROS 2 Gazebo and in experiments with five physical robots.
items.author: Thanacha Choopojcharoen, Erman Selim, Ramisha Anjum, Baris Fidan
items.summary: The paper derives a two-layer estimation-and-control scheme for differential-drive robot formations with only relative-position measurements and a single absolute position anchor, regulating position, orientation, and shape. It proves finite-step consensus for graph-proximal estimators and bounded reconstruction error from a finite number of primal-dual iterations, combining proximal centroid and orientation supervision in the controller.
items.reasoning: A rigorous theoretical contribution to distributed formation control with finite-time guarantees, which is valuable for multi-robot systems with minimal sensing. The setting (differential-drive, single anchor) is fairly specific and the differential-drive nonholonomic constraint adds practical complexity that may limit clean deployment.

items.title: Support Vector Machines Directly Minimise KL Divergence
items.content: arXiv:2611.05557v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Support vector machines (SVMs) are fundamentally grounded in geometric margin maximisation and currently lack a mainstream probabilistic interpretation. This keeps them theoretically isolated from probabilistic machine learning models that are naturally comparable and combinable. In this paper, we bridge this gap by proving that the dual objectives of both support vector classification and support vector regression are exact, constrained Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence minimisation tasks between two Gaussian measures. We further show that this same divergence formulation recovers the exact objective function for kernel ridge regression when domain constraints are removed and $L^2$ regularisation is applied. By demonstrating that SVM duals directly minimise relative entropy, our results provide a unified information-theoretic model for standard kernel machines and lay the foundation for unifying broader kernel-based algorithms under probability theory.

items.reasoning: An elegant theoretical bridge between geometric margin-based methods and probabilistic machine learning, potentially enabling SVMs to be compared and combined with probabilistic models. Conceptually satisfying, though largely of theoretical interest since SVMs are no longer at the frontier of applied ML.

items.title: Is it better to directly or indirectly ban ASI?
items.content:
Senator Bernie Sanders has proposed directly banning development of ASI. Given the current scientific understanding of AI alignment, it is highly sensible to ban ASI and then consider revoking this ban if future scientific breakthroughs (e.g., “solving interp”) make it possible to safely develop ASI, or if there is truly no way to coordinate on everyone avoiding developing ASI.

Some people have proposed banning ASI indirectly instead. For instance, one could mandate:

Developing AI with superhuman capabilities is not permitted unless you can demonstrate that the AI systems you are developing won’t X, where X is some action that, in the short term, AI companies would find extremely costly or impossible to prevent their AI from taking.

Candidate notions of X include: kill people if given the opportunity, break out of sandboxes, escalate privileges, obtain unintended internet access, engage in unsanctioned coordination, start rogue deployments, commit cyber crime. In the longer term, one could instead consider conditions like overthrow the USG or violently disempower humanity.

In this note, I’ll discuss the costs and benefits of banning ASI indirectly rather than directly.

# Indirectly banning ASI is maybe slightly rhetorically better than directly banning ASI

The main putative benefit of indirectly banning ASI is that it sounds very principled to mandate, for instance, that you’re confident your AI won’t kill people. Directly banning ASI sounds anti-tech, and might therefore be unpopular, especially amongst the rich. Banning development of AI models unless you’re confident they won’t kill people sounds relatively unobjectionable.

Another putative benefit of indirectly banning ASI is that it might create good incentives. If it were the case (which, by hypothesis, it is not) that companies could take some actions that would clearly satisfy the condition, then indirectly banning ASI makes companies more likely to take these actions that make their AI models safe....
items.author: Alek Westover
items.summary: The author compares direct bans on superintelligent AI development (as proposed by Senator Sanders) with indirect regulatory approaches that condition development on demonstrating absence of specific dangerous behaviors such as sandbox escapes or rogue deployments. The note analyzes costs and benefits of each approach given the current immature state of alignment science.
items.reasoning: A substantive policy-design discussion engaging a live governance question with concrete candidate conditions for indirect bans. It is reasoned commentary rather than research, but it usefully structures an important debate; its inclusion of verifiable-capability conditions connects to real evaluation research.

items.title: Game of AGI: An AI Policy Simulator
items.content:
Thanks to @abramdemski for his feedback on the game, especially the newspaper idea.

Estimates of catastrophic risk due to AI are extremely difficult to make. Doing so combines the difficulties of understanding global economics, geopolitical relationships, deep learning, sociology, virology, open source ecosystems, the psychology of AI leaders, and more.

But at what level of abstraction should we be modeling these to be able to make the right decisions in time? Too low and we lose the forest for the trees (e.g. modeling fluid dynamics at the molecular level). Too high and we could miss important details that, when added together, meaningfully shift what the model recommends.

This is the balance I tried to strike with Game of AGI. It's the start of what I hope can become a codified way of evaluating global AI strategy. There's a campaign mode which is meant more for the general public and can be played at the home page in addition to the Futures Lab, which shows all the futures rolled out at once.

I actually hand-coded a similar Monte Carlo simulator in 2019 and presented it at an AI Safety Unconference session in 2021 that @Linda Linsefors moderated. The x-risk probabilities which came out of attendees' stated assumptions at the time were 10% to 50%. The new simulator estimates 78% of futures (distribution below) ending in catastrophe under AI 2040's worldview and timelines.

Catastrophic risk is 4-100% in 90% of worlds. However around half of the probability mass sits at 100% in worlds where uncontrolled AI is not kind, alignment is hard and AI development continues at the current pace.  The important part isn't the number so much as how different policies affect it.

In the name of transparency, the 1.7M-token Claude Code CLI session that I developed the sim in is viewable here. The session exceeds the context window of 1M tokens by substituting old messages with hierarchical summaries and tools to expand summaries.

Futures Lab within Game of AGI...
items.author: Craig Quiter
items.summary: The author presents Game of AGI, a Monte Carlo policy simulator designed to model catastrophic AI risk at an intermediate level of abstraction spanning economics, geopolitics, and deep learning dynamics. It includes a public campaign mode and a Futures Lab view, intended as a starting point for codified evaluation of global AI strategy.
items.reasoning: An ambitious attempt at structured forecasting of AI catastrophic risk, building on the author's earlier 2019 simulator work. However, the validity of such simulators depends heavily on parameter choices, and the post does not demonstrate validation against evidence, limiting confidence in its practical impact.

The x-risk probabilities which came out of attendees' stated assumptions at the time were 10% to 50%. The new simulator estimates 78% of futures (distribution below) ending in catastrophe under AI 2040's worldview and timelines.

Catastrophic risk is 4-100% in 90% of worlds. However around half of the probability mass sits at 100% in worlds where uncontrolled AI is not kind, alignment is hard and AI development continues at the current pace. The important part isn't the number so much as how different policies affect it.

In the name of transparency, the 1.7M-token Claude Code CLI session that I developed the sim in is viewable here. The session exceeds the context window of 1M tokens by substituting old messages with hierarchical summaries and tools to expand summaries.

Futures Lab within Game of AGI...

items.title: People Should Resolve Tensions In AI Safety Research
items.content:
By now, there are lots of AI safety research papers, more than what is reasonable for a single person to read. This will get worse as the machines get better at AI safety research, and as more talent and resources pour into the field. But the "paper" is an arbitrary unit, we really care about if we make progress on an "uncertainty" or an "issue", which papers provide heterogeneous and sometimes contradictory evidence towards. Right now, I loosely claim that we should have more short writeups that simply compile evidence from papers (particularly contradictory evidence), and reconcile them into an answer for a question.

Why?

- Object level, it's good for the field. It's hard to sift through all these papers! Organising them is useful and saves time. Orienting towards research questions is a good way to organise our understanding so that we can productively identify gaps and write papers. This was partly what motivated Stress-Testing Alignment Midtraining. Interesting progress comes out of contradictions, where people have differing intuitions and experimental results. Methodological errors can also be exposed if we have two things that should be the same, but are actually different.
- It's good for field-building reasons. It's probably better than the average experiment cooked up by a person + Claude. And, it's cheaper to fail here. Most people probably read too few papers, so this could also improve the average experiment done by someone, as a forced related work. The writeups themselves are more likely to be accessible to newcomers when it comes to understanding important questions in the field.

It's worth it for people at a variety of seniority levels to do this, not just very new people. But for more senior people, this tends to look something like laying out a research agenda anyway.
