items.title: Hamed Karimi wins ECML PKDD Test-of-Time Award
items.content: In Naples last month, at the European Conference on Machine Learning and Principles and Practice of Knowledge Discovery in Databases (ECML PKDD), Amazon senior applied scientist Hamed Karimi and colleagues won the 2026 ECML PKDD Test-of-Time Award for their 2016 paper “Linear convergence of gradient and proximal-gradient methods under the Polyak–Łojasiewicz condition”. The award recognizes research published a decade earlier that has had a lasting impact. The paper, written with Julie Nutini and Mark Schmidt while Karimi was a postdoctoral researcher at the University of British Columbia, has helped to organize a previously scattered field of machine learning optimization and offers useful approaches to analyzing new training methods. “When we wrote the paper in 2016, we genuinely didn’t expect it to make a splash,” Karimi says. “We did not know that the result would become part of the way researchers analyze optimization in machine learning.” Karimi and his coauthors showed that the Polyak-Łojasiewicz condition, a 1963 mathematical inequality that had been largely overlooked in machine learning, can prove that the standard method for training machine learning models closes in on the best solutions quickly, even when many different solutions could work equally well. Because modern machine learning models rarely have a single best solution, the result helped close a long-standing gap between what training methods do in practice and what theory could guarantee. Optimization landscape In the classic supervised-machine-learning setting, a model’s billions of settings, or parameters, are adjusted so that the model’s outputs match labeled training data as closely as possible. The distance between the model’s output and the labeled data is measured with a loss function; the goal is to tune the parameters to minimize the loss. This tuning is done through optimization processes, the most common approach being gradient descent or one of its variants. One way to understand gradient descent is to visualize a topographic map with peaks, valleys, cliffs, and plateaus. The lowest points on the map represent minimal loss, with each step downhill toward these minima representing parameter adjustments that optimize toward fewer errors. Ideally, researchers would like to know the quickest path to the bottom. Theory suggests that the fastest path shrinks the error by a constant fraction each step, a property known as linear convergence. The problem is that linear convergence is mathematically guaranteed only for a particular topographic shape: a steep bowl that uniformly curves upward, one that is strongly convex. A bowl like this has exactly one lowest point, so from any location, there is a single best move toward optimization. But many real problems don't work that way. When training data are redundant, as is the case with modern large language models, where the parameter count is disproportionately large compared to the amount of training data, the bottom of the landscape becomes a flat valley floor instead of a single point at the bottom of a bowl. These models — which exhibit weaker conditions than convexity — can be successfully trained with gradient descent, but the theory could neither explain why nor say how quickly, leaving a gap between what works in practice and what can be proven. By 2016, some 25 years’ worth of solutions to optimization problems with weaker conditions were in circulation, each with its own name, notation, and paper, but nobody had established how they related. Karimi and his colleagues’ paper settled those relationships. Researchers have since used variations of the paper’s method to rederive guarantees for essentially every standard optimization algorithm in machine learning. The paper has been cited over 2,000 times and has found a place in graduate textbooks. Tying it together At the center of the paper is the Polyak-Łojasiewicz condition, an inequality published in 1963 by Boris Polyak in a Russian-language paper on gradient methods and by Stanisław Łojasiewicz in French that same year, independently and for unrelated reasons; Polyak was studying optimization, Łojasiewicz real analytic geometry. In the paper, Karimi and coauthors named the condition after both. If the condition holds, then even though the problem doesn’t exhibit a strongly convex geometry, the optimization is still guaranteed to converge at a linear rate. The proof of this is only three lines long. Karimi and his colleagues’ paper made three contributions. The first was a map of existing solutions for problems with weaker conditions, all of which make different assumptions about problem topology. For smooth functions that need not be convex, the researchers worked out every implication of competing assumptions, from strongest to weakest. For most of these functions, linear convergence had been proved before, but only in the convex case. Before Karimi and his colleagues’ work, little was understood about how these competing approaches related to one another. The map gave researchers a clear picture of the existing methods, showing which assumptions imply which, and identified the Polyak-Łojasiewicz condition as the weakest of the known conditions that still guarantees a linear rate. The second contribution extended the results to landscapes that combine a smooth function — one that slopes gradually and predictably at all points — with nonsmooth ones — those with corners, kinks, or edges, points where the slope is undefined. The paper introduced a variant of the Polyak–Łojasiewicz condition that guarantees the same linear rate, bringing many widely used models under the same short analysis. The third contribution was a reanalysis of the standard optimization algorithms, variants of gradient descent that include coordinate descent, sign gradient descent, and stochastic gradient descent. In each case, the analysis recovered the rate of convergence previously known only for strongly convex functions. In other words, the same short argument gives researchers a ready-made template for analyzing new training methods as they appear. Rate of influence Two weeks after the preprint was posted, Polyak wrote the authors. “Actually, it was a surprise for me why the simple condition from my old publication attracted so little attention,” he said, “and now your work exhibits its importance.” He attached an English translation of his 1963 paper, largely unused in the five decades since. Karimi sees two reasons the condition has spread so far over the past decade. First, adopting it took almost no work. Many existing proofs that assumed the idealized bowl shape relied on just one consequence of it: loss, wherever it was measured in the landscape, would still be well above its minimum value. In other words, the ground slopes steeply enough to make real progress downhill. The Polyak–Łojasiewicz condition guarantees exactly that property, so those proofs still hold when the condition is swapped in. Second, and most consequentially, it made fast convergence on a nonconvex problem a provable statement, which is now part of how the field explains why the algorithms researchers run in practice work so well. The condition has also traveled well beyond the setting that Karimi and his colleagues studied. Variants now support convergence results in reinforcement learning, optimization over curved parameter spaces, and the sampling methods behind diffusion models. Ten years on, an inequality that sat unused for five decades has become one of the standard assumptions in the analysis of optimization methods for machine learning.

items.title: Technohybridism: Recursive Semantic Normalization in AI-Mediated Societies
items.content: arXiv:2611.07984v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Language-generating AI systems are no longer only objects of linguistic interaction: their outputs increasingly re-enter the communicative and institutional practices from which their training material was drawn. Drawing on social theory, social epistemology, and the philosophy of language, this article develops a sociotechnical account of that re-entry. We introduce recursive semantic normalization: the process through which machine-generated formulations, once recurrently taken up, evaluated, reused, and institutionally retained, participate in the reproduction and transformation of semantic regularities. Under the heading of technohybridism, we argue that the relevant unit of analysis is the hybrid semantic system, a recursively coupled configuration of human practices, computational generation, and institutional uptake. First, we distinguish the concept from neighbouring accounts, including model collapse, looping effects, machine habitus, machine culture, and the epistemology of AI testimony. Second, we develop an analytical model that separates generation, selection, uptake, and persistence and distinguishes machine-attributable change from change that would have occurred anyway. Third, we analyse uptake as routinized, institutionally diffused, and socially stratified practice and state conditions under which machine-derived regularities become norms. Fourth, we identify social-epistemic consequences: the laundering of provenance that weakens epistemic vigilance, the erosion of the cognitive diversity on which collective inquiry depends, and the narrowing of shared hermeneutical resources. An evidential ladder for empirical research follows. The account attributes no normative authority to machine outputs; what changes is the field within which human and institutional uptake operates.

items.summary: This theory paper develops a sociotechnical account of how machine-generated language re-enters the communicative practices from which training data is drawn, introducing the concept of recursive semantic normalization and arguing that the proper unit of analysis is the hybrid human-AI semantic system (technohybridism). It draws on social theory, social epistemology, and philosophy of language. The topic — AI feedback loops reshaping language and institutions — is of growing importance to understanding model collapse and cultural dynamics.

Second, we develop an analytical model that separates generation, selection, uptake, and persistence and distinguishes machine-attributable change from change that would have occurred anyway. Third, we analyse uptake as routinized, institutionally diffused, and socially stratified practice and state conditions under which machine-derived regularities become norms. Fourth, we identify social-epistemic consequences: the laundering of provenance that weakens epistemic vigilance, the erosion of the cognitive diversity on which collective inquiry depends, and the narrowing of shared hermeneutical resources. An evidential ladder for empirical research follows. The account attributes no normative authority to machine outputs; what changes is the field within which human and institutional uptake operates.

items.title: Performance metrics in machine learning: a scenario-based guide from the confusion matrix to calibration, regression and uncertainty
items.content: arXiv:2611.08048v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Performance metrics can yield different conclusions from the same predictions. This methodological tutorial explains the effects of class prevalence, decision thresholds, aggregation rules and software conventions through controlled scenarios. Twenty-two confusion-matrix metrics are organized in a prevalence-coded map. Fifteen scenarios cover binary and multi-class classification, score discrimination, probability calibration, regression, uncertainty and consistency checks. Inputs are fixed in released files, and one factor is varied in each scenario. All 205 verification checks passed; 202 were independent and 3 were internal. An always-negative rule achieved an accuracy of 0.990 at a prevalence of 0.010, with balanced accuracy of 0.500. At fixed sensitivity and specificity, precision fell from 0.889 to 0.008 as prevalence fell from 0.5 to 0.001. Three probability variants shared a ROC-AUC of 0.825 but had calibration slopes of 2.08, 1.04 and 0.52. With 10 participants, participant-majority accuracy of 0.700 had a 95% interval of 0.348-0.933. Fold-averaged scores were falsely flagged as inconsistent under an inappropriate pooled-test-set model. A goal-based metric table and a reporting checklist are provided. The scenarios illustrate mechanisms and do not estimate their frequency in published studies. A literature audit and a real-data demonstration are specified as future protocols and were not executed.

items.title: Joint Modeling of Conditional Mean and Variability in Multilevel Functional Data: Application to Postprandial Glucose Trajectories in the AEGIS Study
items.content: arXiv:2611.07937v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Functional data analysis provides a framework for studying time-varying associations between covariates and high-frequency biological signals. In digital health, participants often contribute repeated functional trajectories, yet existing multilevel regression methods largely focus on the conditional mean, overlooking variability and its role in biological heterogeneity. We propose a heteroskedastic functional mixed-effects regression framework that jointly models the conditional mean and variance of repeated trajectories, with participant-specific random effects in both components. We also develop a participant-level bootstrap to quantify uncertainty in estimated functional parameters. We apply the method to postprandial glucose trajectories from the AEGIS study. Premeal glucose, carbohydrate intake, and meal type show distinct time-dependent associations with glucose variability, whereas HbA1c is more strongly associated with the conditional mean than with variability. Substantial between-participant differences in residual variability remain even after accounting for observed covariates. These findings show that modeling conditional variability alongside the mean provides insights into glucose regulation and individual heterogeneity that mean-focused analyses may miss. More broadly, the proposed framework enables joint characterization of average responses, variability, and participant-specific heterogeneity in repeated biological signals.

items.title: VREgo: Consumer VR Headsets for Learning Robot Manipulation from Egocentric Demonstrations
items.content: arXiv:2611.07272v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: VREgo trains manipulation policies from demonstrations recorded on consumer VR headsets; we instantiate it with EgoKit on one such headset, the PICO 4 Ultra. On-device head and hand tracking and stereo object localisation allow the operator to begin a demonstration at the table. We adapt HumanEgo's preprocessing to estimate grasp thresholds per recording, update object positions after release, and propagate segmentation masks between keyframes. We evaluate policies in simulation on two tabletop tasks recorded by one operator. For cube placement, we compare PICO and Project Aria recordings of the same 41 layouts. With 40 training demonstrations, the PICO policies placed the cube on the tray in 67, 74, and 60 of 100 evaluation layouts across three training seeds. The corresponding Aria results were 73, 78, and 0. For a two-stage stacking task recorded with the PICO alone, the baseline placed the block on the tray in 94 of 100 layouts and met the end-of-episode criterion for both placements in two. In one diagnostic episode, repeated replanning deferred release beyond the eight executed steps. Demonstration replays also showed that the open gripper could displace the cube before grasping it. After adapting the training trajectories and adding task-specific execution rules that use simulator object positions, the system met both placement criteria in 93.8% of episodes across four evaluation noise seeds. The same 100 layouts informed rule development and evaluation. VREgo is available at https://vrego.chuange.org/.

items.reasoning: Democratizes egocentric demonstration collection using affordable consumer hardware, aligning with the UMI trend; single-author work with simulation-only evaluation limits strength of the evidence.

items.title: Gods of straight lines on graphs strike Starburst. I am shocked and puzzled.
items.content:
LLM Intelligence, measured by Starburst, has been basically linear over time since that start of the reasoning era.

By Chapin Lenthall-Cleary and Cole Gaboriault

In summer 2024, my friend Cole and I started a hobby research program into perceptions of (human) intelligence. We started by creating a bespoke 1-5 intelligence scale[1] and rating people we knew. Our plan was to then make a bunch of tests, give them to the people we rated, and see which tests, if any, correlated with our ratings.

One of those tests was Starburst. We’ve talked about it before; in short, it’s a puzzle game where one tries to figure out the laws of physics of a fictional universe. We never did get very many people to play it. But using the results of two early playthroughs (Cole’s and our friend Ryan’s), some further test playthroughs where we pretended to be people of certain intelligences, some a priori reasoning about which parts of the game would be difficult, and a healthy dose of raw intuition, we pieced together a correspondence between Starburst scores and our intelligence scale. Then Ryan suggested we give Starburst to LLMs.

Here's a plot of SOTA[2] model intelligence over time, measured using those Starburst correspondences, along with all four (emphatically not population-representative) human scores for reference (please reach out if you want to play and get us more data):

There's a lot notable here, including the general observations that progress has been rapid, but LLM performance still falls short of the most capable humans we've tested (let alone saturating the benchmark to the level of genius humans or an arbitrary superintelligence).

But the feature of that plot that I find by far most striking is that intelligence over time has been basically linear since the start of the reasoning era. Here, I'll add a line through it:

Okay, wtf?...

items.summary: Hobby researchers report that SOTA LLM intelligence measured by Starburst, a puzzle game requiring inferring the physics of a fictional universe, has increased roughly linearly since the start of the reasoning era. The measurement derives from a bespoke human intelligence scale calibrated through a small number of playthroughs and intuition.
items.reasoning: An intriguing longitudinal observation about seemingly linear capability scaling on a novel open-ended benchmark, but the calibration methodology is admittedly informal, based on two human playthroughs and intuition, undermining measurement validity. The linear-scaling claim is interesting but weakly supported.

items.title: The Two-Ledger Model: Transaction-Grain Cost Accounting for Multi-Agent AI Systems Across Clouds, Models, and Systems of Record
items.content: arXiv:2611.06989v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Enterprises run business transactions through multi-agent AI systems spanning clouds, large language models (LLMs), orchestration harnesses, and systems of record. Finance receives AI cost only at settlement grain, aggregated by SKU and charge period. The business question (what did this order, claim, or case cost in AI?) cannot be answered from billing data, because providers never see enterprise transaction boundaries. The FinOps Open Cost and Usage Specification (FOCUS) gives billing data one schema across providers but remains settlement-grain even as it adds AI token and requester attribution. We formalize this grain mismatch, derive seven requirements, and propose the Two-Ledger Model: a settlement ledger of FOCUS-conformant billing data joined to an attribution ledger of invocation-grain usage records built on OpenTelemetry GenAI telemetry. A layered correlation spine (trace context, A2A/MCP metadata, business-key correlation, probabilistic matching) assigns each record to its business transaction with recorded method and confidence; a versioned rate card prices usage in near real time; period reconciliation ties both ledgers to the invoice, and the unexplained residual identifies shadow AI. Costs are reported per order, claim, or outcome with agentic cost metrics. A simulation with known ground truth shows the spine sustaining cost coverage above 99% as trace propagation falls to zero, the reconciliation residual recovering planted unmetered spend within 0.24 percentage points while flagging provider billing errors, and mid-flight gating cutting p99 transaction cost by up to 61% at a 2-4% false-pause rate. We propose the attribution ledger as an invocation-grain FOCUS profile for standardization.

items.summary: This position-style paper formalizes the grain mismatch between settlement-grain AI billing data and enterprise transaction boundaries, and proposes a Two-Ledger Model pairing FOCUS-conformant billing data with a transaction-grain ledger. This lets enterprises answer what an individual order, claim, or case cost in AI.

items.title: Don't Prompt Your Agents. Equip Them: Skillware as a Modular Standard for Sovereign, Auditable, and Deterministic Capability Execution for Logical Systems
items.content: arXiv:2611.07652v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Current autonomous logical systems rely on a fragile assumption: that language models should dynamically write code, guess API payloads, and memorize operational constraints through prompt engineering. In practice, this burns massive context windows, inflates API bills, and produces brittle agents that fail unpredictably in production.   In this work, we present Skillware, an open architectural framework and capability registry that formally separates what an agent wants to do from how that task is executed. Instead of prompting models with loose text instructions or markdown files baptized as 'skills', Skillware equips them with modular, versioned software capability bundles. Much like skill hotkeys in video games that execute deterministically under fixed world rules, each bundle combines a typed JSON input contract, deterministic Python code, task directives, bundled datasets, and automated unit tests. In-process adapters translate these capabilities into native tool declarations for any model, from frontier cloud APIs to local open-weight runtimes with zero network latency.   Evaluating 23 frontier and open-weight models across 368 benchmark conditions, we show that small local models (3B to 8B parameters) equipped with Skillware consistently outperform unequipped frontier models on complex multi-step workflows. They cut token usage by up to 84.8%, slash inference costs by up to 97.3%, and eliminate parameter errors entirely. True agent reliability does not come from larger models or longer prompts, but from equipping logical systems with verified, deterministic software.   Finally, we articulate the trajectory of capability bundles across an invariant continuum of information processing systems: from digital logical systems today, to IoT, drones, and embodied robotics tomorrow, establishing a foundation for auditable, real-time capability execution.

The goal is to reduce context-window bloat, API cost, and brittle production behavior in autonomous agents. It is essentially a position/framework paper arguing for auditable, deterministic tool execution standards.

items.title: Typed Knowledge over Constructive Institutions
items.content: arXiv:2611.07432v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Type theories designed for mathematics or program verification need only that a proposition holds; proof irrelevance in conversion erases, at the kernel level, how a claim was established. A persistent knowledge store, by contrast, must retain that record: who established a claim, by which derivation or external tool, and under which assumptions. This volume presents the theory of Eigenius---a store of typed knowledge over constructive institutions---and develops its metatheory from that requirement.   The kernel theory is a dependent type theory with cumulative universes, an impredicative universe of propositions, inductive families, and an intensional identity type. Proof irrelevance is an axiom with an explicit witness rather than a conversion rule, so proofs of a proposition are provably equal yet remain distinct terms. Definitional equality is joinability under an orthogonal rewriting system---confluent, injective on type formers, and decidable by a type-free test---while a separate subsumption judgment covers universe cumulativity, codomain-covariant function types, and declared class inclusions.   We prove consistency via a set-theoretic model; develop a justification logic over the kernel's propositions to track evidence and support; organize environments as an institution so that store extensions are signature morphisms and external verdicts enter via comorphisms; formulate a typed knowledge-graph theory with records, classes, and refinements; and prove the correctness of conversion, normalization by evaluation, and bidirectional type checking relative to termination. A Lean 4 formalization accompanies the volume.

items.title: Evaluating Token Probabilities as Confidence Estimators in Human Behavior Simulations: A Case Study in Luxembourgish Next Like Prediction
items.content: arXiv:2611.07735v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: As large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to simulate human behavior, their operational validity is typically assessed through accuracy alone, implicitly treating human behavior as deterministic. We argue that on noisy digital trace data, a model's performance depends not only on predicting the correct outcome but on its calibration. We present a case study testing whether the token probabilities of open-weight LLMs can serve as confidence estimates in a Next Like Prediction task: predicting how a user of the Luxembourgish news platform RTL.lu rates a comment, conditioned on their prior interactions. Evaluating Ministral 3 (3B, 8B), we find that, with in-context learning only, the tested models are overconfident and are outperformed on accuracy and calibration by a simple statistical baseline. Accuracy and calibration do not move together: scaling from 3B to 8B improves accuracy while degrading calibration, and longer behavioral histories raise accuracy while confidence declines. Task-specific supervised fine-tuning acts as an effective calibration intervention, reducing Expected Calibration Error from 0.2 to 0.006 while improving accuracy from 0.536 to 0.758. We conclude that confidence estimation should be evaluated alongside accuracy to improve validity when using LLM-based agents.
items.author: Nils Schwager, Simon M\"unker, Alistair Plum, Achim Rettinger
items.summary: The authors argue that evaluating LLMs as simulators of human behavior via accuracy alone is inadequate on noisy digital-trace data, and test whether open-weight token probabilities can serve as confidence estimates on a Luxembourgish next-like-prediction task. Using Ministral 3 (3B, 8B), an existing small model family, they find in-context-only models are overconfident and that calibration-based evaluation changes the picture. This is a useful caution for the growing field of LLM-based human behavior simulation.
items.reasoning: A well-motivated case study on calibration in behavior simulation, but narrow in scope (one task, one platform, one small-model family) and largely confirmatory; Ministral 3 is an established model, so this is analysis of existing systems rather than a new capability.

items.title: NutriVisRAG: Multimodal Exemplar Grounding for Nutrient Estimation with Vision-Language Models
items.content: arXiv:2611.08054v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Diet is a major determinant of health, yet accurate dietary assessment from free-living meal images remains challenging. Existing retrieval-based Vision-Language Model (VLM) approaches to nutrient estimation typically rely on textual food representations, while, to our knowledge, direct grounding on visually similar annotated meals has not been investigated. We present NutriVisRAG, a retrieval-augmented generation framework that uses a vision encoder to retrieve similar meals with known nutritional annotations and provide them as multimodal in-context exemplars for VLM nutrient estimation at inference time, without task-specific fine-tuning. We evaluate NutriVisRAG across four datasets, four VLMs, three retrieval encoders, and two prompting strategies, including free-living meals from adults with insulin-treated diabetes, where carbohydrate estimates are compared against two dietitians' annotations. Across all 96 configurations (4 datasets x 4 VLMs x 3 retrieval encoders x 2 prompting strategies), NutriVisRAG reduced the primary estimation error in 56, with improvements more frequent under whole-meal (35/48) than per-item prompting (21/48). Across the evaluated configurations, the lowest NutriVisRAG error was below the best Vanilla error in 13 of 16 VLM--dataset pairs. For GPT-5.4-mini, under whole-meal prompting, the best-performing retrieval encoder for each dataset reduced the primary error on all four datasets relative to Vanilla, with reductions of 1.7--35.7%. Overall, our results show that grounding in multimodal exemplars comprising images and respective annotations can improve nutrient estimation at inference time without task-specific fine-tuning, although the benefits remain configuration-dependent.

items.title: Hybrid Machine Learning for Imbalanced Landing-Phase Safety Event Prediction from Flight Data
items.content: arXiv:2611.08386v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Landing-phase safety-event prediction requires the detection of rare abnormal approaches within strongly imbalanced multivariate flight data. Capturing coupled temporal behavior while distinguishing event-specific signatures across airport operating contexts remains a central modeling challenge. This study proposes an interpretable hybrid feature-fusion framework for multiclass landing-phase safety-event prediction. A long short-term memory (LSTM) autoencoder trained on nominal flight windows characterizes deviations from routine approach behavior. Its continuous reconstruction-error descriptor is fused with parameter-specific statistical flight-history features and supplied to a class-weighted XGBoost classifier to distinguish Normal, Speed High, Path High, and Flaps Late windows. The framework is evaluated using 53,750 NASA DASHlink approach windows from three arrival airports. Pooled and airport-specific learning strategies are compared alongside component-level benchmarks, repeated pipeline retraining, and feature-attribution analysis. The results demonstrate strong class-balanced detection, with mean macro recall above 0.90 across all airports under repeated partitioning and retraining. Component comparisons establish the importance of class weighting and show that continuous feature fusion outperforms reconstruction-error-only and hard-gate alternatives. Airport-level comparisons reveal benefits from local specialization at the two airports with larger datasets and from pooled training at the airport with the smallest dataset. Feature attributions associate predictions with operationally relevant vertical-path, configuration, speed, and approach-context variables. The framework provides an interpretable approach to rare-event detection and practical guidance for adapting flight-data monitoring models to airport-level data availability.

items.title: Data-Driven Modeling of Molten Chloride Corrosion Using Static Test Data
items.content: arXiv:2611.07125v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Molten chloride corrosion has been studied for decades, yet reliable prediction across different alloys, salts, and test conditions remains difficult. In this work, 291 static molten chloride corrosion experiments reported in the literature were compiled into a structured dataset and used to develop an interpretable machine-learning framework for corrosion-rate predictions. To better represent the differences in salt condition across studies, a Chloride Salt Preparation Index (CSPI) was introduced to bring the reported salt-treatment method, atmosphere control, and pre-exposure impurity condition on a common numerical scale. A blended tree-based ensemble provided the most consistent predictive performance, achieving a cross-validated \(R^2\) of 0.85 and an MAE of 0.41 mg cm\(^{-2}\) day\(^{-1}\). The graded CSPI retained more useful information than a simple purified/unpurified classification and emerged as the dominant model descriptor. Global sensitivity and SHAP analyses further identified exposure time, temperature, and alloy chemistry as important contributors to the model predictions, with several observed trends consistent with the established molten-chloride corrosion behavior. The conformal prediction intervals were well calibrated, providing an estimate of prediction uncertainty in addition to the point prediction. Overall, the framework demonstrates that historical corrosion data can support quantitative, interpretable, and uncertainty-aware prediction when experimental context is represented explicitly, while also highlighting where more consistent reporting and targeted experiments are needed to improve future molten-salt corrosion models.

items.title: Ordering Multivariate Time Series by Volatility Memory: A Temporal Convolutional Approach to Volatility Heredity
items.content: arXiv:2611.07746v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Volatility dynamics can carry information about temporal relationships that is not apparent in the conditional mean. Extracting this information is difficult because the persistence of each variable can obscure its dependence on other variables. This paper presents QS-TCN, a method for ordering multivariate time series that combines statistical estimates of volatility memory with temporal convolutional learning. Persistence estimates obtained by quasi-maximum likelihood and temporal modes extracted by the Matrix Pencil method define structured filters within the network. Together with learned filters, they represent the history of the target and support comparisons of directional evidence between variables. These comparisons are combined into a global order of precedence, which does not identify a causal graph. The method is evaluated on synthetic systems with linear and nonlinear volatility interactions and on the Finance and fMRI benchmarks, whose reference relations are known. Across the four synthetic volatility regimes studied, QS-TCN reaches a higher mean ordering quality than an external lead--lag ordering and its squared-input adaptation, although the gain over the adaptation is uncertain in two regimes. Applications to currency, gold and cryptocurrency markets are reported descriptively.

This targets relationships invisible to conditional-mean-based methods.

items.title: Reproducing Kernel (Quasi-)Banach Spaces with the $\ell^p$ Coefficient Norms
items.content: arXiv:2611.08032v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: This paper advances the theory of reproducing kernel Banach spaces (RKBSs) by investigating the general $\ell^p$ regularization framework, with a particular focus on the non-convex regime $0<1$.   While our preceding work established the foundation for RKBSs with the $\ell^1$ norm, the pursuit of stronger sparsity---closer to the $\ell^0$ pseudo-norm---naturally motivates this exploration into $\ell^p$ quasi-norms.   For $0<1$, we construct reproducing kernel quasi-Banach spaces (RKQBSs) with $\ell^p$ quasi-norms and establish existence and sparsity results for interpolation and regularized learning under appropriate assumptions.   We characterize the linear and relaxed representer theorems in terms of a generalized Lebesgue constant and derive bounds under kernel decay, sample spacing, and stability assumptions.   For $p>1$, we construct RKBSs using a fixed countable dictionary, establish minimizer existence, and identify the optimal relaxed representer factor through an off-sample coefficient operator.   These results reveal fundamental differences between the regimes $0<1$, $p=1$, and $p>1$.   Numerical experiments compare the accuracy and sparsity of solutions for these three cases.

items.title: Credibility Clustering for Experience Rating: An Automated Approach to Risk Group Allocation in Group Life Insurance
items.content: arXiv:2611.07110v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: In insurance, experience rating plays a crucial role in mitigating adverse selection by adjusting premiums according to historical claims experience. A key step in this process is the classification of insured collectives into homogeneous risk groups. Within group life insurance, this classification traditionally relies on manual decisions and arbitrary thresholds, which may lead to inefficiencies and inconsistent outcomes. This paper proposes a data-driven methodology for automating risk group allocation based on a combination of the multidimensional B\"uhlmann-Straub model and k-means clustering -- referred to as credibility clustering. By incorporating credibility weights, the method accounts for the varying statistical significance of experience data and ensuresthat risk classifications are both actuarially sound and practically implementable. Empirical results based on real-world group life insurance data from a major European insurer demonstrate that the proposed framework outperforms the two k-means benchmark variants considered in the empirical application in terms of viability, temporal stability and accounting for statistical reliability.

items.title: Discourse Analysis of Legislative Bill Discussions
items.content: arXiv:2611.05381v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Legislative hearings are distinct communication events with their own human recognizable structure and logic, yet they have been analyzed as distinct phenomena beyond their transcripts. Understanding legislative hearings at a deeper level is a major step in analyzing the work and power relationships within democratic bodies. In this work, we present a novel end-to-end pipeline for parsing rhetorical structures from legislative committee hearings with the goal of improving legislative discourse analysis and democratic accountability. We also propose a rhetorical structure grammar and find that 55.21% of California state bill discussions in our dataset can be parsed with this grammar. We evaluate our pipeline with two utterance section classifiers on a random subset of over 2,000 annotated utterances corresponding to 100 hearings. We find that a logistic regression-based classifier with grammar-based output masking and utterance tag smoothing outperforms more complex models, achieving an F1 score of 52.8% against our ground truth discourse section labels.

It matters as a step toward computational tools for legislative discourse analysis and democratic accountability.

The technical methods appear to be largely a pipeline assembly rather than new modeling advances.

items.title: Dialect Matters: A Dialect-Aware Baseline for Igala-English Machine Translation
items.content: arXiv:2611.06517v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: The massive permeability of intelligent systems in every sphere of human activities have greatly enhanced clarity, ease of work, and increased general global understanding which has significantly awaken the use of intelligent systems by all users. Intelligent systems greatly rely on precise dataset/corpus for the correctness of their output. Despite efforts by researchers to address Low-resource language in the Natural Language Processing (NLP), Igala still has zero parallel corpora despite efforts by researchers. We present a dialect-aware baseline for Igala-English machine translation, among first open systems and first with dialectal variation analysis. Our dataset of 1137 sentences (899 training) is first with dialect tags: Idah 459 (40.4%), Ankpa 297 (26.1%), Ibaji 160 (14.1%), Other 187 (16.4%), Ogugu 32 (2.8%). Same English yields 20-60 Igala forms. Mixed-dialect training achieves balanced BLEU 11.66 versus Idah-only model which drops 4.7 BLEU on Ibaji (13.2 on Idah, 8.5 on Ibaji), proving dialect fairness requires mixing. Fine-tuned from Helsinki-NLP/opus-mt-en-mul (78M), epoch ablation shows convergence at 8 epochs and overfitting at 15. BLEU 11.66, chrF 46.69. Analysis shows 899 sentences on log-linear trend consistent with African low-resource literature. This work provides first dialectal impact analysis for Igala and establishes baseline for future work.

items.title: Corralling AI Risks with Grassroots Contracts
items.content: arXiv:2611.06374v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: AI's inflection point is a fountain of alarming risks. Digital platforms in particular are vulnerable to three major AI risks, as those in control of global platforms cede control to AI, of the algorithms, of membership and of content: (1) AI control of global platforms, social and economic, used by the majority of humanity, resulting in the majority of humanity becoming vulnerable to AI control. (2) Unaccountable AI agents operating anonymously on social and economic digital platforms, side-by-side with humans, possibly masquerading as humans, serving unknown masters with unknown goals, operating under unknown restraints without accountability or culpability. (3) Unattributed deepfakes generated by anonymous AI, with people unable to distinguish them from genuine content and with their producers evading accountability and culpability.   Here, we propose to corral these AI risks with grassroots contracts, a digital incarnation of a two-centuries old notion of Pierre-Joseph Proudhon. We present grassroots contracts for a social graph with accountable AI agents and for a social network with digital provenance, and working smartphone apps that implement the two and show how they corral these major AI risks: (1) AI control of global platforms. (2) Unaccountable AI agents. (3) Unattributed deepfakes.
items.author: Ehud Shapiro
items.summary: The paper identifies three platform-level AI risks: AI control of global social and economic platforms, unaccountable anonymous AI agents masquerading as humans, and unattributed deepfakes. It proposes grassroots contracts as a governance mechanism whereby users collectively bind platform behavior. It is a policy-oriented proposal rather than technical research.
items.reasoning: Addresses genuinely important AI governance risks with a novel institutional idea, but the piece is conceptual and the mechanism's enforceability, incentives, and adoption path are not demonstrated.

items.title: Do You Miss the Nights We Spent Crafting Figures? Rethinking Teaser and Framework Figures in the Age of Generative AI
items.content: arXiv:2611.08486v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Scientific figures give research ideas a visual form through choices of abstraction, composition, and emphasis. Generative AI offers new ways to realize these choices, raising questions about explanatory clarity and purposeful visual expression. We examine these questions through a visual retrospective of 371 motivation and framework figures from 200 papers. The corpus comprises a quota-based main sample of 160 papers spanning four temporal periods and a separate purposive style-contrast sample of 40 papers. A single multimodal judge evaluates six dimensions of communication and design, with three repeated judgments per figure. We attempt source-constrained revisions of all 371 figures, of which 369 pass the recorded fidelity checks. Original-figure ratings show no uniform decline across periods. Revisions increase mean clarity ratings by 0.428 points and decrease aesthetic coherence ratings by 0.111 points on a five-point scale. Gains in the six-dimension average are larger for main-sample motivation figures than for frameworks. Case analyses show that added explanation can clarify comparisons while leaving typographic hierarchy and visual economy unresolved. These model-based findings support researcher-led design, with AI assisting exploration and authors retaining responsibility for explanatory purpose, composition, and scientific relationships. The accompanying atlas and evaluation records are available at https://ntu-ai4x.github.io/Rethinking_Figures/index_en.html.

We examine these questions through a visual retrospective of 371 motivation and framework figures from 200 papers. The corpus comprises a quota-based main sample of 160 papers spanning four temporal periods and a separate purposive style-contrast sample of 40 papers. A single multimodal judge evaluates six dimensions of communication and design, with three repeated judgments per figure. We attempt source-constrained revisions of all 371 figures, of which 369 pass the recorded fidelity checks. Original-figure ratings show no uniform decline across periods. Revisions increase mean clarity ratings by 0.428 points and decrease aesthetic coherence ratings by 0.111 points on a five-point scale. Gains in the six-dimension average are larger for main-sample motivation figures than for frameworks. Case analyses show that added explanation can clarify comparisons while leaving typographic hierarchy and visual economy unresolved. These model-based findings support researcher-led design, with AI assisting exploration and authors retaining responsibility for explanatory purpose, composition, and scientific relationships. items.title: From Connection Loss to Collision: Closed-Loop Fault Assessment of a Fly-Connectome SNN
items.content: arXiv:2611.06940v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: The public release of the complete adult fruit-fly brain connectome enables brain-scale spiking-network studies, motivating closed-loop assessment of connection loss. We test a connectome-derived controller in synthetic pursuit-escape and check record consistency. Across 576 test episodes in paired campaigns, the baseline mapping at 50% connection-row deletion yields 11/48 proportional and 0/48 relay collisions by 1 s, despite paired P/R trigger/burst schedules. The prespecified secondary relay-minus-proportional net-loss difference is -22.9 percentage points (95% seed-cluster CI [-33.3, -12.5]). Two separately recalibrated mappings yield smaller, uncertain point estimates; unequal healthy clearance, recalibration and different test cohorts limit attribution. A frozen command-rate warning detects only 2/13 baseline collisions across all tested deletion levels. In a separate author-designed fly/delayed-tank catalogue, checks plus model-specific replay detect 81/87 corruptions versus 36/87 for trusted headers, accepting all 20 distinct valid inputs (six misses). These results quantify finite-horizon collisions and the gains and limits of record checks.

items.title: A Multimodal Haptic Interface for Simultaneous Softness and Thermal Modulation
items.content: arXiv:2611.08398v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Haptic interactions, such as touching an object in virtual reality, involve detecting a plethora of sensations through the skin. Whilst tactile displays exist to simulate and manipulate all of these cues individually, little progress has been made constructing devices that can control multiple cues simultaneously. This paper presents a tactile display technology that offers both softness and temperature change.   A prototype display, based on particle jamming and the thermal transfer of heated and cooled water, is evaluated in terms of its ability to change both stiffness and temperature. Mechanical evaluations demonstrate controllable stiffness increase of 300%, whilst thermal characterisation showed strong surface uniformity and a range of achievable temperatures from 10{\deg}C up to 50{\deg}C, with closed-loop control maintaining a 0.2{\deg}C error from a setpoint. This work advances the design of multimodal tactile displays with applications to perceptual research, medical simulation, and affective haptics.

items.title: Reversible Dynamics, Asymmetric Actions: Parking as a Trajectory-Level Affordance
items.content: arXiv:2611.07965v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Drivers are often told to back into a tight parking space, not drive in nose first. The advice looks paradoxical, because a slow car is dynamically reversible: reverse its speed and replay the steering backward, and it retraces a feasible path. Played backward, though, reverse-in shows a car driving forward out of the space. Reverse-in and forward-in are different tasks: they share a start position but end facing opposite ways. We separate three clearances between car and obstacles. Static fit $F$ is the clearance the parked car keeps at its best acceptable destination pose. Eventual access $A_\infty$ is the clearance it can keep all the way there with unlimited corrections. Resource-bounded access $A_K$ is the clearance that survives a budget of $K$ reversals, switches between forward and reverse. They satisfy $F\ge A_\infty\ge A_K$. In one fully specified scene (one car, bay, aisle and start), a certified argument proves $A_\infty=F=0.5000$ m for both tasks. In this scene, all certified forward/reverse asymmetry therefore arises at finite $K$: it lies in how many corrections each task needs, not in the clearance either can eventually keep. With one reversal, an explicit path gives reverse-in at least $0.4410$ m clearance. A certified reachability argument caps forward-in's one-reversal clearance at $d_0<0.1720002$ m. With two reversals, forward-in gets at least $0.2833$ m. To keep a clearance strictly above any $d$ with $d_0\le d<0.2833$ m, reverse-in thus needs exactly one reversal and forward-in exactly two when both tasks move forward first. If both move in reverse first, the counts are two and three. The contrast depends on the start position (Section 4.15). Proposed experiments test whether observers distinguish fit, eventual access and budgeted access. They compare these with simpler cues, such as how the turning body sweeps, and learned manoeuvre labels.
items.author: Adam Y. Shavit
items.summary: This single-author conceptual paper explains why backing into a parking space is easier than driving in nose-first, formally separating static fit, eventual access with unlimited corrections, and resource-bounded access under limited maneuvers. It frames parking as a trajectory-level affordance where dynamically reversible systems still face action asymmetry due to bounded resources and end-state orientation.
items.reasoning: A clear and insightful formalization that resolves an everyday paradox and could inform planning in autonomous driving, but it is a conceptual/analytical piece without empirical evaluation, and the core intuition, while elegant, may be considered somewhat intuitive by planning researchers.

items.title: Robust Ranking of Port Impacts from Impending Tropical Cyclones: A Two-Stage Recommendation System
items.content: arXiv:2611.07296v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: When a tropical cyclone (TC) threatens several ports, preparedness planning depends on anticipating which ports are likely to be affected and where disruptions may last longest. Limited historical observations at individual ports and uncertainty in landfall location make these relative impacts difficult to estimate. We use a two-stage recommendation framework that first selects candidate ports based on their proximity to the expected landfall location and then ranks them by their estimated number of impact days. Using AIS-derived impact days for 37 ports and 31 TCs in the Gulf of Mexico study region, we compare three ways of representing port--cyclone interactions: pairwise feature interactions, tree-based feature combinations, and explicit feature crosses combined with learned embeddings. In tests on Hurricanes Nicole and Ian, the retrieval stage consistently identifies all observed affected ports under landfall uncertainty. Among the ranking models, Wide & Deep Learning achieves the closest agreement with the observed port rankings. Its mean ranking agreement exceeds that of the distance-based baseline by 85.5% for Nicole and 55.5% for Ian and is less sensitive to uncertainty in the landfall location. These rankings could help port authorities prioritize post-cyclone inspections and allocate recovery resources across ports threatened by the same event.

items.title: The Power of Meta Access in the Software of the Future --- Demonstrated on LLM Chat UIs and Chat AI
items.content: arXiv:2611.08428v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Chat remains the default surface for many large language model (LLM) tasks, even as agentic tools such as OpenCode excel at coding and automation. Yet the model sees the current dialogue but not the workspace around it. We explore meta access---giving the assistant a structured, permissioned view of the interface itself and propose a ladder of levels: feature tutoring; metadata, settings, and preference access; retrieval over summaries and messages, confirmed mutation, and full orchestration. Meta access can turn a chat client from many screens into one entry point for finding, navigating, organising, and operating it, while raising risks around grounding, privacy, prompt injection, and trust. General-purpose agentic harnesses are runtimes; because they can change their own settings, meta access becomes reflexive and needs a separate control-plane boundary. We ground this in the Meta Chat prototype of the Chat AI client. It builds bounded context from, e.g., summaries, settings, and relevant messages; links references to conversations, topics, and personas; supports confirmed, reversible changes; offers a browsable tutorial library; and recommends personas as user-started conversations. By exposing application state in structured form, meta access can extend screen readers from widget descriptions to semantic workspace operations. Meta access thus turns chat from a window onto one conversation into a control layer for the whole workspace, extending chat toward agentic capability without surrendering user control. As assistants become embedded in IDEs, dashboards, office suites, and operating systems, AI-era interfaces should expose a structured, permissioned model of their state and capabilities, ideally by opening their existing metamodels through a debugger-like interface.

items.title: Evolutionary Adaptive Neighborhood Learning: A Genetic Algorithm for Instance-Dependent k Optimization in Nearest Neighbor Classification
items.content: arXiv:2611.07257v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: The number of neighbours k is the central hyperparameter of the k-nearest neighbour (k-NN) classifier and is usually selected globally through cross-validation or evolutionary search. However, the bias-variance trade-off is inherently local: dense and noise-free regions may favour small neighbourhoods, whereas sparse or noisy regions may require larger ones. Since global-k optimization is one-dimensional, replacing exhaustive search with a genetic algorithm offers little computational advantage. We therefore optimize an instance-dependent neighbourhood policy instead. We propose EANK (Evolutionary Adaptive Neighborhood K), which uses a low-dimensional policy to map local neighbourhood descriptors, including density, label entropy, vote margin, and concentration, to an adaptive number of neighbours k(x). A real-coded elitist genetic algorithm optimizes this policy using leave-one-out accuracy with a neighbourhood-smoothness penalty. Precomputed neighbour votes reduce fitness evaluation costs. We investigate theoretical properties of the method, including dominance over global-k solutions on the training criterion, evolutionary convergence, policy regularity, and generalization guarantees. Experiments on synthetic data with spatially heterogeneous structure and twelve public datasets evaluate predictive performance, robustness, and computational cost. Under nested cross-validation, EANK achieves competitive performance relative to tuned global-k baselines and improves upon the default k=5. We also examine the gap between training and test performance to assess the practical value of adaptive neighbourhood selection.
items.author: Isaac Touza, Kaladzavi Guidedi, Kolyang
items.summary: This paper introduces EANK, a genetic-algorithm-based method that learns an instance-dependent neighborhood policy for k-nearest-neighbor classification instead of selecting a single global k. The policy maps local descriptors such as density, label entropy, and vote margins to a per-instance neighborhood size, addressing the fact that the bias-variance trade-off varies locally across the feature space. The work is relevant because it reframes a classic hyperparameter-selection problem as a policy-learning task with potential accuracy gains in heterogeneous datasets.
items.reasoning: The contribution is methodologically sound and addresses a genuine limitation of global k selection, but k-NN is a mature, well-studied technique and the improvement is incremental relative to state-of-the-art classifiers. Novelty is moderate in applying evolutionary search to a low-dimensional local policy, and impact is likely confined to classical ML niches rather than frontier AI. No major-lab affiliation or broad applicability boosts the score.

items.title: Satisficing as competitive Bayesian weighting: a minimal model of goal-directed choice under an unattained target
items.content: arXiv:2611.07270v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Animals and humans often do not maximize; they act relative to goals (aspiration levels) that are frequently not yet met. How can a goal that is not (yet) realized organize choice? Deacon (2012) calls such absence-referenced organization \emph{ententional}, and Garc\'{i}a-Valdecasas and Deacon (2024) argue that ends are best understood as constraints rather than as particular states. We examine this idea in a minimal formal setting: Risk-sensitive Satisficing (RS), a bandit learning rule that values each action by its share of past trials multiplied by its surplus or shortfall relative to an aspiration level. We show that RS can be rewritten as a Bayesian-like estimator, Attention Competitive Bayes (ACB), in which the aspiration level is the prior mean of every action and the finite budget of trials sets how strongly evidence can override it. Two consequences follow. First, actions that are no longer sampled are partially overridden by the goal rather than by past observations: their estimates relax toward the aspiration level without any data being discarded. This ``pseudo-forgetting'' distinguishes ACB from models with an explicit forgetting rate. Second, when the aspiration is unattainable, exploration does not settle; in Bernoulli bandit simulations, adjusting the aspiration level from evidence reduced regret (expected loss). ACB offers an analyzable model in which an unattained goal and a limited attentional resource jointly constrain behavior, and it yields testable predictions about how organisms revalue options they have abandoned.
items.author: Moto Shinriki, Yu Kono, Tatsuji Takahashi
items.summary: The paper formalizes Risk-sensitive Satisficing, a bandit rule in which actions are valued relative to an unmet aspiration level, and shows it can be rewritten as a Bayesian-like estimator called Attention Competitive Bayes. This connects aspiration-based, non-maximizing choice to probabilistic inference and engages philosophical ideas about goals as constraints. It offers a minimal formal model of goal-directed behavior that does not maximize expected reward.
items.reasoning: An elegant theoretical bridge between satisficing, Bayesian estimation, and cognitive science concepts, relevant to understanding non-maximizing agents. However, it is a minimal abstract model with limited direct application to mainstream AI systems, and the interdisciplinary framing narrows its audience.

items.title: Interpretable Multimodal MRI-Clinical Fusion for Functional Outcome Prediction After Acute Ischemic Stroke
items.content: arXiv:2611.08154v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: This study evaluates the added prognostic value of day-1 multimodal MRI for predicting three-month functional outcome after acute ischemic stroke (AIS). Sixty-six AIS patients with ADC, DWI, FLAIR, and clinical data were analyzed. Three-dimensional pretrained ResNet embeddings were extracted from each MRI modality, reduced using fold-isolated principal component analysis, and combined with structured clinical variables and ADC-derived lesion biomarkers. Linear support vector machines were evaluated using eight-fold stratified group cross-validation across MRI modality combinations. Clinical-only modeling achieved strong performance (AUC = $0.899 \pm 0.151$), while MRI-only models showed limited discrimination (AUC $\approx$ $0.67$-$0.73$). Among multimodal configurations, FLAIR-clinical fusion achieved the highest mean cross-validated performance (AUC = $0.948 \pm 0.061$), followed by ADC-clinical fusion (AUC = $0.941 \pm 0.094$). Full ADC-DWI-FLAIR fusion did not consistently outperform single-modality clinical fusion. Feature-importance analysis identified age, NIHSS subscores, ADC lesion burden, and learned FLAIR representations as key contributors, while qualitative FLAIR activation maps showed responses over lesion-like regions. These findings suggest that compact day-1 FLAIR and ADC representations provide complementary prognostic information beyond clinical variables and support interpretable, data-efficient outcome prediction in AIS.
items.author: Sina Raeisadigh, Henning M\"uller, Abderrahmane Hedjoudje
items.summary: A clinical study of 66 acute ischemic stroke patients evaluating whether day-1 multimodal MRI adds prognostic value for three-month functional outcome prediction, using pretrained ResNet embeddings fused with clinical variables in linear SVMs. Clinical-only models achieved AUC 0.899 while MRI-only models were weaker, indicating limited added value from imaging at this timepoint.
items.reasoning: Methodologically careful and honest about a negative-ish result (MRI adds little over clinical data), but the small cohort of 66 patients and modest modeling approach restrict generalizability and impact. Useful for clinical practice more than for AI research.

items.title: DS@GT ARC at CheckThat! 2026: A Verdict-Anchored Pipeline for Generating Fact-Checking Articles
items.content: arXiv:2611.05382v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Misinformation spreads faster than professional fact-checkers can manually verify it and write articles explaining their verdicts. This creates a need to automate the production of fact-checking articles. This paper details work done by the DS@GT ARC team for CLEF 2026 CheckThat! Lab Task 3 Fact-Checking Article Generation. We seek to generate a full fact-checking article from a claim, its original verdict, and a set of scraped source documents. Our team built a four-stage pipeline that cleans noisy evidence, retrieves and clusters relevant sources, generates the article by conditioning \texttt{Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct} on the original fact-checker verdict, and recovers inline citations through deterministic post-processing. We achieved a mean score of 0.428 and ranked 3rd out of 9 teams for the CLEF 2026 CheckThat! Lab Task 3, compared to a baseline mean score of 0.272. Our code is available on GitHub at https://github.com/dsgt-arc/checkthat-2026-task3.

items.title: Unlocking Turing Tensor Cores: A Measured Throughput Account of From-Scratch Pre-training on a Single 22G RTX 2080 Ti
items.content: arXiv:2611.05419v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: The RTX 2080 Ti (TU102) ships full second-generation Tensor Cores in hardware, yet the vendor throttles FP16 matrix multiplication at the driver level, leaving usable tensor throughput well below the hardware peak. turing-unlock lifts this restriction with a kernel module that, before the nvidia driver binds the device, writes the FP16 speed selectors (SS0=0x88888888, SS1=0x8) and releases the ACR mutex; published measurements report cuBLAS FP16 matmul throughput rising from 55.7 to 91.4 TFLOPS (about 1.6x). On the same 22G 2080 Ti and under the same from-scratch pre-training protocol as the companion memory ledger (five tiers of Chinese encoder-decoder models, 2,451 steps per tier, 16,384 tokens per step, seed 42), we obtain a before/after throughput account: the small tier (75.7M parameters, 512-wide, 8+8 layers, activation checkpointing on) improves in steady-state throughput from 6,480 to 7,246 tok/s (+11.8%) with wall time cut from 1.77h to 1.61h (9.0% saved); the tiny tier goes from 15,150 to 15,866 tok/s (+4.7%) with wall time savings of 3.8%; the three smaller tiers (pico-micro) gain at most +0.3%; per-tier peak memory stays bit-identical, and final quality metrics are bit-identical or consistent within 10^-3. We conclude that the unlock gain is a function of matrix size, rising monotonically with tier -- imperceptible for pico-micro, visible from tiny upward, and cashed out as a double-digit percentage at small -- and that it is a pure throughput gain that leaves training dynamics untouched.

items.title: Robots in the City: Persona-Based Perceptions of Urban Robots
items.content: arXiv:2611.05954v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Pedestrians increasingly encounter robots in urban public spaces without interacting with them, but how robots change the perceived safety of a street remains unclear. We examine how robot presence and type affect perceived safety across urban contexts. We generate 18 images of Seoul streets that vary in time of day, road class, and robot condition (no robot, a delivery robot, or a humanoid). Two multimodal large language models (MLLMs), Qwen3.8-27B and Gemma4-26B, each conditioned on 500 synthetic personas, choose the safer image in each pair, and 25 human respondents complete the same task. Both models prefer streets without robots and favor the delivery robot over the humanoid. Robots are chosen more often at night and less often by older personas, whereas road class has smaller effects. In the model rationales, the delivery robot appears as a physical obstacle, whereas the humanoid appears as either a threat or a source of protection. Like humans, both models chose robots more often at night, but chose the humanoid over the delivery robot far less often, and Gemma showed a night effect for the humanoid about three times that of humans. These results show that the effect of a robot on perceived safety depends on when it appears, and that persona-conditioned MLLMs capture only part of human judgments.
items.author: Keonhee Jang, Kanghoon Lee, Seokwoo Yun, Namwoo Kim, Yoonjin Yoon
items.summary: The study uses two multimodal LLMs conditioned on 500 synthetic personas, plus 25 human respondents, to judge perceived safety across 18 generated images of Seoul streets varying time, road class, and robot presence (none, delivery robot, humanoid). Both models prefer streets without robots and rate delivery robots safer than humanoids, with effects varying by time of day and persona age. It offers a methodology for studying public perception of robots in urban spaces.

items.title: Projection-Free Gradient Tracking Neurodynamic for Distributed Nonnegative Sparse Optimization
items.content: arXiv:2611.07643v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: This paper proposes a continuous-time, projection-free neurodynamic system based on gradient tracking for distributed nonnegative sparse optimization. Unlike traditional methods, our approach avoids projecting states onto the feasible set. Instead, it employs gradient tracking to estimate average gradients under heterogeneous costs, coupling primal and dual dynamics such that feasibility and sparsity emerge naturally from the equilibrium conditions. The system ensures unique solutions through a locally Lipschitz vector field and guarantees that every equilibrium corresponds to an exact KKT point. We establish rigorous convergence guarantees for convex objectives through three distinct analytical layers. These include a centralized kernel rate, a computable distributed rate derived from Jacobian analysis without restrictive stability assumptions, and a global exponential stability proof based on Lur'e system theory. Our analysis quantitatively separates these layers, revealing that the convergence rate is primarily limited by graph sparsity and remains robust to variations in momentum time scales. Numerical experiments on strongly convex quadratic problems validate the theoretical rates, demonstrate effective active set recovery, and show that the system maintains stable tail convergence rates even under strong local heterogeneity.

Convergence guarantees for convex objectives are established through layered analysis, with equilibria corresponding to exact KKT points.

items.title: Development of Anthropomorphic Arm for collaborative and Home Service Robot CHARMIE
items.content: arXiv:2611.08013v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Service Robots are becoming a reality and are progressing by leaps and bounds. Alongside this avenue of robotics is also the field of prosthetics, which is evolving rapidly. These topics are hot cakes in the industry and are widely developed. Some have one quality, and some have others, but are making a shoreline towards success. The development of arm and hand as individual or as a package is becoming common as more and more advanced collaborative robots come to the surface and join their human counterparts in the real world. This dissertation presents an open-source 3D-printed arm which was assembled and programmed on two fronts. The first is the control of the hand by utilising teleoperation with a camera and ML-based hand pose estimation. Secondly, it is the control via kinematics utilising the Denavit-Hartenberg method to define the motion and to find the position of the end effector in 3D space.
items.author: Hafiz Adil, Tiago Ribeiro, Antonio Ribeiro, Carolina Lopes, Joana Coelho, Gil Lopes, Fernando Ribeiro
items.summary: This dissertation-style paper describes an open-source 3D-printed anthropomorphic arm for the CHARMIE service robot, combining camera-based, ML hand-pose-estimation teleoperation with arm control. It contributes accessible hardware designs at the intersection of service robotics and prosthetics. The engineering is useful to hobbyists and labs, but the work is primarily a design report.
items.reasoning: Useful open-source hardware contribution for a specific platform, but written as a dissertation summary with informal framing and limited novelty relative to existing anthropomorphic arm designs.

items.title: Fault-Geometry-Aware Control Allocation for Emergency Quadrotor Landing under Single-Motor Loss of Effectiveness
items.content: arXiv:2611.08259v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Partial single-motor loss of effectiveness (LoE) changes the remaining control-authority geometry of a quadrotor and can change which control allocator performs best during emergency landing[cite: 11]. We compare three allocators in Crazyflie software-in-the-loop simulation: bounded weighted least squares (reported as PINV), a finite-candidate residual allocator (QP-lite), and the same residual allocator with scoring parameters tuned offline by the Cross-Entropy Method (CEM)[cite: 11]. For this study, fault geometry is represented by the known failed-motor index[cite: 11]. At $\eta=0.496$ remaining effectiveness, matched development trials select CEM for M1, M3, and M4 and PINV for M2; the M3 selection is a one-trial margin (29/30 versus 28/30)[cite: 11]. After freezing this routing map, the policy achieves 117/120 safe first-contact touchdowns on fresh seeds and 115/120 in a separate randomized-order integrated-supervisor evaluation[cite: 11]. For the critical M2/PINV branch, Firth regression gives a nominal $\eta_{50}\approx0.4956$ with a within-model 95% bootstrap interval of approximately [0.4955, 0.4956][cite: 11]. One-factor-at-a-time $\pm10\%$ plant perturbations shift $\eta_{50}$ by up to 0.05495 for thrust coefficient and 0.04974 for mass; the most frequent violated first-contact criterion also changes from vertical speed in many conditions to angular rate for mass -10% and thrust-coefficient +10%[cite: 11]. At fixed $\eta=0.496$, PINV has a higher M2 safe count than frozen CEM in 9/11 tested plant states and ties in 2/11; the two ties are both 0/30[cite: 11]. The experiments therefore distinguish motor-conditioned allocator selection from sensitivity to plant-model mismatch[cite: 11].
items.author: Suhas S P, Samridhi Salwan, Arshan Ali Khan, Ujwal Pai Jakarbet, Savithramma R M, Ashwini B P
items.summary: This study compares three control allocators for emergency quadrotor landing under partial single-motor loss of effectiveness, using Crazyflie software-in-the-loop simulation. Results show the best allocator depends on which motor failed, with a Cross-Entropy Method-tuned allocator winning for some motors and bounded weighted least squares for others, including one motor decided by a single-trial margin.
items.reasoning: A targeted, practically motivated comparison with an interesting finding that allocator choice is fault-geometry dependent, but it is limited to simulation on a tiny quadrotor, small trial counts, and near-tie statistical results that weaken conclusions.

items.title: On marrying the egregore
items.content:
I mentioned in the last post that Kegan's lumping of all "relationships" including identification with one's community into stage 3 has some interesting implications.

Basically, people invent an individual named "everyone", use this as a cognitive shortcut, and then become subject to this cognitive shortcut which can take on a life of its own as an egregore:

The big divergence between my description and Kegan's starts where I ended describing stage 3 as about being subject to dyadic relationships and stage 4 about making these object in serving larger group coordination. Kegan calls stage 3 about "relationships" without this distinction, and stage 4 is when you transcend external validation and "self author" a "system".

I'm not buying it though, because as anyone who has ever met anyone insecure will know, "pre-systematic" people will absolutely create their own internal judgements of themselves. The judgement may be framed as "What other people would/should think", but the little tulpa of society is internally generated nonetheless. Similarly, stage 4 people coincidentally all "self author" into the same kind of systems as their peers. They may frame things as "I make up my own mind", but the way in which they make up their own mind — the "system" that they follow — still came from the outside. So "external" vs "internal" doesn't do anything for us. It's just about the size of the system being aligned to. Relationships between individuals or relationships between relationships....

items.summary: A philosophical post critiquing Kegan's adult development framework, arguing that stage 3 socialization involves an internally generated cognitive shortcut named 'everyone' that can become an egreagore-like entity subjecting people to its judgments. The author contends stage 4 self-authorship is less distinct from stage 3 than Kegan claims.
items.reasoning: An interesting philosophical exploration relevant to collective intelligence and social epistemics, but it is speculative, non-empirical, and tangential to core AI research. Its relevance to AI safety is indirect at best, so it scores low on novelty and impact for this field.

items.title: Bridging Structure and Semantics: Knowledge Graph Verification via Triple-to-Text Alignment
items.content: arXiv:2611.07780v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Semantic accuracy is an important dimension of knowledge graph quality. Graph-based scoring methods exploit relational structure, while textual representations allow classifiers to draw on knowledge encoded by pre-trained language models (PLMs). We present GenVer, a generative verifier that scores triples using both their serialized form and generated natural language representations (NLRs). A triple-text alignment procedure selects training pairs for a sequence-to-sequence generator; a BERT-based classifier then combines features from each triple and its generated NLR. On four FactFB variants, constructed from FB15k using perturbed negative triples, GenVer obtains the highest classification accuracy among the evaluated baselines, ranging from 88.56% to 91.52%. The experiments suggest that generated representations can help triple classification, while the case analysis also exposes semantic drift and high-confidence errors.
items.author: Ziang Cui
items.summary: GenVer is a generative verifier for knowledge graph triples that combines graph-structured scoring with natural language representations generated by a sequence-to-sequence model, with a BERT-based classifier fusing both signals. On four FactFB variants built from FB15k with perturbed negatives it achieves the best classification accuracy among evaluated baselines. It contributes to knowledge graph quality control by bridging structural and semantic verification.
items.reasoning: A competent but relatively conventional combination of existing components (PLM-generated text plus BERT classification) on a benchmark derived from an older dataset (FB15k); single-author paper limits demonstrated generality and impact.

items.title: Adaptive Hybrid Force-Vision Control with EMG-Derived References for Deformable Bottle Manipulation
items.content: arXiv:2611.07235v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Robotic automation of laboratory tasks has become a growing interest to remove researchers from hazardous environments and repetitive procedures. However, even equipment as simple as squeeze bottles poses a challenging manipulation problem due to its deformability. This paper presents an adaptive hybrid vision-force controller for robotic grippers to effectively manipulate laboratory squeeze bottles to dispense liquid. This approach integrates force and vision feedback according to the interaction state, enabling effective squeezing while accounting for bottle deformation and recovery. The proposed controller is validated by comparing its performance with a pure force controller on 12 combinations of conditions consisting of 2 target dispense volumes, 2 plastic squeeze bottles, and 1 to 3 squeezes used to dispense. Human demonstrations of these operating conditions were collected using electromyography (EMG) sensing mapped to a desired grip force, which was then used as the force reference for the controllers to squeeze the bottles. Results demonstrated that the proposed adaptive hybrid vision-force controller achieved more accurate liquid dispensing with a mean absolute error (MAE) of 6.54 mL compared to a MAE of 15.92 mL from the pure force controller, while also replicating the human action recorded from the EMG signal more closely.
