items.title: Create Your Own Work Stack: Deploying Self-hosted AI and Tooling in a Tech Startup
items.content: arXiv:2611.08116v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Self-hosting AI is often presented as a way to reduce inference costs and increase control, but deployment introduces its own costs. We report our experience deploying a hybrid AI stack at Grayhat Developers, a small software company with an AI-intensive development workflow. Our initial motivation was to counter the growing cost of commercial AI usage: Claude/Codex incurred approximately \$325 per month, with more than 25.93 billion recorded tokens. We experimented with local open-source models as replacements for commercial coding agents, but after learning that their performance and inference speed were insufficient, we adopted a hybrid approach in which commercial agents remained responsible for complex tasks while local models handled lower-complexity tasks, organizational information retrieval, and synchronization with self-hosted tools including Outline, Plane, and ERPNext.   We estimated that approximately 30--40\% of our commercial AI workload was associated with context transfer, documentation synchronization, task management, and related operational coordination. By moving this work to local models, we estimate that approximately 90\% of this coordination workload could be handled without commercial inference, corresponding to an estimated 27--36\% reduction in overall commercial-AI workload or cost-equivalent usage. Our first internal deployment nevertheless failed to achieve adoption because it introduced UX friction. Replacing it with a centrally configured deployment substantially improved feedback and adoption. We conclude that local inference is most useful not as a wholesale replacement for commercial AI, but as part of a hybrid architecture that assigns tasks according to their capability requirements, cost, context demands, and operational sensitivity.

items.title: From Maps to Metabolism: Historical Precedents and a Unified Critique of Computationalism
items.content: arXiv:2611.06936v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Alexander Lerchner's recent work on the 'abstraction fallacy' argues that computational functionalism confuses physical processes with abstract descriptions, and that symbolic computation alone cannot instantiate consciousness. Yet these claims were anticipated by Korzybski's map-territory distinction, Searle's critique of strong artificial intelligence, Floridi's levels of abstraction, Spencer et al.'s observer-relativity arguments, Winograd and Flores's account of computation as socially grounded practice, and Nasuto and Bishop's biological arguments. Synthesizing these contributions, this paper advances a form of non-computational physicalism: consciousness depends upon intrinsically organized, metabolically grounded physical dynamics rather than abstract computation, whilst leaving open the possibility of artificial consciousness.   An objection is that this critique targets an outdated computationalism. Mechanistic computationalism, associated with Milkowski, Piccinini, Craver, Bechtel, and Kaplan, treats computation as a property of physically realized mechanisms rather than substrate-independent formalism. Although this represents an important advance, it does not dissolve the abstraction fallacy. Computational attributions remain dependent upon choices of state individuation, system boundaries, and interpretive mapping that are not determined by physical facts alone. Kaplan and Craver's 'model-to-mechanism mapping' constrains computational descriptions without eliminating their dependence upon an external observer. Grounding computation in neural mechanisms does not confer intrinsic significance or the normativity explored by Bickhard and Nasuto and Bishop. The abstraction fallacy persists wherever computational descriptions are treated as constitutive of, rather than descriptive of, physical reality.

items.title: STAG-Net: Structure-Aware Attention over Landmark Groups for Lightweight Head Pose Estimation
items.content: arXiv:2611.07828v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Head pose estimation is important for human computer interaction and driver monitoring, but many image based methods remain too costly for resource constrained deployment. We propose STAG-Net, a structure-aware attention over landmark groups for lightweight head Pose estimation that estimates head pose from facial landmarks using movement aware selection, spatial clustering, compact DeepSet encoders, self attention, and a global geometry descriptor. We develop variants using FaceMesh and Face Alignment Network landmarks and evaluate them under cross dataset and subject independent protocols on 300W-LP, AFLW2000, and BIWI. STAG-Net achieves the lowest mean absolute error among all compared landmark based methods in every evaluated setting. On BIWI frames with valid detections, the FAN variant also records the lowest overall error among all compared methods, reaching $3.51^\circ$ under cross dataset evaluation and $2.39^\circ$ under subject independent evaluation. The regressors use only 0.012 to 0.043 million parameters and 24.1 to 83.6 thousand FLOPs, about three orders of magnitude fewer FLOPs than FSA-Net. Despite including landmark extraction and regression, the FaceMesh pipeline reaches 322.9 frames per second on a Tesla T4 GPU, nearly twice the 164.5 frames per second of the fastest measured image based baseline, and 111.0 frames per second on CPU. After normalization by dataset size, STAG-Net processes training samples seven to eight times faster than FSA-Net and more than one hundred times faster than HopeNet and TokenHPE, while complete training finishes within 28 minutes. These results show that STAG-Net combines leading landmark based accuracy with substantially lower training and inference cost.

items.title: Label-Wording Augmentation in a Typed-Decision Encoder: Gains on Unfamiliar Words, Not on Abbreviations or Codes
items.content: arXiv:2611.08439v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Typed-decision models score options that the caller supplies at request time, so their accuracy depends on label wording that the model's developer does not control. We compare two releases of a 307M-parameter multilingual cross-encoder, Ru-Jev, trained on thirteen Russian-language tasks; the later release adds an augmentation that presents labels in several surface forms. Holding questions fixed and varying only how eighteen routing labels are worded, we evaluate ten label vocabularies, produced by three separate processes and checked for overlap with the training data, with five candidates per question and, for eight of them, also with eighteen. On held-out vocabularies made of ordinary or borrowed words (English-derived jargon, office slang, department names), the augmented release is more accurate in every setting, by up to 0.24. Eleven of these fourteen gains survive a Holm correction (slang with eighteen candidates and descriptive sentences with five do not), and for jargon on all labels the label-level interval excludes zero in both settings. On abbreviations and opaque codes it gives no usable gain: on abbreviations it is not better, and worse on the clean slice, and on opaque codes both releases stay at or below chance once labels related to training options are removed. In most cells where accuracy rises, the risk-coverage area falls, but with eighteen candidates confident errors rise on jargon and slang. On two datasets neither release saw, accuracy moves by -8.4 and +5.6 points. We also report four evaluation hazards from comparing the two releases.

items.title: A Theoretical Analysis of a Bilevel Optimization Formulation for Combined Local-Global Optical Flow Models
items.content: arXiv:2611.08359v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: This paper analyzes a bilevel formulation for learning the regularization parameter of combined local-global (CLG) optical flow models. The lower-level problem computes the flow from a Lucas--Kanade data term and a quadratic or total variation (TV) regularizer, and the upper-level problem selects the parameter that minimizes the squared distance to a ground-truth flow. The setting is finite-dimensional, and a full-rank assumption makes the lower-level solution unique. For the quadratic model we derive sufficient conditions for the existence of an optimal parameter, for every optimal parameter to be positive, and for strict local optimality. For TV regularization an optimal parameter always exists, because the lower-level solution vanishes for large parameters, and we give a sufficient condition for positivity that accounts for the coupling of the two flow components through the local structure tensors. Synthetic examples illustrate the conditions, including cases in which they fail.
items.author: El Mostafa Kalmoun
items.summary: This paper provides existence, positivity, and strict local optimality conditions for bilevel optimization of regularization parameters in combined local-global (CLG) optical flow models, covering both quadratic and TV regularizers. It is a finite-dimensional theoretical treatment with full-rank assumptions ensuring unique lower-level solutions.

items.title: Kinematic analysis of a double-closed-loop four-bar chain-based leg for a multimodal quadruped-pentarotor robot
items.content: arXiv:2611.07470v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: This paper presents the kinematic modeling and singularity analysis of a three-degree-of-freedom, double four-bar closed-loop quadruped leg mechanism. This leg is essential for transitioning between the two operational modes; therefore, it is examined in both joint and task spaces, leading to the development of its Jacobian matrix, which is vital for designing the gaits required for terrestrial mode and mid-air aerial reconfiguration (for aerial mode). Various gaits are devised for the system's motion in the MATLAB simulation, and their practical implementation on the single-leg test rig is demonstrated.

items.title: What are the concrete arguments for "AI pause would significantly hurt the economy."
items.content:
I've seen a bunch of people claiming "well, we need to make sure whatever our AI policy is doesn't hurt the economy because people will feel that in their wallets and hate it (and hurting the economy is bad."

This might hypothetically be true, but I've never seen anyone argue for it in any detail.

Meanwhile, I'd naively expect if shut down AI anytime soon, it'd dampen growth, and maybe it'd be a minor economic dip, but I wouldn't expect it to be a major recession. (It makes sense that it'd become a bigger deal as AI takes over more of the economy. But it feels like the people saying "it'd hurt the economy" are often the people implying that means we should do less of a pause and do it later).

I don't know much about economic recessions.

But, like, for reference, here's the 2007-2009 recession and the Covid blip.

GDP

https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/GDP

Unemployment

https://www.bls.gov/charts/employment-situation/civilian-unemployment-rate.htm

I asked Claude

If the frontier AI industry and datacenter build out completely halted, what do you predict would happen to US unemployment and GDP?

Claude said:

My central estimate: a sudden, complete halt would likely cause a US recession. Unemployment would probably peak around 5.5–6.5%, up from roughly 4.2–4.4% today. Real GDP would end up about 2–4% below where it would otherwise be within 12–18 months. That would be worse than the 2001 dot-com bust but well short of 2008.

Full response

items.title: An Ordering Optimization for Fruit-Vegetable in High-Density Environment based on Genetic Algorithm
items.content: arXiv:2611.07293v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: This paper presents a robotic harvesting method that combines RGB-D fruit localization, GA-based harvest ordering, and waypoint-based robot motion in dense and unstructured crop environments. The global RGB-D camera provides 3D fruit positions for ordering, while the end-effector-mounted camera provides close-range observation during execution. The GA determines the harvesting sequence, and static or dynamic waypoints define the intermediate robot motion. The method was evaluated in a controlled laboratory testbed and in four-, five-, and six-fruit field conditions. GA solutions were compared with exhaustive enumeration, and both waypoint offsets were examined by parameter sensitivity analysis. Continuous execution reduced unnecessary Home-return motion, while the dynamic waypoint changed with the remaining fruit distribution without changing the GA sequence. In the field evaluation, the dynamic-waypoint continuous strategy produced 40 collision events and a 70.7% target-approach success rate, compared with 55 collision events and 65.3% for the static-waypoint continuous strategy.

items.title: Category differences in similarity between fixation density maps and psychological potential fields for sketches
items.content: arXiv:2611.06930v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: When an object comes into view, humans can instantaneously recognize it if known to them. However, assessing how this recognition takes place remains challenging. A few studies using simple sketches have reported varying degrees of image similarity between the fixation density map (FDM), which visualizes eye movements and durations, and the psychological potential field (PPF), which visualizes part of the visual cognition process, depending on the object category. This study reports how the similarity behaves across three categories---animal, non-animal, and meaningless shape---and under rotated presentation, which is known to increase cognitive load during object recognition. The similarity was quantified through area under the curve (AUC) measures, including a baseline-adjusted AUC that isolates the early rise in similarity from stimulus-dependent baseline levels. A variability score was introduced to assess individual differences, and linear mixed models were used to evaluate category and orientation effects. Results indicated that the baseline-adjusted AUC yielded significant differences among all three categories with large effect sizes, whereas the raw AUC did not distinguish between the animal and non-animal categories due to the influence of sketch representation. No significant Category $\times$ Orientation interaction was observed, indicating that rotated presentation did not produce a category-specific effect. The meaningless shape stimuli yielded consistently low similarity and variability scores, clearly separating them from the two meaningful object categories. These results characterize the behavior of the FDM--PPF similarity under free viewing and indicate that baseline adjustment is necessary to separate category-related variation from stimulus-dependent baseline levels.

items.summary: This psychophysics/vision paper quantifies how similarity between fixation density maps (eye movement visualizations) and psychological potential fields varies across animal, non-animal, and meaningless shape sketch categories, including under rotated presentation that increases cognitive load. Similarity is measured via area under the curve, offering insight into how human object recognition is deployed.

These results characterize the behavior of the FDM--PPF similarity under free viewing and indicate that baseline adjustment is necessary to separate category-related variation from stimulus-dependent baseline levels.

items.title: Educational robotics beyond ROS: a custom library for direct transfer of Webots controllers in the Turtlebot3
items.content: arXiv:2611.08142v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Robot Operating System (ROS) is becoming a standard in robotics courses at higher education, but its installation, configuration and distributed programming model can introduce a significant entry barrier in the new landscape of AI-based master and degree studies, where many students do not have a strong informatics background. This paper presents an educational experience that enables students to program a TurtleBot3 Burger directly in Python, while preserving a direct transfer path from simulation to the physical robot. The approach is based on a custom library that mirrors the Webots API, allowing the same controller code to be executed in the simulator and on the real TurtleBot3 with minimal modification. The library provides access to the robot motors, wheel encoders, inertial sensors and LiDAR, and is complemented by scripts that automate deployment and execution on the physical platform. It was used in a master-level course on introductory autonomous vehicles, and initial student feedback suggests that the approach reduces the perceived complexity of ROS-related infrastructure and helps learners focus on algorithmic logic and real-world behaviour.

It aims to lower the installation and configuration barrier of ROS for students in AI programs without strong informatics backgrounds.

items.title: Nociceptors as a simple heuristic for the subjective experience of pain
items.content: Animal welfare is an important cause area within effective altruism. Every year, billions of animals suffer, both in factory farms and in the wild. The scale of that suffering means interventions have the potential to measurably improve billions of lives. Yet the organizations most motivated to address these problems have limited resources, so heuristics are required to direct those resources toward the most impactful interventions. One way to measure an intervention’s impact is by how much suffering it reduces, and a critical part of that calculation is an animal’s capacity to feel subjective pain. This is difficult to assess: animals cannot describe their experiences to us, and precise, generalizable neural correlates of subjective pain remain elusive. We are therefore left to rely on heuristics. An obvious heuristic is the number of nociceptors. Nociceptors are sensory neurons that respond to damaging or potentially damaging stimuli. They are distributed throughout the skin, muscles, joints, bones, and viscera, and they form the basis of the sensation of pain. It seems reasonable, then, to expect the number, density, or quality of an animal’s nociceptors to track how much pain it subjectively experiences. So what does research say? I focus on studies in humans, the only animal that can describe its experience of pain....
items.author: Archit Gupta
items.summary: The author examines whether nociceptor count, density, or quality is a defensible heuristic for assessing animals' capacity for subjective pain, motivated by resource allocation in animal-welfare interventions within effective altruism. The post weighs the promise and pitfalls of such a heuristic given the lack of generalizable neural correlates of pain.
items.reasoning: A reasonable, clearly written discussion relevant to welfare science and cause prioritization, but it is conceptual commentary without new data or formal methods and is peripheral to AI research.

items.title: Enhanced MRI brain tumor detection using deep learning in conjunction with explainable AI SHAP based diverse and multi feature analysis
items.content: arXiv:2611.07843v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Recent innovations in medical imaging have markedly improved brain tumor identification, surpassing conventional diagnostic approaches that suffer from low resolution, radiation exposure, and limited contrast. Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) is pivotal in precise and accurate tumor characterization owing to its high-resolution, non-invasive nature. This study investigates the synergy among multiple feature representation schemes such as local Binary Patterns (LBP), Gabor filters, Discrete Wavelet Transform, Fast Fourier Transform, Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN), and Gray-Level Run Length Matrix alongside five learning algorithms namely: k-nearest Neighbor, Random Forest, Support Vector Classifier (SVC), and probabilistic neural network (PNN), and CNN. Empirical findings indicate that LBP in conjunction with SVC and CNN obtained high specificity and accuracy, rendering it a promising method for MRI-based tumor diagnosis. Further to investigate the contribution of LBP, Statistical analysis chi-square and p-value tests are used to confirm the significant impact of LBP feature space for identification of brain Tumor. In addition, The SHAP analysis was used to identify the most important features in classification. In a small dataset, CNN obtained 97.8% accuracy while SVC yielded 98.06% accuracy. In subsequent analysis, a large benchmark dataset is also utilized to evaluate the performance of learning algorithms in order to investigate the generalization power of the proposed model. CNN achieves the highest accuracy of 98.9%, followed by SVC at 96.7%. These results highlight CNN's effectiveness in automated, high-precision tumor diagnosis. Code: https://github.com/asifrahman557/BrainTumorDetection

items.summary: This study combines handcrafted feature representations (LBP, Gabor, wavelet, FFT, GLRLM) with CNN features and multiple classical classifiers for MRI brain tumor detection, using SHAP-based explanations for interpretability. It reports improved detection over conventional diagnostic approaches.
items.reasoning: Applies well-established feature engineering and classifier combinations rather than contributing novel methods; this pipeline style is common in the applied medical imaging literature. Limited novelty and unclear clinical validation reduce significance despite the explainability angle.

items.title: Contextual Pictograms for Repairing Multilingual ASR Errors
items.content: arXiv:2611.05637v2 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Speech transcription errors can be difficult to recognize when competing word hypotheses are unfamiliar or visually similar. We describe an interface that combines alternative transcripts, replay and contextually checked pictograms for selected uncertain concepts. The system will initially support French and Spanish functional utterances. A counterbalanced study will assess whether pictorial feedback helps listeners recover the speaker's intended action beyond text alternatives alone. We will also quantify semantic mismatch and additional interaction time, since an inappropriate image can reinforce the wrong interpretation rather than repair it.
items.author: Mariana Hernandez, Hector Luna, Carlos Bruno, Luis Ricardo Santos, Elena Simoes
items.summary: This paper describes a proposed interface for speech transcription repair that combines alternative transcripts, audio replay, and contextually checked pictograms for uncertain concepts, initially targeting French and Spanish functional utterances. A counterbalanced user study is planned to assess whether pictorial feedback helps listeners recover intended meaning beyond text alternatives, while quantifying risks like semantic mismatch and added interaction time. It is largely a design proposal with a planned evaluation.
items.reasoning: This is a work-in-progress interface design with no completed evaluation; the abstract describes studies that will be run, so there are no results yet. The idea of pictorial disambiguation is interesting but unproven, and the scope (functional utterances in two languages) is narrow.

items.title: An Evolutionary Hypothesis for White's Illusion: Constant Percentage Correction and Modern Individual Variation
items.content: arXiv:2611.06935v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: White's illusion is a striking demonstration of context-dependent brightness and lightness perception. In earlier work, we developed a forward translucency-based formula capable of producing approximately constant perceived appearance across varying backgrounds. While validating that formulation, we observed a notable population-level pattern: individuals selected slightly different correction percentages for "constant perception," while the population average remained remarkably stable across experiments. In this paper, we propose an evolutionary hypothesis for this phenomenon. We suggest that a simple constant-percentage correction function could have emerged as an adaptive mechanism for maintaining useful material and reflectance judgments under variable illumination. Under this interpretation, the stability of the population mean may reflect a conserved perceptual mechanism, whereas individual differences may reflect learning, adaptation, or variation around a shared computational response. Using a modification of our previously published forward model, we show that White's illusion can be reproduced by applying a constant-percentage correction to background luminance. The model therefore provides a compact computational account of the observed population-level regularity and motivates a testable evolutionary interpretation of individual variation in contextual lightness judgments.

items.summary: The authors propose an evolutionary explanation for why people use slightly different brightness correction percentages under White's illusion while the population average remains stable, suggesting constant-percentage correction evolved as an adaptive mechanism for material and reflectance judgment. The work builds on a forward translucency-based formula producing constant perceived appearance across backgrounds.
items.reasoning: A theoretical/speculative hypothesis paper on an optical illusion; the evolutionary framing is interesting but lacks strong empirical validation and has little AI impact.

items.title: Where's all the blackmail?
items.content:
It is interesting how little blackmail I see, that I know is blackmail. A lot of people probably do some things they would be embarrassed by if they were made public at some degree of detail and explicitness, and it probably isn’t that hard to get evidence of these, and quite a few people seem to be amoral. Also, in order to properly embarrass someone, I imagine you would make your information relatively public, so that for instance I—Katja—should hear about some fraction of cases. Yet I very rarely receive information I know to be public for the purpose of embarrassing someone. I’m not sure I remember it ever happening. Why not?

If I imagine being morally inclined toward blackmailing someone, one salient reason to avoid it is that my wrongdoing is extremely obvious and in-the-face of the recipient, so they seem likely to react destructively, for instance by telling everyone that I’m a dirty blackmailer. It’s like stealing from right in front of someone’s face.

Another possibility is that there is a lot of blackmail, but it mostly remains private because the blackmailers mostly get the price right to have their threats heeded. This is an interesting theory, because it suggests blackmail is much more common than we observe, so people may be greatly underestimating the chance of it happening to them.

One place I have heard about blackmail occurring is from AI systems. Which is interesting, if it isn’t a thing humans seem to be doing much. What to make of that?
items.author: KatjaGrace
items.summary: This speculative post observes the apparent rarity of observed blackmail despite widespread embarrassing information and many amoral actors, exploring explanations such as blackmail being obviously visible wrongdoing and the possibility of well-priced private threats. It is a musings-style essay connected loosely to AI-safety concerns about deceptive strategic behavior.
items.reasoning: Interesting sociological speculation with tangential relevance to game-theoretic and AI-safety reasoning, but no data, formal analysis, or direct AI research content.

items.title: AI-Driven SaaS Platform Integration: AI Express for Unified Generative AI Services with Pay-As-You-Go Credit Systems and Scalable Microservice Architecture
items.content: arXiv:2611.05389v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Generative AI is currently fragmented, with separate subscriptions required for text generation, image synthesis, and code assistance, leading to high costs and workflow disruptions. AI Express is a SaaS platform that consolidates these capabilities into a unified pay-as-you-go service. The platform provides a range of AI tools, including a Core Code Reviewer that evaluates GitHub repositories, a Text-to-Website generator that converts text into fully functional websites, script generation, grammar checking, data analysis, and watermark removal, all accessible through a single interface without requiring technical expertise.
items.author: Deepit Sapru
items.summary: AI Express is a SaaS platform consolidating text generation, image synthesis, and code assistance behind a unified pay-as-you-go interface, including a GitHub code reviewer, text-to-website generator, script generation, grammar checking, data analysis, and watermark removal. It aims to reduce subscription fragmentation and cost for non-technical users. The paper is essentially a system description of a product rather than a research contribution.
items.reasoning: A product description with no apparent novel technical contribution, evaluation, or research methodology; consolidating existing APIs behind a microservice wrapper is engineering work, not research. The inclusion of watermark removal raises additional ethical concerns. It is poorly matched to a research venue.

items.title: Useful Junk
items.content:
Occasionally people will get excited about a minimalism fad, where you
figure out which of your possessions you need and keep only those.  As
someone who generally doesn't like getting rid of things, I've been
thinking some about why, and the main thing I keep coming back to is
that random objects can be helpful in unpredictable ways.  Here are
some things that I kept without a specific use in mind, but that ended
up being useful.  You could say they saved time or money, but often
the biggest gain was from being able to do a project in one go with
what I already had on hand:

- Ethernet cable.  Back in 2019 if you'd asked me whether I would
ever use ethernet again, I would have said probably not.  WiFi was
good enough for everything I was doing.  But then I (like a lot of us)
suddenly started working from home and got frustrated about how poorly
my internet was working for video calls and
ran ethernet to my desk.  Having cable on hand already meant I could
just set it up.

- Plexiglass.  When I built my accidental
electronic instrument I wanted to protect it, and had plexiglass
left over from when I added an insulating layer to a single-pane
window.

- Scrap wood.  So many things.  To give one example, when one of
the stairs in our basement fell apart, I was able to replace it with
extras from past projects that I'd kept around. Similarly, when Lily came back from visiting a friend enamored of
their prop axe, she had everything she needed to make one already in
the basement:

- Computer mouse.  One of my housemates was having wrist
issues, and wanted to try out using a mouse
on the floor.  They ended up hating it after a day or so, but
being able to pull one out of the junk electronics pile and try it
made for quick experimentation.

- Plastic sheeting.  When we wanted to divide our apartment in
two so we could isolate a
new housemate I had sheeting left over from an earlier project....
items.author: jefftk
items.summary: A personal essay by jefftk reflecting on why keeping ostensibly useless possessions pays off, cataloging examples like ethernet cable, plexiglass, and scrap wood that later enabled projects to be completed in one go. The post argues against minimalism fads on pragmatic grounds.
items.reasoning: An amicable personal essay with no connection to AI research, safety, or technology analysis. It has essentially no relevance to the analytical focus of this batch beyond the author's presence in the rationalist community.
